4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Tokenisation splits raw text into smaller units (tokens) that a model or pipeline can process: words, sentences, or sub-word pieces (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece). It is the first step of essentially every NLP pipeline.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: Models operate on discrete units with a finite vocabulary, not on raw character streams. Tokenisation converts unbounded text into a sequence of indices from a fixed vocabulary, balancing vocabulary size against sequence length and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) handling.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Word tokenisers split on whitespace/punctuation with language-specific rules (handling contractions, hyphens, abbreviations). Sentence tokenisers use punctuation + abbreviation lists + ML models to find sentence boundaries. Subword tokenisers (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram) start from characters/bytes and iteratively merge frequent pairs, producing a vocabulary that represents common words whole and rare words as pieces — e.g. 'unhappiness' -> ['un', 'happi', 'ness']. This eliminates OOV since any string can be built from the base vocabulary (bytes/chars).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Word/sentence tokenisation for classical NLP (BoW, TF-IDF, POS tagging) where each token should be a linguistic unit. Subword tokenisation for any modern Transformer (BERT, GPT, T5) since it gives a small fixed vocabulary, handles rare/new words/typos gracefully, and keeps sequence lengths manageable.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Don't use naive whitespace-splitting for languages without spaces (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) — need dedicated segmenters. Don't use a classical word tokeniser's output directly as input IDs for a pretrained Transformer — you must use that model's exact tokeniser, or embeddings will be meaningless.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Mismatched tokenisers between training and inference silently corrupt inputs (model sees garbage IDs but doesn't error). Naive split() breaks on punctuation-heavy text ('don't' -> 'don', "'t'"), contractions, URLs, emojis, and hashtags. Subword tokenisation can split numbers inconsistently, hurting arithmetic reasoning. Sentence tokenisers fail on abbreviations like 'Dr.', 'U.S.A.' without abbreviation lists.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: spacy.load('en_core_web_sm')(text) correctly tokenises "Dr. Smith won't go to the U.S." into ['Dr.', 'Smith', 'wo', "n't", 'go', 'to', 'the', 'U.S.'] — handling the abbreviation 'Dr.' as one token, splitting the contraction "won't" into 'wo'+"n't", and keeping 'U.S.' intact, none of which a naive .split(' ') would get right.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Stemming reduces a word to its 'stem' by chopping off suffixes using fixed rules, without consulting a dictionary or considering part of speech. The Porter stemmer (1980) and its successor Snowball are the most widely used algorithms.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: To normalise word variants ('running', 'runs', 'ran' -> ideally 'run') so that downstream tasks like search and BoW/TF-IDF treat morphological variants as the same feature, reducing vocabulary size and sparsity.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Porter applies a cascade of ~5 rule steps (e.g. 'sses' -> 'ss', 'ies' -> 'i', 'ational' -> 'ate', trailing 'e' removal under conditions) based on measures of consonant-vowel sequences in the stem. It's purely string-pattern based — no morphological or dictionary knowledge. Snowball is a more consistent, configurable reimplementation supporting more languages.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Fast, lightweight normalisation for search indexing, information retrieval, or BoW/TF-IDF pipelines where speed matters more than linguistic correctness and the output never needs to be a real word.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid when output readability matters (chatbots, summaries) or when downstream tasks need valid dictionary words (e.g. WordNet lookups, POS-aware processing) — use lemmatisation instead. Avoid for languages with rich morphology unless a dedicated stemmer exists.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Over-stemming merges unrelated words ('university' and 'universe' both -> 'univers'), hurting precision. Under-stemming fails to merge true variants ('alumnus'/'alumni'). Output is often not a real word ('studies' -> 'studi'), which breaks anything expecting valid tokens. Porter is English-only and aggressive; results vary across Porter vs Snowball for the same word.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: PorterStemmer().stem('caresses') -> 'caress', stem('ponies') -> 'poni' (not a real word), and stem('university') -> 'univers' which collides with stem('universe') -> 'univers' — a classic over-stemming collision that would make a search engine return university pages for a query about 'the universe'.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Lemmatisation reduces a word to its dictionary base form (lemma) using vocabulary and morphological analysis, e.g. 'better' -> 'good', 'running' -> 'run', 'mice' -> 'mouse'. Unlike stemming, the output is always a valid word.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: To normalise text to a linguistically correct canonical form, which is necessary when the normalised tokens need to be valid words (for readability, dictionary lookups, WordNet-based features, or downstream generation).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: A lemmatiser uses a vocabulary/dictionary plus morphological rules and typically the word's part of speech (POS) to pick the correct lemma — e.g. 'meeting' as a noun stays 'meeting' but as a verb becomes 'meet'. spaCy's lemmatiser uses lookup tables and rule-based exceptions keyed on POS tags produced earlier in the pipeline.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Any task where normalised output must be real words: search with readable facets, feature extraction for interpretable models, text analytics dashboards, or as a preprocessing step before lexicon-based sentiment analysis (which relies on dictionary entries like 'good').
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid when speed is critical and approximate normalisation suffices (stemming is much faster). Avoid for modern Transformer pipelines entirely — subword tokenisation makes lemmatisation unnecessary and can even remove useful morphological signal.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Lemmatisation quality depends heavily on accurate POS tagging — get the POS wrong and you get the wrong lemma ('meeting' as noun lemmatised as if verb -> 'meet', changing meaning). It's slower than stemming due to dictionary lookups and POS dependency. Lemmatisers may not cover domain-specific jargon, slang, or misspellings, leaving them unchanged.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: spaCy: doc = nlp('The geese were better than the mice running around'); [token.lemma_ for token in doc] correctly returns 'goose' for 'geese', 'good' for 'better', 'mouse' for 'mice', and 'run' for 'running' — all valid dictionary words, unlike a stemmer which would produce 'gees', 'better', 'mice', 'run' (inconsistent and non-words).

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Stop word removal filters out very common, low-information words ('the', 'is', 'at', 'a', 'and') from text before further processing, based on a predefined list per language.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: These high-frequency words add noise and dimensionality to BoW/TF-IDF representations without carrying much topical signal, so removing them reduces vocabulary size, speeds up computation, and can improve signal-to-noise ratio for tasks like topic modelling and keyword extraction.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: A fixed or customisable list of stop words (NLTK, spaCy, scikit-learn each ship slightly different lists) is checked against each token (often after lowercasing), and matches are dropped from the token stream before vectorisation.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Classical bag-of-words/TF-IDF pipelines, topic modelling (LDA), keyword/keyphrase extraction, and search indexing where reducing the vocabulary to content words improves topic separability and index size.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks where function words carry meaning: sentiment analysis (negation words like 'not', 'no' are often in stop lists and removing them flips meaning), machine translation, text generation, syntactic parsing, or any Transformer-based pipeline (subword models need the full sequence including function words for context).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Removing 'not'/'no'/'never' from sentiment text turns 'not good' into 'good', inverting the label. Generic stop lists may remove domain-important words (e.g. 'will' is a stop word but critical in legal documents about 'last will and testament'). Different libraries' stop lists disagree, making results non-reproducible across tools.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: scikit-learn's CountVectorizer(stop_words='english') strips 'the', 'is', 'a' from 'The movie is not a good use of time', leaving 'movie good use time' — the negation 'not' is removed, so a naive sentiment classifier trained on this BoW could misclassify a negative review as positive.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Bag of Words represents a document as a vector of word counts (or binary presence) over a fixed vocabulary, completely discarding word order and grammar — hence 'bag'.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: It provides the simplest possible numerical representation of text for classical ML algorithms (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM) that require fixed-size numeric feature vectors, enabling fast text classification baselines with minimal preprocessing.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Build a vocabulary of all unique tokens across the corpus (size V). Each document becomes a length-V vector where entry i is the count (or 0/1) of vocabulary word i in that document. CountVectorizer in scikit-learn handles tokenisation, lowercasing, stop-word removal, and n-gram extraction in this step.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Quick baselines for text classification or clustering on small-to-medium datasets, when interpretability matters (each feature maps directly to a word), or when training data is too small for embeddings to learn meaningful representations.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid when word order/context matters (sentiment with negation, sarcasm), when vocabulary is huge (high-dimensional sparse vectors become memory-heavy), or whenever a pretrained embedding/Transformer is feasible — BoW cannot capture synonymy ('good' and 'great' are unrelated dimensions) or polysemy.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Vocabulary explosion on large corpora creates huge sparse matrices. Out-of-vocabulary words at inference time are silently dropped (zero vector contribution). BoW treats 'not good' and 'good not' identically and cannot distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'. High dimensionality with limited data causes overfitting in downstream classifiers.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: CountVectorizer().fit_transform(['the cat sat', 'the dog sat']) builds vocabulary {'the':0,'cat':1,'sat':2,'dog':3} and produces rows [1,1,1,0] and [1,0,1,1] — 'cat' and 'dog' get completely independent dimensions even though they're semantically similar, a limitation that Word2Vec/embeddings directly address.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: TF-IDF is a weighting scheme that scores each word in a document by how often it appears in that document (TF) multiplied by how rare it is across the whole corpus (IDF), giving high weight to words that are frequent locally but rare globally.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: Plain word counts (BoW) over-weight common words that appear in almost every document ('the', 'said') and under-weight distinctive content words. TF-IDF down-weights ubiquitous terms and up-weights terms that distinguish a document from the corpus, improving search relevance and classification features.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: TF(t,d) = count of term t in document d (often normalised by document length). IDF(t) = log(N / df(t)) where N is total documents and df(t) is the number of documents containing t — rare terms get a large IDF, terms in every document get IDF near 0. TF-IDF(t,d) = TF(t,d) * IDF(t). Resulting document vectors are usually L2-normalised.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Search/information retrieval ranking, keyword extraction, document similarity (cosine similarity on TF-IDF vectors), and as features for classical classifiers when embeddings aren't available or interpretability is desired.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid when semantic similarity beyond exact word overlap matters ('car' vs 'automobile' get zero similarity) — use dense embeddings/sentence transformers instead. Avoid for very short texts (sparse, noisy IDF estimates) or streaming corpora where IDF statistics constantly shift.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: IDF is corpus-dependent: a term rare in the training corpus but common in production gets an inflated weight. New vocabulary at inference (OOV) gets zero weight entirely. TF-IDF still can't capture word order or synonymy. Cosine similarity on TF-IDF can be fooled by keyword stuffing (repeating a term inflates TF).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus) on a corpus of news articles assigns 'the' an IDF near 0 (appears in nearly every doc) but assigns a rare term like 'cryptocurrency' a high IDF — so a query for 'cryptocurrency regulation' ranks documents containing that specific phrase far higher than generic documents, exactly the behaviour classic BM25-based search engines (an evolution of TF-IDF) rely on.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: An n-gram language model estimates the probability of a word given the previous n-1 words, using simple frequency counts from a training corpus. Bigram = condition on 1 previous word; trigram = condition on 2 previous words.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: Before neural language models, n-gram models provided a tractable way to estimate P(word | context) and P(sentence) for tasks like speech recognition, spelling correction, and machine translation, using the Markov assumption to make the problem computationally feasible.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: P(w_i | w_{i-n+1},...,w_{i-1}) is estimated as count(w_{i-n+1},...,w_i) / count(w_{i-n+1},...,w_{i-1}) from corpus frequencies. The probability of a full sentence is the product of these conditional probabilities (chain rule with Markov truncation). Higher n captures more context but suffers worse data sparsity.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Lightweight, interpretable language modelling for spelling/grammar correction, simple autocomplete, or as a baseline/comparison point for perplexity when teaching language modelling concepts. Still used inside some ASR decoders for fast rescoring.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid for any task requiring long-range context or semantic understanding — n-grams beyond trigrams suffer extreme sparsity, and even trigrams can't capture dependencies spanning more than 2 words. Modern tasks use neural (Transformer) language models instead.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Sparsity: most higher-order n-grams in test data were never seen in training, giving zero probability and breaking the whole sentence probability (product with a zero) — this is exactly why smoothing (Laplace, Kneser-Ney) is required. Storage grows combinatorially with n and vocabulary size. Pure n-gram models can't generalise to paraphrases or novel word combinations.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: A trigram model trained on news text computes P('president'|'the','vice') from how often 'the vice president' appeared vs how often 'the vice' appeared — but a novel trigram like 'the vice chancellor' (correct English) may have zero training count, giving probability 0 and making the whole sentence 'impossible' under the raw model, which is precisely the sparsity problem smoothing techniques fix.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Smoothing techniques that adjust n-gram probability estimates to avoid assigning zero probability to unseen n-grams. Laplace (add-one) smoothing is the simplest; Kneser-Ney is the most sophisticated and widely used in practice.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: Raw maximum-likelihood n-gram estimates assign probability 0 to any n-gram not seen in training, which is both unrealistic (unseen != impossible) and catastrophic for sentence-probability computation (a single zero makes the whole product zero). Smoothing redistributes some probability mass to unseen events.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Laplace smoothing adds a constant (usually 1) to every count before normalising: P(w|context) = (count(context,w)+1) / (count(context)+V), which is simple but over-allocates probability to rare/unseen events when V is large. Kneser-Ney instead uses 'absolute discounting' (subtract a fixed discount from each count) and redistributes the freed mass to lower-order n-gram distributions weighted by a 'continuation probability' — how many distinct contexts a word follows in, capturing that words like 'York' mostly follow 'New' rather than being generally frequent.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Building or studying classical statistical n-gram language models (for ASR, spelling correction, or pedagogical purposes) where some probability mass must be reserved for unseen n-grams.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Not applicable to neural language models — softmax over a vocabulary already assigns non-zero probability to every token via the output distribution, so smoothing in this sense is unnecessary in Transformer-based LMs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Laplace smoothing is too aggressive when vocabulary V is large — it can give unseen events more relative probability than is realistic, hurting perplexity badly compared to no smoothing on seen events. Implementing Kneser-Ney correctly (especially the recursive backoff to lower-order models and continuation counts) is notoriously tricky and easy to get subtly wrong.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: On a corpus where 'San Francisco' is common but 'San Diego' never appears, Laplace smoothing gives every unseen bigram following 'San' equal small probability, while Kneser-Ney's continuation-probability term recognises that 'Diego' appears after very few words in general (mostly 'San'), giving 'San Diego' a more realistic, higher probability than an unrelated unseen bigram like 'San Xylophone' — this distinction is why Kneser-Ney consistently outperforms Laplace in perplexity benchmarks.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: TextBlob is a beginner-friendly Python library built on top of NLTK and pattern, providing a simple object-oriented API for common NLP tasks: tokenisation, POS tagging, noun phrase extraction, sentiment analysis, translation, and spelling correction.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: NLTK's API is powerful but verbose and requires understanding many submodules. TextBlob wraps common NLTK/pattern functionality behind a simple `TextBlob(text).sentiment` style interface, making it ideal for quick prototypes, teaching, and small scripts.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Wrapping a string in TextBlob(text) gives a rich object with properties: .words, .sentences, .tags (POS), .noun_phrases, .sentiment (polarity -1 to 1, subjectivity 0 to 1, using a lexicon-based pattern.en analyser), and .correct() for spelling. Under the hood it composes NLTK tokenisers/taggers and a pattern-based sentiment lexicon.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Quick prototyping, teaching NLP fundamentals, simple sentiment analysis on small text volumes, or scripts where a one-line `.sentiment` call is more valuable than fine control.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid in production systems requiring accuracy, speed, or scale — its lexicon-based sentiment is far weaker than fine-tuned Transformer sentiment models, and it's slower than spaCy for pipeline-style processing. Avoid when you need customisable, language-specific pipelines.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: The default sentiment analyser is a static lexicon (pattern.en) that doesn't understand context, sarcasm, or negation well, giving naive polarity scores. Performance on large corpora is poor compared to spaCy. Some features (translation) depend on external APIs that may be deprecated or rate-limited.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: TextBlob('I am not happy with this product').sentiment can return a near-neutral or even slightly positive polarity because the lexicon-based approach weights 'happy' heavily and may not correctly apply the negation 'not' — illustrating why production sentiment systems use fine-tuned Transformers (e.g. DistilBERT-SST2) rather than lexicon lookups.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: Gensim is a Python library specialised in unsupervised topic modelling and word embedding training on large text corpora — it implements Word2Vec, FastText, Doc2Vec, LDA, and LSA with memory-efficient streaming over data that doesn't fit in RAM.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: Training word embeddings or topic models on millions of documents requires algorithms that stream data rather than load it all into memory, plus efficient C-optimised implementations (Cython) of the core training loops — Gensim provides this without requiring a deep learning framework.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Gensim's `corpora` and `Dictionary` classes build streaming bag-of-words representations from disk. `models.Word2Vec` trains skip-gram/CBOW embeddings with negative sampling over tokenised sentences. `models.LdaModel` runs variational Bayes / Gibbs sampling to discover latent topics as distributions over words, and documents as distributions over topics.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Training custom word embeddings on a domain-specific corpus (medical, legal text where general embeddings underperform), exploratory topic discovery on large unlabelled document collections, or computing document similarity via LSA/LDA topic vectors.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid for state-of-the-art semantic tasks — pretrained Transformer embeddings (Sentence-BERT, E5) outperform Word2Vec/LDA on almost all downstream benchmarks today. Avoid LDA when you need stable, reproducible topics across runs (LDA is sensitive to random initialisation and hyperparameters).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: LDA requires choosing the number of topics k in advance, and results are highly sensitive to k, alpha/beta priors, and preprocessing (stop words, lemmatisation) — poor preprocessing yields topics dominated by junk tokens. Word2Vec trained on small corpora produces poor embeddings (needs millions of tokens). Topic interpretability ('topic 7 = sports') requires manual inspection of top words, which doesn't scale.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: gensim.models.Word2Vec(sentences, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=5, sg=1) trains skip-gram embeddings on a custom corpus of customer support tickets, producing domain-specific vectors where 'refund' and 'reimbursement' end up close together — a relationship a general-purpose embedding trained on Wikipedia might not capture as strongly for this domain's jargon.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: NLP (Natural Language Processing) is the umbrella field covering all computational text/speech processing. NLU (Natural Language Understanding) is the subset focused on extracting meaning/intent from text (classification, parsing, entity extraction). NLG (Natural Language Generation) is the subset focused on producing text (summarisation, translation output, dialogue responses).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: These distinctions clarify what a given system or component is doing: a search query parser is doing NLU (interpreting intent), while a chatbot's reply or a summariser's output is NLG (producing text). Modern LLMs blur the lines by doing both in one model, but the distinction remains useful for system design and evaluation.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: NLU tasks map text -> structured meaning (intent classification, slot filling, NER, sentiment, semantic parsing) and are typically evaluated with accuracy/F1 against gold labels. NLG tasks map structured input or context -> fluent text (machine translation, summarisation, dialogue generation, data-to-text) and are evaluated with metrics like BLEU/ROUGE or human judgement. A full conversational AI pipeline often chains NLU (understand the user) -> dialogue management/reasoning -> NLG (generate response).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Use the NLU/NLG framing when designing a pipeline with separable components (e.g. a voice assistant: ASR -> NLU intent classifier -> business logic -> NLG response template/model -> TTS), or when discussing which evaluation metrics apply to which subtask.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Don't force the distinction onto end-to-end generative LLMs where a single model performs understanding and generation jointly in one forward pass (e.g. GPT-4 answering a question) — the boundary becomes an implementation detail rather than a system design choice.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Conflating NLU and NLG evaluation metrics is a common error — using BLEU (an NLG metric comparing generated vs reference text) to evaluate an NLU classification task makes no sense, and vice versa using F1 to evaluate open-ended generation quality misses fluency/coherence. Teams sometimes over-engineer separate NLU+NLG pipelines for tasks an end-to-end LLM now handles better and more simply.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: A customer service bot: the NLU component classifies 'I want to cancel my subscription' as intent=CANCEL_SUBSCRIPTION (an understanding task, evaluated by intent classification accuracy), while the NLG component generates 'I can help you cancel — can you confirm your account email?' (a generation task, evaluated by fluency and task success rate) — separating these lets teams swap in a better intent classifier without touching the response generator.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: A conceptual hierarchy of linguistic analysis levels that classical NLP pipelines process in order: lexical (word-level: tokenisation, morphology), syntactic (sentence structure: POS tagging, parsing), semantic (meaning: word sense, semantic roles), and pragmatic (context-dependent meaning: discourse, intent, implicature).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: This layered framework reflects linguistic theory and historically guided how NLP systems were architected — each stage's output feeds the next, allowing modular development and debugging (you can inspect whether an error originates from tokenisation, parsing, or semantic interpretation).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: Lexical analysis: tokenisation, stemming/lemmatisation, morphological analysis. Syntactic analysis: POS tagging, constituency/dependency parsing to determine grammatical structure. Semantic analysis: word sense disambiguation, named entity recognition, semantic role labelling (who did what to whom) to determine literal meaning. Pragmatic analysis: coreference resolution, discourse structure, speech act interpretation — meaning that depends on context beyond the sentence.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Designing or debugging traditional NLP pipelines (spaCy-style), teaching NLP fundamentals, or diagnosing where a pipeline's understanding breaks down (e.g. parsing is correct but semantic role labelling assigns the wrong agent/patient).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid treating this as a literal required pipeline for modern Transformer-based systems — end-to-end neural models don't have explicit separable stages; the levels are useful for analysis/interpretability research but not a mandatory architecture.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Errors compound across stages in pipeline architectures — a tokenisation mistake propagates to bad POS tags, which propagates to a wrong parse tree, which propagates to wrong semantic roles ('garbage in, garbage out' cascading failure). Pragmatic-level phenomena (sarcasm, implicature) remain hard for both classical pipelines and modern LLMs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: For the sentence 'The chicken is ready to eat': lexical analysis tokenises it normally; syntactic analysis produces a valid parse; but semantic/pragmatic analysis must resolve the ambiguity of whether the chicken is the eater or the food — a classic example showing that even with correct lower-level analysis, semantic/pragmatic ambiguity can remain unresolved without world knowledge.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: spaCy is a production-oriented NLP library in Python/Cython that processes text through a configurable pipeline of components: tokeniser (always first, non-optional), then statistical components like tagger (POS), parser (dependencies), and NER (named entities), each adding annotations to a shared Doc object.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: NLTK was designed for teaching/research and is slow with inconsistent APIs across tools. spaCy was built for production: fast (Cython), opinionated single best-practice algorithms per task, pretrained pipelines for many languages, and a unified Doc/Token/Span API where every annotation lives on the same object.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: nlp = spacy.load('en_core_web_sm') loads a pretrained pipeline. doc = nlp(text) runs the tokeniser, then each pipeline component in sequence (tok2vec -> tagger -> parser -> ner -> lemmatizer etc.), writing annotations onto Token objects (token.pos_, token.dep_, token.head) and doc.ents for entities. Components share a common tok2vec embedding layer for efficiency. The pipeline is configurable via nlp.pipe_names, and components can be disabled for speed (nlp.disable_pipes).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Production NLP pipelines needing tokenisation + POS + dependency parsing + NER together efficiently, information extraction systems, preprocessing for downstream ML, or whenever you need fast batch processing (nlp.pipe()) of large text volumes.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks spaCy's pretrained models don't cover well out-of-the-box (domain-specific entities require custom NER training) and avoid using spaCy's general statistical models when a fine-tuned Transformer (via spacy-transformers or HuggingFace directly) would give materially better accuracy for your specific task.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Loading the wrong model size (en_core_web_sm vs lg vs trf) trades accuracy for speed — sm models have weaker parsing/NER. Disabling a component that a later component depends on (e.g. disabling tagger when parser needs POS) silently degrades downstream quality. Custom domain entities (drug names, product SKUs) are not recognised by general pretrained NER without retraining.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: doc = nlp('Apple is looking at buying U.K. startup for $1 billion'); for ent in doc.ents: print(ent.text, ent.label_) outputs ('Apple','ORG'), ('U.K.','GPE'), ('$1 billion','MONEY') — all extracted in a single nlp(text) call that also populated POS tags and a dependency parse, illustrating spaCy's single-pass multi-annotation design versus NLTK's separate function calls per task.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_it_is: NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is the original comprehensive Python NLP library, providing tokenisers, stemmers, POS taggers, parsers, classifiers, and access to many linguistic corpora (WordNet, treebanks, etc.) — widely used for teaching and research.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.why_it_exists: Created as an educational and research toolkit to make classical computational linguistics algorithms and corpora accessible in Python, with extensive documentation and a companion book ('NLP with Python') that has trained generations of NLP students.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.how_it_works: NLTK provides standalone functions/classes for each task: nltk.word_tokenize(), nltk.pos_tag(), nltk.ne_chunk(), PorterStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer, and access to corpora via nltk.corpus (e.g. wordnet, treebank, stopwords) — most require downloading data packages via nltk.download(). It also includes classic ML classifiers (Naive Bayes, decision trees) for text classification exercises.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.use_when: Teaching/learning NLP fundamentals where seeing each algorithmic step explicitly is valuable, accessing linguistic resources like WordNet (synsets, hypernyms) for lexical semantics tasks, or quick exploratory analysis/prototyping in notebooks.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.avoid_when: Avoid for production pipelines needing speed and a unified annotation object — spaCy is faster and more consistent. Avoid for state-of-the-art accuracy on any task where pretrained Transformers exist (NLTK's taggers/parsers are pre-deep-learning quality).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.what_goes_wrong: Requires separate nltk.download() calls for each corpus/model, which can fail silently in offline/restricted environments. Its POS tagger and parser are noticeably less accurate than spaCy's or Transformer-based taggers. Mixing NLTK tokenisation with a different library's models (e.g. feeding NLTK tokens to a HuggingFace model) causes vocabulary mismatches.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Text Preprocessing|.real_example: from nltk.corpus import wordnet; wordnet.synsets('bank') returns multiple synsets (financial institution, river bank, etc.) with definitions and hypernym/hyponym relations — a lexical resource still useful for word-sense-disambiguation research and rule-based systems, even though it predates and is less powerful than contextual embeddings for the same task.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.what_it_is: CBOW (Continuous Bag of Words) is one of the two Word2Vec training architectures: it predicts the centre word given its surrounding context words, producing dense word embeddings as a byproduct of this prediction task.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.why_it_exists: Sparse representations like BoW/TF-IDF give every word an independent dimension with no notion of similarity. Word2Vec's goal is to learn dense, low-dimensional vectors where semantically similar words end up close together, by exploiting the distributional hypothesis ('words that occur in similar contexts have similar meanings').
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.how_it_works: For a window of context words around position i (e.g. w_{i-2},w_{i-1},w_{i+1},w_{i+2}), CBOW averages (or sums) their embedding vectors and feeds that through a linear layer + softmax to predict w_i. Training via gradient descent on this prediction objective (with negative sampling for efficiency) pushes the embedding matrix toward representations where context-predictive words cluster together. CBOW trains faster than skip-gram because it averages multiple contexts into one prediction per centre word.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.use_when: Training word embeddings on large corpora where training speed matters and the corpus has many frequent words — CBOW tends to perform better on frequent words due to the averaging/smoothing effect.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.avoid_when: Avoid when the corpus is small or dominated by rare words — skip-gram generally captures rare-word representations better since it generates more training pairs per occurrence. Avoid for any task needing contextual (per-occurrence) representations — CBOW gives one static vector per word regardless of context.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.what_goes_wrong: Static embeddings mean polysemous words ('bank' = river bank vs financial bank) get a single blended vector, conflating distinct senses. Training requires large corpora (millions of tokens) — small corpora produce noisy, low-quality embeddings. The averaging of context vectors can blur fine-grained distinctions compared to skip-gram.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.real_example: gensim.models.Word2Vec(sentences, sg=0, vector_size=300, window=5) trains CBOW embeddings; on a large news corpus, the resulting vectors place 'king', 'queen', 'prince' near each other in vector space because they share many contextual neighbours ('the X announced', 'X of England'), even though CBOW never saw an explicit 'royalty' label.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.what_it_is: Skip-gram is the second Word2Vec architecture: it predicts each context word individually given the centre word — the inverse direction of CBOW.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.why_it_exists: Skip-gram generates many (centre, context) training pairs per sentence (one per context position), which gives rare words more training signal than CBOW's single averaged prediction — making skip-gram the preferred choice when rare-word quality matters.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.how_it_works: For centre word w_i and window size c, skip-gram creates training pairs (w_i, w_{i-c}),...,(w_i, w_{i+c}) and trains the model to maximise P(context word | centre word) via a softmax over the vocabulary (made tractable with negative sampling or hierarchical softmax). Each pair is a separate gradient update, so rare centre words still get many updates if they appear with diverse contexts.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.use_when: Training embeddings where rare-word quality matters (specialised domains with long-tail vocabulary), or when corpus size is moderate rather than massive — skip-gram is more sample-efficient per occurrence than CBOW.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.avoid_when: Avoid when training speed/compute is the binding constraint on a huge corpus and frequent-word quality is sufficient — CBOW trains faster. Avoid when contextual (sense-disambiguated) embeddings are required — use ELMo/BERT instead.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.what_goes_wrong: Skip-gram is slower to train than CBOW because it makes one prediction per context position rather than one per centre word. Like CBOW, it produces static embeddings — no context-sensitivity. Choice of window size c is a critical hyperparameter: too small misses topical relations, too large blurs syntactic relations.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Wor.real_example: Word2Vec(sentences, sg=1, vector_size=300, window=5, negative=10) trains skip-gram with negative sampling; this is the configuration originally used by Mikolov et al. to demonstrate the famous analogy 'king - man + woman ≈ queen', which works well specifically because skip-gram produces enough well-separated directions in embedding space to encode such relational structure.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.what_it_is: Negative sampling is a training trick that replaces the full softmax over the entire vocabulary (which requires computing scores for every word, e.g. 1M+ words) with a much cheaper binary classification: distinguish the true (centre, context) pair from a handful of randomly sampled 'negative' (centre, random-word) pairs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.why_it_exists: Computing softmax over a vocabulary of hundreds of thousands to millions of words for every training step is computationally infeasible — the normalisation term alone requires a sum over the whole vocabulary. Negative sampling makes Word2Vec training tractable on large vocabularies by turning a V-way classification into k+1 binary classifications.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.how_it_works: For each true pair (centre, context), sample k negative words (typically 5-20) from a noise distribution (often unigram frequency raised to the 0.75 power, which slightly flattens the distribution to oversample rare words relative to raw frequency). The training objective becomes: maximise sigmoid(v_centre . v_context) for the true pair and minimise sigmoid(v_centre . v_negative) for each negative — a logistic regression-style loss instead of softmax cross-entropy.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.use_when: Training any embedding model (Word2Vec, FastText, and contrastive learning more broadly such as SimCLR/InfoNCE) where the output space is too large for full softmax, and approximate probability estimates suffice.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.avoid_when: Avoid when exact probability calibration is required (negative sampling gives a model that's good at ranking/similarity but not a calibrated probability distribution over the vocabulary). Hierarchical softmax is an alternative when exact normalised probabilities matter more than speed.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.what_goes_wrong: Choosing too few negatives (k) under-trains the model (insufficient contrastive signal); too many slows training without proportional benefit. Using raw unigram frequency as the noise distribution over-samples extremely common words like 'the' as negatives, wasting capacity — hence the 0.75 power smoothing. The resulting dot products are not true log-probabilities, so they shouldn't be interpreted as P(context|centre) directly.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Neg.real_example: Word2Vec(sentences, negative=5) means for every true (centre, context) pair, 5 random words are sampled as negatives — for the pair ('eat','pizza'), negatives might include ('eat','astronomy'), ('eat','Tuesday') etc., and the model learns to push 'pizza' close to 'eat' in vector space while pushing unrelated words away, all without ever computing a softmax over the full ~3M-word vocabulary.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.what_it_is: GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation) is a word embedding method that learns vectors by factorising a global word-word co-occurrence matrix, explicitly optimising so that vector differences capture ratios of co-occurrence probabilities.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.why_it_exists: Word2Vec is a 'local context window' method — it only ever sees small windows during training and never directly leverages global corpus-wide co-occurrence statistics. GloVe was designed to combine the strengths of global matrix-factorisation methods (like LSA, which use global statistics but capture analogy structure poorly) with the local-context analogy performance of Word2Vec.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.how_it_works: First build a global co-occurrence matrix X where X_ij = how often word j appears in the context of word i across the whole corpus. GloVe's training objective minimises (v_i . v_j + b_i + b_j - log(X_ij))^2 weighted by a function that down-weights very rare and very frequent co-occurrences. The key insight is that ratios of co-occurrence probabilities P(k|i)/P(k|j) encode meaning (e.g. for i='ice', j='steam', words k like 'solid'/'gas' have very different ratios), and the log-bilinear model form makes vector differences correspond to these log-ratios.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.use_when: When you want pretrained general-purpose static embeddings and value training efficiency on a fixed corpus (GloVe trains directly on precomputed co-occurrence counts, which can be more memory/compute efficient than streaming through Word2Vec's window-by-window training for very large corpora).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.avoid_when: Avoid for any task needing contextual embeddings (use BERT/Sentence-Transformers). Avoid when the corpus is small — the co-occurrence matrix becomes too sparse for stable statistics. Avoid building the full co-occurrence matrix for huge vocabularies without sparse-matrix techniques (memory cost is O(V^2) in the worst case).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.what_goes_wrong: Like Word2Vec, GloVe produces a single static vector per word — no polysemy handling. The co-occurrence matrix can be memory-intensive for large vocabularies/window sizes. Pretrained GloVe vectors (e.g. from Common Crawl) reflect biases and word distributions of their training corpus, which may mismatch a target domain (e.g. medical text).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Glo.real_example: Pretrained glove.6B.300d vectors (trained on Wikipedia + Gigaword) are commonly loaded directly into a Keras/PyTorch Embedding layer as initial weights for a text classifier — giving the model a 'head start' with meaningful word relationships before task-specific fine-tuning, a common pre-Transformer transfer-learning pattern.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.what_it_is: FastText is an extension of Word2Vec (from Facebook/Meta) that represents each word as a bag of character n-grams plus the whole word itself, summing their embeddings — enabling it to produce embeddings for words never seen during training.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.why_it_exists: Word2Vec and GloVe assign a completely separate vector to every word form, so morphological variants ('run', 'running', 'runner') share no parameters, and any out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word at inference gets no embedding at all. FastText fixes both issues by decomposing words into shared subword units.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.how_it_works: A word like 'running' (with boundary markers '<running>') is decomposed into character n-grams of length 3-6: '<ru', 'run', 'unn', 'nni', ... plus the full word '<running>'. Each n-gram has its own embedding vector; the word's embedding is the sum of all its n-gram vectors. Training uses skip-gram with negative sampling, same as Word2Vec, but gradients update the shared n-gram vectors. At inference, an OOV word is embedded by summing the embeddings of whatever n-grams it shares with training vocabulary.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.use_when: Morphologically rich languages (German, Finnish, Turkish) where many word forms share roots, domains with frequent typos/misspellings or rare word forms (social media text), or any application needing to embed words never seen during training without retraining.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.avoid_when: Avoid when word order/contextual meaning matters more than morphology — FastText is still a static embedding (one vector per word, summed from n-grams), so it doesn't solve polysemy. Avoid for languages where character n-grams don't carry morphological signal (e.g. logographic languages like Chinese, where character n-grams behave differently).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.what_goes_wrong: The n-gram decomposition increases vocabulary/parameter count substantially (every n-gram needs a vector), increasing model size and training time vs plain Word2Vec. OOV embeddings via n-gram summation are approximations — for very short or unusual OOV words, the resulting vector quality can be poor. Choosing n-gram length range (default 3-6) affects which morphological patterns are captured.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Fas.real_example: A FastText model trained on English text has never seen 'unfollowable', but because it has learned vectors for n-grams like 'un', 'follow', 'able', 'ow', it can still produce a reasonable embedding for 'unfollowable' by summing those shared subword vectors — something Word2Vec/GloVe simply cannot do (they'd have no vector at all for an unseen word).

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.what_it_is: Doc2Vec (also called Paragraph Vector) extends Word2Vec to learn a dense vector representation for an entire document/paragraph, not just individual words, by treating each document as having its own learned 'pseudo-word' vector that participates in context predictions alongside word vectors.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.why_it_exists: Averaging word vectors to represent a document (a common ad-hoc approach) loses word-order information and dilutes signal in long documents. Doc2Vec was designed to directly learn fixed-length document vectors that capture document-level semantics, usable for document similarity, clustering, and as classifier features.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.how_it_works: Two variants mirror Word2Vec: PV-DM (Distributed Memory, analogous to CBOW) prepends a document ID vector to the context word vectors when predicting the next word, so the document vector must encode information helpful across all predictions in that document. PV-DBOW (analogous to skip-gram) trains the document vector to predict randomly sampled words from the document directly, ignoring word order. At inference on a new document, word vectors are frozen and only the new document's vector is trained via the same prediction objective.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.use_when: Document similarity/clustering/retrieval tasks on a fixed corpus where training a dedicated model is feasible, or as a baseline before adopting Transformer-based sentence/document embeddings (Sentence-BERT).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.avoid_when: Avoid for new/few documents — Doc2Vec needs many documents to learn meaningful document vectors, and inferring a vector for a brand-new document requires additional gradient-descent steps (slow compared to a single forward pass through a pretrained Sentence-BERT model). Avoid when state-of-the-art semantic similarity is needed — Sentence-BERT/E5 embeddings substantially outperform Doc2Vec on retrieval benchmarks today.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.what_goes_wrong: Inferring vectors for new documents at inference time requires running additional training iterations (infer_vector with multiple epochs), which is slow and has stochastic results depending on random initialisation/seed. Quality is highly sensitive to hyperparameters (vector size, window, epochs) and corpus size. Document vectors from PV-DBOW ignore word order entirely, similar to BoW limitations.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Doc.real_example: gensim.models.Doc2Vec(documents, vector_size=100, dm=1) trained on a corpus of product reviews can produce a 100-dim vector per review such that cosine similarity between two reviews about the same product defect is high — useful for clustering similar complaints, though modern systems would more likely use a pretrained sentence-embedding model for this with zero training required.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.what_it_is: LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis, also called LSI) reduces a TF-IDF term-document matrix to a lower-dimensional 'latent semantic' space using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), revealing relationships between terms and documents that aren't apparent from raw co-occurrence.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.why_it_exists: Raw TF-IDF vectors are sparse and high-dimensional, and treat exact word matches as the only similarity signal — 'car' and 'automobile' share zero TF-IDF dimensions. LSA was developed to find a lower-rank approximation that captures latent topics/concepts, so documents about the same topic using different vocabulary end up with similar reduced vectors.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.how_it_works: Build the term-document TF-IDF matrix X (terms x documents). Apply truncated SVD: X ≈ U_k * Σ_k * V_k^T, keeping only the top k singular values/vectors. U_k gives term vectors in the k-dimensional latent space, V_k gives document vectors, and Σ_k contains the singular values (importance of each latent dimension). Documents/terms close in this k-dimensional space share latent semantic structure even without exact word overlap, because SVD captures patterns of co-occurring terms across documents.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.use_when: Dimensionality reduction for TF-IDF-based pipelines, exploratory topic analysis on smaller corpora, or as a fast unsupervised baseline for document similarity/clustering before considering neural embeddings.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.avoid_when: Avoid for large vocabularies/corpora where SVD becomes computationally expensive (though truncated/randomised SVD helps). Avoid when polysemy or fine-grained semantic nuance matters — LSA's linear algebra captures broad co-occurrence patterns, not nuanced meaning. Modern embeddings (Word2Vec onward) generally outperform LSA on semantic tasks.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.what_goes_wrong: Choosing k (number of latent dimensions) is a hyperparameter with no principled selection rule — too small loses information, too large retains noise. SVD on large matrices is memory/compute intensive without randomised approximation algorithms. LSA's latent dimensions are not directly interpretable as 'topics' the way LDA's are (they can have negative values and mix concepts).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Lat.real_example: TruncatedSVD(n_components=100).fit_transform(tfidf_matrix) reduces a 50,000-term TF-IDF matrix to 100 dimensions per document; a search query 'automobile' transformed into this latent space can now retrieve documents about 'car maintenance' even if those documents never contain the literal word 'automobile', because SVD captured the co-occurrence pattern linking 'car' and 'automobile' contexts.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.what_it_is: ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models) produces contextual word embeddings — a different vector for the same word depending on its sentence context — by combining internal states from a deep bidirectional LSTM language model trained on large text corpora.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.why_it_exists: Word2Vec/GloVe/FastText give every word a single fixed vector regardless of context, so 'bank' has the same representation in 'river bank' and 'savings bank'. ELMo was the first widely-adopted method to produce genuinely context-sensitive embeddings, directly addressing the polysemy limitation of static embeddings — a major step toward what BERT later perfected with Transformers.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.how_it_works: ELMo trains a multi-layer bidirectional LSTM as a language model (forward LM predicts next word, backward LM predicts previous word) on a large corpus. For a given word in a given sentence, ELMo concatenates/combines the hidden states from each LSTM layer (for both directions) at that word's position into a single vector — so the same word token gets different embeddings depending on its surrounding sentence. These contextual embeddings are then used as (frozen or fine-tuned) input features for downstream task-specific models.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.use_when: Historically used as a drop-in replacement for static embeddings to boost performance on tagging/parsing/QA tasks via feature-based transfer learning (before full Transformer fine-tuning became standard).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.avoid_when: Avoid in any new project today — BERT and its successors (via full Transformer self-attention rather than LSTM) provide strictly better contextual representations with simpler fine-tuning workflows, and the entire NLP field has moved to Transformer-based contextual embeddings.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.what_goes_wrong: LSTMs process sequentially, making ELMo slower to train and run than parallelisable Transformers. Bidirectional LSTMs combine forward and backward passes somewhat shallowly compared to Transformer self-attention's direct token-to-token interactions, limiting representational power. ELMo embeddings are typically used as frozen features with a separate downstream model, which is less effective than end-to-end fine-tuning (BERT's approach).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|ELM.real_example: Before BERT (2018), state-of-the-art NER and SQuAD QA systems used ELMo embeddings as input features to a BiLSTM-CRF tagger or attention-based QA model, achieving notable gains over GloVe-initialised models — but within a year, BERT's fine-tuned Transformer representations surpassed ELMo-based systems on the same benchmarks by a wide margin, making ELMo largely obsolete in practice.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.what_it_is: A famous demonstration that Word2Vec embeddings capture linear relational structure: vector arithmetic on word embeddings — vec('king') - vec('man') + vec('woman') — yields a vector closest to vec('queen'), showing that the gender relationship is encoded as a roughly consistent vector offset across word pairs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.why_it_exists: This result became the canonical illustration of why dense embeddings are powerful: relationships between concepts (gender, capital-of, plural-of) are encoded as consistent directions/offsets in vector space, enabling analogy reasoning ('a is to b as c is to ?') purely through vector arithmetic — something impossible with sparse one-hot or BoW representations.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.how_it_works: Word2Vec's training objective (predict context from centre or vice versa) tends to place words that participate in similar relational patterns at similar offsets — because 'king' and 'queen' appear in structurally similar contexts to 'man' and 'woman' respectively (e.g. 'the king/queen announced', 'he/she is a man/woman'), the offset vec('king')-vec('man') ends up approximately parallel to vec('queen')-vec('woman'). Analogy queries are answered by computing the target vector via arithmetic and finding the nearest actual word vector (often excluding the input words) by cosine similarity.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.use_when: Useful as an intuitive teaching example of embedding geometry, and as a component of intrinsic embedding evaluation (analogy benchmarks like the Google analogy dataset test exactly this kind of relation).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.avoid_when: Don't rely on this property for production reasoning tasks — the analogy works cleanly for a curated set of famous examples but is much less reliable across the broader vocabulary, and modern LLMs handle analogical reasoning through entirely different (in-context, attention-based) mechanisms that don't require explicit vector arithmetic.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.what_goes_wrong: The famous examples are somewhat cherry-picked — many analogies don't hold as cleanly, especially for less frequent words or more abstract relations. The result is sensitive to training corpus, hyperparameters, and whether the queried words themselves are excluded from the nearest-neighbour search (otherwise 'king' itself might be the nearest match trivially). Cosine similarity ties can make results unstable.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|wor.real_example: Using gensim's model.most_similar(positive=['king','woman'], negative=['man']) computes vec('king') - vec('man') + vec('woman') and returns 'queen' as the top result on models trained on large corpora like Google News — a result frequently cited in NLP courses as the first compelling evidence that neural embeddings capture meaningful semantic structure beyond simple word similarity.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.what_it_is: Methods for measuring embedding quality intrinsically (without a downstream task): analogy tasks (does vec(a)-vec(b)+vec(c) retrieve vec(d) for known a:b::c:d relations?) and similarity benchmarks (does cosine similarity between word pairs correlate with human-judged similarity scores, e.g. WordSim-353, SimLex-999).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.why_it_exists: Training embeddings is expensive, and you want a quick, task-independent signal of quality before plugging embeddings into a full downstream pipeline. Intrinsic evaluations provide fast, standardised, reproducible benchmarks for comparing embedding methods/hyperparameters.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.how_it_works: Analogy evaluation: for a dataset of (a,b,c,d) quadruples (e.g. Athens:Greece::Berlin:Germany), compute vec(b)-vec(a)+vec(c) and check whether the nearest vector (excluding a,b,c) is vec(d); accuracy = fraction correct. Similarity evaluation: for word pairs with human similarity ratings (e.g. 'cat'-'dog' rated 8/10), compute cosine similarity between the corresponding embeddings and compute Spearman correlation between model scores and human scores across all pairs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.use_when: Quickly comparing different embedding training runs/hyperparameters/corpora during development, or sanity-checking a newly trained embedding model before expensive downstream fine-tuning. For modern sentence/document embeddings, the analogous standardised benchmark is MTEB.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.avoid_when: Don't treat intrinsic benchmark performance as a proxy for downstream task performance in all cases — research has repeatedly shown that analogy/similarity scores don't always correlate strongly with performance on real tasks like classification or retrieval. Avoid using these for contextual embeddings (BERT etc.) where a single word doesn't have one fixed vector to evaluate this way.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.what_goes_wrong: Overfitting hyperparameter choices to a specific analogy/similarity benchmark can produce embeddings that look good on that benchmark but underperform on actual applications ('Goodhart's law' for embedding evaluation). Human similarity judgements themselves have inter-annotator disagreement, putting an upper bound on achievable correlation. Analogy datasets often skew toward certain relation types (capitals, gender) that may not represent the relations your application cares about.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|Word Embeddings|Eva.real_example: Comparing two Word2Vec runs — one trained with window=2 and another with window=10 — on the Google analogy dataset might show the larger window scoring higher on semantic analogies (country-capital) but lower on syntactic analogies (verb tense), guiding the choice of window size based on which relation type matters more for the downstream application (e.g. syntactic parsing favours smaller windows).

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.what_it_is: NER identifies and classifies spans of text into predefined entity categories (PERSON, ORG, LOCATION, DATE, etc.). BIO (Beginning-Inside-Outside) and BIOES (adds End and Single) are tagging schemes that convert span extraction into a per-token classification problem.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.why_it_exists: Many NLP tasks (information extraction, search, knowledge graph construction, redaction) need to locate and categorise specific entities in text. Framing NER as sequence labelling (one tag per token) lets it be solved with standard sequence models (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, or fine-tuned Transformers) rather than requiring a separate span-extraction architecture.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.how_it_works: Each token gets a tag: B-TYPE marks the beginning of an entity of type TYPE, I-TYPE marks tokens inside a multi-token entity, O marks non-entity tokens. BIOES adds E-TYPE (end of entity) and S-TYPE (single-token entity) for finer-grained boundary signal. A sequence model (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, or token-classification head on BERT) predicts a tag per token; contiguous B/I/E tags are then merged into entity spans with their type.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.use_when: Information extraction pipelines (extracting names, organisations, dates from documents), building knowledge graphs, anonymising/redacting PII, or any task requiring locating specific entity mentions in unstructured text.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.avoid_when: Avoid plain BIO when entities can be nested or overlapping (e.g. 'Bank of America' containing 'America' as a separate LOCATION entity) — standard BIO sequence labelling can't represent overlapping spans; need span-based or nested-NER architectures instead.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.what_goes_wrong: Tag inconsistency at entity boundaries (predicting I-PER without a preceding B-PER) requires post-processing/constrained decoding. Domain-specific entities (drug names, product codes, legal clause types) require labelled training data — pretrained NER models (PERSON/ORG/LOC/MISC) won't recognise them. Class imbalance is severe (most tokens are 'O'), requiring careful loss weighting or evaluation via entity-level F1 rather than token accuracy.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Named Ent.real_example: For 'Marie Curie discovered radium in Paris', BIO tagging gives: Marie/B-PER Curie/I-PER discovered/O radium/O in/O Paris/B-LOC — a fine-tuned BERT token-classification model (bert-base + linear head) trained on CoNLL-2003 produces exactly this tagging, which is then post-processed into entities: ('Marie Curie', PER), ('Paris', LOC).

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.what_it_is: POS tagging assigns each word in a sentence a grammatical category (noun, verb, adjective, adverb, etc.) based on both its definition and its context.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.why_it_exists: Many downstream tasks depend on knowing a word's grammatical role: parsing needs POS as input features, lemmatisation needs POS to pick the correct base form ('meeting' as noun vs verb), and information extraction uses POS patterns (e.g. noun phrases) to find candidate entities.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.how_it_works: Classical approaches used Hidden Markov Models or CRFs over tag sequences, modelling P(tag_i | tag_{i-1}) and P(word_i | tag_i). Modern approaches use a Transformer encoder (or BiLSTM) with a per-token classification head trained on tagged corpora like the Penn Treebank (using tag sets such as Universal POS tags: NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV, PRON, DET, ADP, etc.). The model uses both the word itself and surrounding context to disambiguate ('book' as NOUN in 'read a book' vs VERB in 'book a flight').
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.use_when: As a feature/preprocessing step for parsing, lemmatisation, or rule-based information extraction (e.g. extracting noun phrases via POS patterns), or for linguistic analysis of text corpora.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.avoid_when: Avoid treating POS tagging as a standalone end-task in modern pipelines — it's almost always a means to another end (parsing, lemmatisation), and end-to-end Transformer models for downstream tasks (classification, NER) don't require explicit POS as an intermediate step.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.what_goes_wrong: Ambiguous words depend heavily on context ('The old man the boat' — 'man' is a verb here, a classic garden-path sentence that trips up taggers). Domain shift hurts: a tagger trained on news text may mis-tag social media text with non-standard grammar/abbreviations. Tag set mismatches (Penn Treebank's ~45 tags vs Universal POS's ~17 tags) cause confusion when combining tools/datasets.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Part-of-s.real_example: spaCy's doc = nlp('Time flies like an arrow'); [(t.text, t.pos_) for t in doc] tags 'flies' as VERB and 'like' as ADP (preposition) in this sentence — correctly resolving an ambiguous sentence that famously has multiple valid parses depending on whether 'flies' or 'time' is read as the verb.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.what_it_is: Dependency parsing analyses the grammatical structure of a sentence by establishing directed binary relations ('dependencies') between a 'head' word and its 'dependent' words, forming a tree where every word (except the root) has exactly one head.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.why_it_exists: Knowing which words modify or relate to which other words is essential for extracting structured meaning — e.g. to find 'who did what to whom' (subject, object, modifiers), which constituency parsing's nested-phrase structure makes less direct to query.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.how_it_works: Each word gets a head (the word it grammatically depends on) and a dependency label (nsubj=nominal subject, dobj=direct object, amod=adjectival modifier, etc.), forming a tree rooted at the main verb. Modern parsers (transition-based or graph-based) use neural networks (often Transformer encoders) to score possible head-dependent arcs and find the highest-scoring valid tree (e.g. via the Chu-Liu/Edmonds algorithm for graph-based parsing, or a stack-based transition system for transition-based parsing).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.use_when: Information extraction needing structured relations (subject-verb-object triples), grammar checking, question answering systems that need to identify the relationship between entities in a question, or as a feature for relation extraction.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks where end-to-end neural models can directly learn the needed relationships from raw text without explicit parse trees (most modern classification/QA/generation tasks). Avoid for languages/text styles (social media, code-mixed text) where parsers trained on formal text perform poorly.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.what_goes_wrong: Long sentences with complex coordination/subordination produce parses with many possible valid analyses; parser errors compound when used as input to downstream extraction. Parsing ungrammatical or fragment text (common in chat/social media) degrades badly since parsers assume roughly well-formed sentences. Different treebank annotation schemes (Universal Dependencies vs Penn Treebank-style) produce incompatible trees.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Dependenc.real_example: For 'The cat that chased the mouse ran away', a dependency parse identifies 'ran' as the root verb with 'cat' as its nsubj, while 'chased' is in a relative clause (acl:relcl) modifying 'cat' with its own subject 'that' and object 'mouse' — this structure lets an information extraction system correctly attribute 'ran away' to 'the cat' rather than 'the mouse', which a flat BoW or POS-only approach couldn't disambiguate.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.what_it_is: Coreference resolution identifies all expressions in a text that refer to the same real-world entity, e.g. linking 'Marie Curie', 'she', and 'the scientist' across a passage to the same person.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.why_it_exists: Text naturally uses pronouns and varied referring expressions for brevity and style, but downstream tasks (information extraction, summarisation, question answering, dialogue systems) need to know that 'she' in sentence 3 refers to 'Marie Curie' from sentence 1 to correctly attribute facts and actions.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.how_it_works: Mention detection finds candidate referring expressions (pronouns, named entities, noun phrases). For each pronoun/mention, a scoring model (historically rule-based with Hobbs' algorithm or centering theory; now neural, often a Transformer encoder with span representations) computes compatibility scores between the mention and all preceding candidate antecedents, considering gender/number agreement, syntactic constraints, recency, and semantic plausibility. Mentions are then clustered into coreference chains, each representing one entity.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.use_when: Document-level information extraction and summarisation (to correctly attribute actions/attributes to entities across sentences), dialogue systems tracking entities across turns, and knowledge graph construction from text.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.avoid_when: Avoid for single-sentence tasks where cross-sentence reference doesn't arise. Avoid assuming off-the-shelf coreference resolvers handle domain-specific reference patterns well (e.g. legal documents with defined terms like 'the Purchaser') without adaptation.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.what_goes_wrong: Pronoun resolution ambiguity is genuinely hard even for humans in some cases ('The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it's too big' — what does 'it' refer to? — the famous Winograd Schema problem, requiring world knowledge). Long documents with many entities create combinatorial complexity. Gender-neutral pronouns and cross-lingual coreference add further difficulty. Errors cascade into downstream extraction (wrong entity gets credited with an action).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Coreferen.real_example: In 'Dr. Smith examined the patient. She prescribed antibiotics.', a coreference resolver must link 'She' to 'Dr. Smith' (not 'the patient') — getting this right is essential for a clinical NLP system summarising 'who prescribed what', and getting it wrong could (in a real clinical context) misattribute a medical decision to the wrong person.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.what_it_is: A text classification pipeline is the end-to-end process of assigning predefined category labels to text documents: preprocessing (tokenisation, cleaning), feature extraction (BoW/TF-IDF or embeddings), model training (Naive Bayes/SVM/logistic regression or fine-tuned Transformer), and evaluation.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.why_it_exists: Text classification underlies an enormous range of applications — spam detection, sentiment analysis, topic categorisation, intent classification, content moderation — and a standard pipeline structure (preprocess -> vectorise -> classify -> evaluate) provides a reusable template across these applications.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.how_it_works: Classical pipeline: clean text -> tokenise -> remove stop words/lemmatise -> vectorise with TF-IDF -> train a linear classifier (logistic regression, SVM, or Naive Bayes) -> evaluate with accuracy/precision/recall/F1, often with cross-validation. Modern pipeline: tokenise with the model's subword tokeniser -> fine-tune a pretrained Transformer (BERT/RoBERTa) with a classification head on [CLS] -> evaluate the same way. Both require a labelled training set and a held-out test/validation split to avoid overfitting.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.use_when: Any supervised task where documents/texts map to a fixed set of categories: spam/ham, sentiment (positive/negative/neutral), topic tags, intent classes for chatbots, or content moderation categories.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.avoid_when: Avoid building a custom classification pipeline when a pretrained zero-shot/few-shot LLM classifier (via prompting) achieves sufficient accuracy without labelled training data — for many low-volume or rapidly-changing label sets, prompting an LLM is faster to deploy than training a classifier.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.what_goes_wrong: Class imbalance (99% non-spam, 1% spam) makes accuracy a misleading metric — need precision/recall/F1 per class or balanced accuracy. Train/test leakage (e.g. splitting by random row when documents share near-duplicate content) inflates reported performance. TF-IDF-based classical pipelines fail to generalise to vocabulary/phrasing not seen in training; Transformer fine-tuning needs enough labelled examples per class (typically hundreds+) to avoid overfitting.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text clas.real_example: A support-ticket routing system: TfidfVectorizer + LogisticRegression baseline achieves 82% F1 on routing tickets to {billing, technical, account} categories; fine-tuning distilbert-base-uncased on the same labelled tickets pushes F1 to 91% by capturing context and synonymy ('can't log in' vs 'login failure') that TF-IDF treats as unrelated features.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.what_it_is: Sentiment analysis classifies the emotional tone of text — typically as positive/negative/neutral, or on a finer scale (1-5 stars) — and is one of the most common applied text classification tasks.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.why_it_exists: Businesses need to monitor opinion at scale: product reviews, social media mentions, customer support tickets, survey responses. Manual reading doesn't scale, so automated sentiment classification provides aggregate metrics (e.g. 'sentiment trending negative this week') and flags individual items for human follow-up.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.how_it_works: Lexicon-based approaches (older, e.g. VADER, TextBlob) sum/average precomputed sentiment scores for words in the text, with rules for negation and intensifiers. ML-based approaches train a classifier (from Naive Bayes on BoW to fine-tuned Transformers like DistilBERT-SST2 or RoBERTa) on labelled examples to predict sentiment class directly from text, implicitly learning context, negation, and domain-specific sentiment words.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.use_when: Aggregate monitoring of opinion across large volumes of text (reviews, social media, support tickets) where approximate sentiment trends are useful, or as a feature in a larger pipeline (e.g. flagging negative-sentiment support tickets for priority routing).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.avoid_when: Avoid relying on coarse positive/negative/neutral sentiment for nuanced business decisions — sarcasm, mixed sentiment within one text ('great product, terrible customer service'), and domain-specific sentiment words (in finance, 'volatile' might be neutral-to-negative, not the everyday connotation) all reduce reliability. For actionable insight, aspect-based sentiment (Opinion Mining) is usually more useful.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.what_goes_wrong: Lexicon-based methods fail on negation ('not bad' scored as negative due to 'bad') and sarcasm ('Oh great, another delay' scored positive due to 'great'). Domain mismatch: a model trained on movie reviews (SST-2) may misclassify financial news sentiment. Class definitions are subjective — what counts as 'neutral' varies, causing label noise in training data and inconsistent evaluation.
