4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Sentiment.real_example: distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english correctly classifies 'This movie was a complete waste of time' as NEGATIVE with high confidence by attending to 'waste of time' in context — but the same lexicon-based VADER analyser applied to 'not terrible, actually' might score it negative because of 'terrible', missing the negation's effect, illustrating why context-aware Transformer models outperform lexicon approaches on nuanced phrasing.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.what_it_is: Topic modelling discovers latent thematic structure in a collection of documents — representing each document as a mixture of topics, and each topic as a distribution over words — without requiring labelled data. LDA and NMF are classical probabilistic/algebraic approaches; BERTopic is a modern embedding-based approach.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.why_it_exists: Large unlabelled document collections (news archives, customer feedback, research papers) need automatic thematic organisation for exploration, summarisation, and trend analysis — manually reading and categorising every document doesn't scale.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.how_it_works: LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) is a generative probabilistic model assuming each document is a mixture of K topics (Dirichlet-distributed), and each topic is a distribution over words; inference (variational Bayes or Gibbs sampling) recovers these distributions from the observed word counts. NMF (Non-negative Matrix Factorisation) factorises the TF-IDF document-term matrix into two non-negative matrices (documents x topics, topics x words) via iterative multiplicative updates. BERTopic instead embeds documents with a sentence-transformer, reduces dimensionality (UMAP), clusters (HDBSCAN), and extracts representative words per cluster via class-based TF-IDF — leveraging semantic embeddings rather than just word co-occurrence.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.use_when: Exploratory analysis of large unlabelled text corpora to discover themes (LDA/NMF for fast classical baselines; BERTopic when semantic coherence and handling of synonyms/short documents matters and embeddings are affordable).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.avoid_when: Avoid LDA when documents are short (tweets, titles) — word co-occurrence statistics are too sparse for stable topics; BERTopic (embedding-based) handles short text much better. Avoid topic modelling entirely when you have labelled categories already — supervised classification will be more accurate and interpretable for a fixed taxonomy.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.what_goes_wrong: LDA/NMF require choosing the number of topics K upfront, with no universally correct method to pick it (coherence scores help but are imperfect). Topic labels must be manually assigned by inspecting top words per topic — 'topic 7: game, team, player, season, win' must be human-labelled as 'Sports'. BERTopic's clustering (HDBSCAN) can produce many small 'outlier' clusters or be sensitive to UMAP's stochastic dimensionality reduction, making results non-deterministic across runs without fixed seeds.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Topic mod.real_example: Running BERTopic on a corpus of app store reviews might surface a topic cluster with top words ['crash', 'freeze', 'restart', 'app', 'closes'] (clearly a 'stability bugs' topic) and another with ['subscription', 'price', 'expensive', 'cancel', 'refund'] ('pricing complaints') — giving a product team an automatic thematic breakdown of feedback volume without anyone manually tagging a single review.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.what_it_is: Word Sense Disambiguation determines which meaning (sense) of a polysemous word is intended in a given context, e.g. deciding whether 'bank' in a sentence means a financial institution or a riverbank.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.why_it_exists: Many words have multiple distinct meanings, and downstream tasks (machine translation, information retrieval, question answering) need the correct sense to behave correctly — translating 'bank' (financial) into French requires 'banque', while 'bank' (river) requires 'rive', and using the wrong one produces nonsensical or incorrect output.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.how_it_works: Classical approaches use dictionaries/sense inventories (WordNet synsets) and either knowledge-based methods (Lesk algorithm: pick the sense whose dictionary definition has the most word overlap with the surrounding context) or supervised classifiers trained on sense-annotated corpora (SemCor) using context features. Modern approaches use contextual embeddings (BERT) directly — since BERT already produces different vectors for 'bank' depending on context, WSD can be framed as nearest-neighbour matching between a word's contextual embedding and sense-representative embeddings, or as fine-tuning a classifier over BERT representations.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.use_when: Machine translation (choosing the correct target-language word for a polysemous source word), information retrieval (disambiguating query terms to improve relevance), and any lexical-resource-based application (WordNet-based reasoning) where sense-level precision matters.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.avoid_when: Avoid treating WSD as a separate explicit step in modern end-to-end neural pipelines — contextual Transformer models implicitly disambiguate word sense as part of computing contextual representations, without needing a discrete WSD module.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.what_goes_wrong: Sense inventories (WordNet has ~17 senses for some common verbs like 'run') are often too fine-grained for practical use — many distinctions don't matter for a given task. Sense-annotated training data is expensive and limited (SemCor covers far fewer words than the full vocabulary). The Lesk algorithm's simple word-overlap heuristic is easily fooled by short or generic dictionary definitions.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Word Sens.real_example: In 'He went to the bank to deposit a check' vs 'He sat by the bank fishing', a contextual model (BERT) produces noticeably different embeddings for 'bank' in each sentence because the surrounding words ('deposit', 'check' vs 'sat', 'fishing') shift the representation toward the financial-institution sense vs the riverbank sense — a capability that lets downstream tasks like translation pick 'banque' vs 'rive' correctly without an explicit WSD step.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.what_it_is: Relationship (relation) extraction identifies semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text, e.g. extracting (Marie Curie, discovered, radium) or (Apple, headquartered_in, Cupertino) as structured (subject, relation, object) triples.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.why_it_exists: Unstructured text contains a vast amount of factual information that, if extracted into structured triples, can populate knowledge graphs, enable structured querying, and support downstream reasoning — manually curating such facts doesn't scale to the volume of available text.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.how_it_works: Pipeline approaches first run NER to identify entity mentions, then for each pair of entities within a sentence (or document), classify whether/which relation holds between them — using a classifier over features derived from the dependency path between entities, or a fine-tuned Transformer with the entity pair marked in the input (entity markers around each mention). Distant supervision approaches automatically label training data by aligning text with an existing knowledge base (if KB says (Curie, discovered, radium), any sentence containing both entities is assumed to express that relation, though this introduces label noise).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.use_when: Knowledge graph construction/population from text corpora, structured fact extraction from scientific literature or news, or building searchable databases of entity relationships from unstructured documents.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.avoid_when: Avoid when relations are highly contextual/temporal and a simple triple loses critical nuance (e.g. 'was CEO from 2010-2015' reduced to a static 'is_CEO_of' triple loses the time bound). Avoid distant supervision without quality filtering — the label noise from assuming all co-occurrences express the target relation can be severe.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.what_goes_wrong: Relation extraction inherits NER errors (can't extract a relation about an entity that wasn't correctly identified). Distant supervision introduces false positives (entities co-occur but the sentence doesn't actually express the assumed relation). Long-distance relations spanning multiple sentences (cross-sentence relation extraction) are much harder than within-sentence relations. Relation schemas (the fixed set of relation types) must be predefined, limiting extraction to anticipated relation types.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Relations.real_example: Given 'Marie Curie, born in Warsaw, discovered radium and polonium', a relation extraction system identifies entities (Marie Curie: PERSON, Warsaw: LOCATION, radium: SUBSTANCE, polonium: SUBSTANCE) and extracts triples (Marie Curie, born_in, Warsaw) and (Marie Curie, discovered, radium), (Marie Curie, discovered, polonium) — these triples could then populate a knowledge graph queryable with 'who discovered radium?'.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.what_it_is: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA), also called opinion mining, identifies specific aspects/features of a product or service mentioned in text and determines the sentiment expressed toward each aspect individually, rather than assigning one overall sentiment to the whole text.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.why_it_exists: Overall sentiment analysis loses crucial information: a review like 'great battery life but the screen is disappointing' is sentiment-mixed — overall sentiment classification might call it 'neutral' or pick one dominant sentiment, hiding that the business needs to know battery=positive, screen=negative separately to prioritise improvements.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.how_it_works: ABSA typically involves (1) aspect term extraction — identifying the specific features/aspects mentioned ('battery life', 'screen', 'price'), often via sequence labelling similar to NER, and (2) aspect-sentiment classification — for each extracted aspect, classifying the sentiment expressed toward it specifically, using the local context around the aspect mention. Modern approaches fine-tune Transformers with the aspect term included in the input (e.g. '[CLS] review text [SEP] aspect: battery life [SEP]') to produce aspect-specific sentiment.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.use_when: Product/service review analysis where actionable, feature-level feedback is needed (which aspects drive satisfaction/dissatisfaction), or any domain where a single document discusses multiple evaluable entities/features with potentially conflicting sentiment.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.avoid_when: Avoid for short texts with a single clear topic and sentiment, where overall sentiment analysis is simpler and sufficient — ABSA adds complexity (aspect extraction + per-aspect classification) that isn't worth it if there's typically only one aspect per document.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.what_goes_wrong: Implicit aspects (sentiment expressed without naming the aspect explicitly, e.g. 'lasted only 2 hours' implies battery life) are missed by extraction methods relying on explicit aspect terms. Aspect categories must often be predefined for a domain (battery, screen, camera, price for phones), requiring domain expertise to build the taxonomy. Sentiment toward one aspect can be expressed via comparison to another ('better camera than my old phone but worse battery'), requiring relational reasoning beyond simple aspect-sentiment pairs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Opinion M.real_example: For the review 'The camera is excellent but battery drains too fast and customer service was unhelpful', an ABSA system extracts three aspect-sentiment pairs: (camera, positive), (battery, negative), (customer service, negative) — giving a product team a precise breakdown that a single overall-sentiment score ('mixed' or 'neutral') would completely obscure.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.what_it_is: Transformer-XL is a Transformer variant that extends the effective context length beyond a fixed segment by introducing a 'segment-level recurrence mechanism' that carries hidden states from previous segments forward, plus relative positional encoding to make this recurrence work correctly.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.why_it_exists: Standard Transformers process fixed-length segments independently (e.g. 512 tokens), with no information flowing across segment boundaries — long documents get artificially chopped, and context from earlier segments is lost ('context fragmentation'). Transformer-XL was designed to let language models attend to information beyond a single fixed-length segment, improving long-document modelling without the quadratic cost of attending over the entire document at once.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.how_it_works: When processing segment t, Transformer-XL caches and reuses the hidden states computed for segment t-1 (without backpropagating through them — they're treated as fixed context, like a memory). Attention in segment t can attend to both the current segment's tokens and the cached hidden states from segment t-1, effectively extending the receptive field across segments. Because absolute positional encodings would be ambiguous when reusing cached states from a 'previous' segment, Transformer-XL introduces relative positional encoding, where attention scores depend on the relative distance between query and key positions rather than absolute positions.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.use_when: Useful conceptually for understanding how long-context handling evolved in Transformers (a precursor to ideas in modern long-context architectures), and historically used for language modelling on long documents where segment-level recurrence improved perplexity over vanilla Transformers with the same segment length.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.avoid_when: Avoid for new projects — modern long-context approaches (RoPE/ALiBi-based models with extended context windows, FlashAttention enabling longer sequences directly, retrieval-augmented approaches) have largely superseded the segment-recurrence approach for practical long-context LLMs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.what_goes_wrong: The cached hidden states are not updated by gradients (stop-gradient), so the 'memory' is a frozen snapshot — it helps provide context but doesn't let the model fully integrate long-range dependencies the way true long-context attention would. The recurrence introduces sequential dependency between segments, somewhat reducing the parallelism advantage that made Transformers attractive over RNNs in the first place.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Transform.real_example: Transformer-XL was shown to achieve significantly better perplexity than a vanilla Transformer with the same 512-token segment length on long-document language modelling benchmarks (e.g. enwik8, WikiText-103), specifically because it could leverage the relative positional encoding + segment recurrence to model dependencies spanning thousands of tokens, despite each individual attention computation staying within a manageable segment size.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.what_it_is: Machine translation (MT) automatically translates text from one language to another. The field evolved from rule-based systems, to Statistical Machine Translation (SMT, phrase-based models using co-occurrence statistics), to Neural Machine Translation (NMT, end-to-end neural sequence-to-sequence models, now Transformer-based).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.why_it_exists: Cross-lingual communication, content localisation, and multilingual information access all require automatic translation at scales no human translator workforce could match. Each generation of MT addressed limitations of the previous: rule-based systems were brittle and required hand-written grammars; SMT learned from parallel corpora but produced disfluent output; NMT produces much more fluent, context-aware translations end-to-end.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.how_it_works: SMT (e.g. phrase-based models like Moses) learns alignment probabilities between source and target phrases from large parallel corpora, then uses a decoder to find the highest-probability target sentence combining phrase translation probabilities and a target-language model. NMT uses an encoder-decoder architecture: the encoder reads the source sentence into representations, and the decoder generates the target sentence token-by-token, attending to the encoder representations (originally RNN-based with attention, now Transformer-based as in the original 'Attention is All You Need' paper, which was specifically designed for translation). Training uses parallel sentence pairs with cross-entropy loss on the target sequence.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.use_when: Any cross-lingual text translation task — modern systems use Transformer-based NMT (and increasingly, multilingual LLMs prompted for translation) almost universally; understanding the SMT-to-NMT evolution is useful for grasping why attention/Transformers were originally developed.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.avoid_when: Avoid SMT for new systems entirely — NMT (and LLM-based translation) outperforms it on fluency and most accuracy metrics with far less manual feature engineering. For low-resource language pairs with very little parallel data, pure NMT may underperform without techniques like back-translation or multilingual transfer.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.what_goes_wrong: NMT can produce fluent but factually wrong translations ('hallucination') — output that reads naturally but doesn't match the source meaning, which is harder to detect than SMT's more obviously broken output. Domain mismatch (training on news, translating legal text) degrades quality. Low-resource language pairs suffer from insufficient parallel training data. Evaluation metrics (BLEU) correlate imperfectly with human judgments of translation quality, especially for fluency vs adequacy trade-offs.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Machine t.real_example: The original Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017, 'Attention is All You Need') was introduced and evaluated specifically on English-to-German and English-to-French translation (WMT datasets), where it achieved state-of-the-art BLEU scores while training significantly faster than RNN-based NMT — the success of Transformers on MT was the direct catalyst for their adoption across all of NLP, including BERT and GPT.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.what_it_is: Text summarisation condenses a document into a shorter version that retains its key information. Extractive summarisation selects and concatenates existing sentences/phrases from the source; abstractive summarisation generates new sentences that paraphrase and condense the content.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.why_it_exists: Long documents (articles, reports, legal contracts, meeting transcripts) are time-consuming to read in full; automatic summarisation lets users quickly grasp the key points, supports downstream applications (search result snippets, digest emails), and helps process large volumes of text (e.g. summarising thousands of customer reviews into key themes).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.how_it_works: Extractive methods score sentences by importance (using features like TF-IDF centrality, position in document, or graph-based methods like TextRank that treat sentences as nodes with similarity-weighted edges and rank by a PageRank-style algorithm) and select the top-N sentences, often reordering for coherence. Abstractive methods use sequence-to-sequence models (originally RNN-based, now Transformer encoder-decoder models like BART, T5, or Pegasus, pretrained specifically with summarisation-like objectives) that read the full document and generate a novel summary token-by-token, potentially using words/phrasings not present in the source.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.use_when: Extractive: when factual accuracy/faithfulness to source wording is critical and some redundancy/lack of fluency is acceptable (legal/medical document highlights). Abstractive: when fluent, concise, human-readable summaries are needed and some paraphrasing risk is acceptable (news digest, meeting notes).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.avoid_when: Avoid abstractive summarisation for high-stakes factual domains without careful hallucination mitigation (legal, medical) — generated summaries can state things not actually in the source. Avoid extractive summarisation when source sentences are individually long/complex — concatenating them may not produce a genuinely 'short' or coherent summary.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.what_goes_wrong: Abstractive models can hallucinate facts not present in the source document, a serious problem for factual domains — this is one of the most cited failure modes of generative summarisation. Extractive summaries can be incoherent when concatenated sentences lack the original transitions/context. Both approaches struggle with very long documents exceeding the model's context window, requiring chunking strategies that can lose cross-chunk information. ROUGE scores (the standard evaluation metric) reward word overlap with reference summaries but don't directly measure factual accuracy or coherence.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Text summ.real_example: Summarising a 10-page research paper: an extractive method (TextRank) might pull the abstract's key sentence plus 2-3 high-centrality sentences from the conclusion verbatim — faithful but potentially disjointed; an abstractive method (fine-tuned BART) generates a flowing paragraph synthesising the contribution, but might (incorrectly) state a specific accuracy number that was actually for a different experiment in the paper — a hallucination that extractive methods structurally cannot produce since they only ever copy real source sentences.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.what_it_is: Question answering (QA) systems automatically answer questions posed in natural language. Extractive QA finds the answer as a span within a given passage; open-domain QA retrieves relevant passages from a large corpus first, then extracts/generates an answer; generative QA produces a free-form answer that may not be a literal span from any source text.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.why_it_exists: Users want direct answers to questions rather than having to read through documents/search results themselves — QA systems power search engine featured snippets, customer support bots, and document-grounded assistants.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.how_it_works: Extractive QA (e.g. fine-tuned BERT on SQuAD): given a (question, passage) pair, the model predicts start and end token positions of the answer span within the passage, using two classification heads over the encoder's token representations. Open-domain QA adds a retrieval step (Dense Passage Retrieval or BM25) to first find relevant passages from a large corpus (e.g. all of Wikipedia), then runs extractive (or generative) QA on the retrieved passages — this retrieve-then-read architecture is the precursor to modern RAG. Generative QA (e.g. T5 fine-tuned on QA, or LLMs) generates the answer as free text token-by-token, which can synthesise information across multiple retrieved passages or rephrase the answer naturally, but isn't constrained to copy exact spans.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.use_when: Extractive QA: when the answer is guaranteed to be a literal span in a given context document (reading-comprehension-style tasks, document Q&A). Open-domain QA: when answers could come from anywhere in a large corpus and retrieval is needed first. Generative QA: when answers require synthesis, rephrasing, or aren't literal spans (e.g. 'summarise the key risks' from multiple documents).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.avoid_when: Avoid extractive QA when no single contiguous span in the source answers the question (the answer requires combining information from multiple places) — generative QA or RAG with a generative reader is needed. Avoid generative QA without retrieval grounding for factual questions — pure generative models hallucinate facts not in any source.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.what_goes_wrong: Extractive QA fails when the question has no exact-span answer in the passage (the model is forced to pick some span anyway, often wrong). Open-domain QA accuracy is bounded by retrieval quality — if the right passage isn't retrieved, even a perfect reader can't answer correctly ('retrieval ceiling'). Generative QA can produce fluent but factually incorrect answers (hallucination), especially for questions outside the model's training distribution or when retrieved context is insufficient/contradictory.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Question.real_example: SQuAD-style extractive QA: given the passage 'The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 and is 330 metres tall', for the question 'How tall is the Eiffel Tower?' the model predicts the span '330 metres' directly from the passage. In contrast, an open-domain RAG system answering 'How tall is the Eiffel Tower?' with no passage given first retrieves relevant Wikipedia passages via dense retrieval, then either extracts or generatively phrases the answer from the retrieved text — the retrieval step is what makes this 'open-domain' versus the closed-passage SQuAD setting.

4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.what_it_is: A Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a probabilistic model for sequences where there's an underlying ('hidden') sequence of states generating observable outputs — used classically for sequence labelling tasks like POS tagging, where hidden states are POS tags and observations are words.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.why_it_exists: Sequence labelling tasks need to assign a label to each element of a sequence while accounting for dependencies between adjacent labels (a verb is more likely to follow a noun than another verb) — HMMs provide a principled probabilistic framework for this 'label depends on neighbouring labels and current observation' structure, with efficient exact inference algorithms.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.how_it_works: An HMM defines: (1) transition probabilities P(tag_i | tag_{i-1}) — how likely one tag follows another, (2) emission probabilities P(word_i | tag_i) — how likely a given word is observed given a tag, and (3) initial state probabilities. Given an observed word sequence, the Viterbi algorithm (dynamic programming) finds the most probable tag sequence in O(n*T^2) time (n=sequence length, T=number of tags) by efficiently considering all tag sequences without enumerating them explicitly. Parameters are estimated from a tagged training corpus via counting (maximum likelihood) or the Baum-Welch algorithm if labels are unobserved.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.use_when: Teaching/understanding the foundations of sequence labelling and the Viterbi algorithm (which remains relevant — CRFs and even neural CRF layers use Viterbi-style decoding), or for lightweight sequence labelling where training data is limited and a simple generative model is preferred.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.avoid_when: Avoid for state-of-the-art sequence labelling — CRFs (which model P(tags|words) directly, discriminatively, and can use arbitrary features) and neural sequence models (BiLSTM-CRF, fine-tuned Transformers) substantially outperform HMMs by using richer features and not making the strong independence assumptions HMMs require.
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.what_goes_wrong: HMMs make a strong Markov assumption (each tag depends only on the immediately preceding tag) and assume emissions depend only on the current tag, ignoring richer context — this limits accuracy compared to models that can use the whole sentence as context. HMMs are generative models (model P(words,tags) and derive P(tags|words) via Bayes' rule), which is generally less accurate for labelling tasks than discriminative models (CRFs, neural networks) that directly model P(tags|words).
4|🟡 T2 Classical NLP|NLP Tasks|Hidden Ma.real_example: A simple bigram HMM POS tagger estimates P(VERB|NOUN) and P(NOUN|DET) from a tagged corpus, then for the sentence 'The dog runs', the Viterbi algorithm finds the tag sequence DET-NOUN-VERB as most probable by combining transition probabilities (DET->NOUN is common, NOUN->VERB is common) with emission probabilities (P('dog'|NOUN) is high, P('runs'|VERB) is high) — achieving reasonable accuracy on common sentence patterns, though a modern BiLSTM-CRF or Transformer tagger would handle ambiguous cases ('The old man the boat') far better by using full-sentence context.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Scaled dot-product attention is the core computation of the Transformer: for each query, compute similarity (dot product) with all keys, scale by 1/sqrt(d_k), apply softmax to get attention weights, then take a weighted sum of the values — formula: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Attention lets every token directly look at every other token in a sequence and weight their contributions by relevance, replacing the sequential bottleneck of RNNs. The scaling factor sqrt(d_k) exists because without it, dot products grow large in magnitude as dimensionality d_k increases, pushing softmax into regions with extremely small gradients (saturation), which destabilises training.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: Q (queries), K (keys), V (values) are matrices of shape (seq_len, d_k) derived by linear projections of the input. QK^T computes a (seq_len x seq_len) matrix of raw similarity scores between every pair of positions. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the variance of these scores roughly constant regardless of d_k (since the dot product of two random d_k-dimensional vectors has variance proportional to d_k). Softmax over each row converts scores to a probability distribution (attention weights) summing to 1. Multiplying by V produces, for each query position, a weighted combination of all value vectors — the output representation for that position.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: This is the foundational operation inside every Transformer layer (encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention, cross-attention) — used whenever you need each position to aggregate information from other positions based on learned relevance.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Not applicable as a 'choice' — it's the default attention formulation. The main design choices layered on top (masking, multi-head, relative position encodings) are what vary; the scaled-dot-product core itself is near-universal in Transformer architectures.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: Without the sqrt(d_k) scaling, large d_k causes dot products to have high variance, pushing softmax inputs to extremes where gradients vanish (softmax saturates near 0/1), making training unstable or slow to converge. Numerical precision issues (especially in fp16/bf16) can cause softmax overflow for very large attention scores without careful implementation (subtracting the max before exponentiating). The O(n^2) cost in sequence length n is the fundamental scalability bottleneck that FlashAttention and sparse-attention variants address.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: In the original 'Attention is All You Need' paper, d_k=64 per head; without the 1/sqrt(64)=1/8 scaling factor, dot products of 64-dimensional vectors with unit-variance components have variance ~64, making softmax outputs nearly one-hot (extremely peaked) from the start of training — the scaling keeps the initial attention distribution closer to uniform, allowing gradients to flow and the model to gradually learn which positions to attend to.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Q (Query), K (Key), and V (Value) are three learned linear projections of the same input representations, used in attention to determine 'what am I looking for' (Q), 'what do I contain/offer' (K), and 'what information do I provide if attended to' (V).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Using a single representation for all three roles would conflate 'how relevant is this token to others' (matching, Q/K) with 'what content does this token contribute' (V) — separating them into distinct learned projections gives the model more expressive freedom: the criteria for matching (Q/K) can differ from the information actually retrieved (V).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: Given input embeddings X (seq_len x d_model), three separate weight matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V (each d_model x d_k) project X into Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, V=XW_V. The dot product Q.K^T measures compatibility between a query position's 'search criteria' and a key position's 'identity/label' — high compatibility means that key's value should contribute more to the query's output. V is then the actual content retrieved. The analogy: a database lookup where Q is your search term, K is the indexed field you're matching against, and V is the record content returned.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Understanding/implementing any attention mechanism — this Q/K/V decomposition is the conceptual building block for self-attention, cross-attention, and all attention variants.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Not a 'when to use' choice — it's a core architectural primitive. The relevant design questions are about head count, dimensions per head, and whether Q/K/V come from the same sequence (self-attention) or different sequences (cross-attention).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: A common misconception is treating Q, K, V as conceptually identical just because in self-attention they're all derived from the same input X — they are different learned projections with different roles, and the model learns distinct W_Q/W_K/W_V during training. Dimension mismatches (d_k for Q/K must match for the dot product; d_v for V can differ) are a common implementation bug. Sharing weights across Q/K (as some efficient-attention variants do) changes the model's expressivity and must be a deliberate design choice, not an accident.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: In self-attention for the sentence 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired', when computing the output for the token 'it', its Query vector encodes 'I need to find what I refer to'; the Key vectors for 'animal' and 'street' encode their respective identities; the dot product Q_it . K_animal ends up higher than Q_it . K_street (learned through training on data where this resolution pattern is consistent), so V_animal contributes more to the output representation of 'it' — this is how attention implicitly performs coreference-like resolution.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Multi-head attention runs h independent attention computations ('heads') in parallel, each with its own learned Q/K/V projections into a smaller dimension (d_model/h), then concatenates all heads' outputs and applies a final linear projection back to d_model.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: A single attention computation can only capture one 'type' of relationship per position (one weighted average). Multiple heads let the model simultaneously attend to different aspects of the input — e.g. one head might track syntactic dependencies, another might track coreference, another might focus on adjacent tokens — without these different relationship types interfering with each other in a single weighted average.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: Input X (seq_len x d_model) is projected by h different sets of W_Q^i, W_K^i, W_V^i (each producing d_k = d_model/h dimensional Q/K/V), and scaled dot-product attention is computed independently for each head i, producing head_i output of shape (seq_len x d_k). All h outputs are concatenated along the feature dimension back to (seq_len x d_model), then passed through a final linear layer W_O (d_model x d_model) to mix information across heads.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Standard in every Transformer layer — the choice of h (number of heads) is a hyperparameter trading off per-head dimensionality vs number of distinct 'attention patterns' the model can learn simultaneously (common values: 8, 12, 16, 32, with larger models using more heads).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Not really an avoidable component, but extremely high head counts with very small per-head dimensions (d_k too small, e.g. <32) can hurt each head's ability to represent meaningful relationships — there's a practical lower bound on useful d_k.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: Research has found that many attention heads in trained Transformers are redundant or can be pruned with minimal performance loss, suggesting multi-head attention is often over-parameterised relative to what's strictly needed (motivating techniques like Multi-Query Attention and Grouped-Query Attention that share K/V across heads to reduce memory). Interpreting individual heads as having clean, consistent 'roles' (this head = syntax, that head = coreference) is appealing but often only partially true — many heads have mixed or unclear functions.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: In BERT-base (12 heads per layer, d_model=768, so d_k=64 per head), visualisation studies (e.g. BertViz) show some heads consistently attending to the previous/next token (local context), some heads attending broadly across the sentence, and some heads specialising in syntactic relations like attending from a verb to its direct object — these different specialised patterns coexist because each head computes attention independently before being concatenated and mixed by W_O.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Masked (causal) self-attention restricts each position to only attend to itself and earlier positions in the sequence, preventing it from 'seeing' future tokens — essential for autoregressive generation where the model must predict each token using only previously generated context.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Decoder-only models (GPT-style) are trained to predict the next token given all previous tokens. If attention could see future tokens during training, the model could trivially 'cheat' by copying the answer it's supposed to predict, making the training objective meaningless and the model unusable for actual left-to-right generation at inference (where future tokens don't exist yet).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: Before applying softmax to the QK^T attention score matrix, a mask is added that sets all positions (i,j) where j > i (future positions relative to query position i) to negative infinity. After softmax, these masked positions become exactly 0 — so position i's output is a weighted combination of only values from positions 0 through i. This is implemented efficiently as a single additive mask (an upper-triangular matrix of -inf) applied to the score matrix before softmax, allowing the entire sequence to still be processed in parallel during training (teacher forcing) while respecting causality.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Any decoder-only autoregressive model (GPT, LLaMA, etc.) for language generation, or the decoder side of an encoder-decoder model (T5, BART) when generating output tokens one at a time.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Don't use causal masking in encoder-only models (BERT) where bidirectional context is desired and there's no autoregressive generation constraint — masking would needlessly restrict the encoder's ability to use full-sentence context for tasks like classification or NER.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting the causal mask during training of a generative model causes 'information leakage' — the model learns to attend to future tokens during training (where they're available via teacher forcing) but at inference those tokens don't exist, causing a severe train/inference mismatch and degenerate generation. Implementing the mask incorrectly (off-by-one in the triangular boundary) can leak exactly one future token, a subtle bug that may not be obvious from training loss alone but corrupts generation quality.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: When GPT-2 processes the prompt 'The cat sat on the', causal masking ensures that when computing the representation used to predict the next token, position 'the' (the last token) can attend to 'The', 'cat', 'sat', 'on', 'the' (positions 0-4, all <= its own position 4) but the mask sets attention scores to positions 5+ (which don't exist yet at inference, and would be 'future' tokens during training) to -inf — guaranteeing the prediction for position 5 ('mat') is based purely on the preceding context, matching exactly how generation works at inference time token-by-token.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Cross-attention is an attention mechanism where queries come from one sequence (typically the decoder) while keys and values come from a different sequence (typically the encoder's output) — allowing the decoder to 'look up' relevant information from the source sequence at each generation step.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: In encoder-decoder architectures (translation, summarisation), the decoder needs to condition its output generation on the full input sequence (e.g. the source-language sentence being translated), not just on previously generated output tokens. Cross-attention provides the mechanism for the decoder to dynamically focus on different parts of the encoder's representation as it generates each output token.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: In each decoder layer, after the causal self-attention sub-layer (which lets the decoder attend to its own previously generated tokens), a cross-attention sub-layer computes Q from the decoder's current hidden states but K and V from the encoder's final output representations. This lets each decoder position compute attention weights over all source positions and retrieve a weighted combination of source representations — effectively a learned, soft, dynamic alignment between target and source tokens (the neural successor to explicit word-alignment models in SMT).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Any encoder-decoder (sequence-to-sequence) Transformer: machine translation (T5, original Transformer), summarisation (BART), and any task where the output must be grounded in/conditioned on a separate input sequence rather than purely autoregressive continuation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Not applicable to decoder-only architectures (GPT-style) which have no separate encoder — they use only causal self-attention. Don't use cross-attention when the 'context' to condition on can simply be prepended to the input sequence and handled via self-attention instead (as decoder-only LLMs do, e.g. putting a document and a question both in the prompt).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: Cross-attention adds computational cost (another attention sub-layer per decoder layer, with cost proportional to source_len x target_len). If the encoder's representations are poor (e.g. the encoder hasn't adequately captured some part of a long source document), cross-attention has nothing useful to retrieve, and the decoder may generate fluent but ungrounded text. Visualisation of cross-attention weights is often used for interpretability (alignment visualisation in translation), but attention weights don't always correspond to true 'importance' in a causally meaningful sense.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: In a T5 model translating 'The cat sat on the mat' to French, when generating the French word for 'mat' ('tapis'), the decoder's cross-attention weights at that generation step are typically highest on the encoder's representation of 'mat' in the source sentence — the decoder is 'looking up' the relevant source-side information at each step, similar to how a human translator re-reads the relevant part of the source sentence while writing each word of the translation.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Sinusoidal positional encoding is the original Transformer's method for injecting position information into token representations: each position is assigned a fixed vector computed from sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, added to the token embedding.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Self-attention itself is permutation-invariant — without position information, the attention mechanism treats input as an unordered set, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would produce identical representations. Positional encoding injects order information so the model can distinguish token positions.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: For position pos and dimension index i (0 to d_model/2 - 1), PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)) — different dimensions oscillate at different frequencies, from very fast (low i) to very slow (high i). This vector is added element-wise to the token's embedding before the first Transformer layer. The sinusoidal design has a useful property: PE(pos+k) can be expressed as a linear function of PE(pos), which the authors hypothesised would help the model learn to attend by relative position.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Historically used in the original Transformer for translation; conceptually useful for understanding why position encoding is needed at all, and as a fixed (non-learned, no extra parameters) encoding that can in principle generalise to sequence lengths longer than seen during training (since it's a deterministic function of position, not a learned lookup table).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Largely superseded in modern LLMs by relative position encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) which generalise better to longer sequences and integrate position information directly into the attention computation rather than just additively at the input. Avoid for tasks requiring strong extrapolation to much longer sequences than seen in training — empirically, sinusoidal encoding's theoretical extrapolation benefit doesn't hold up well in practice.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: In practice, despite the theoretical claim that sinusoidal encodings could extrapolate to unseen lengths, models trained with sinusoidal PE often generalise poorly to sequences longer than the training length — the additive combination with token embeddings means position information can get diluted or entangled with content information through the network's layers. This was a major motivation for developing RoPE and ALiBi.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: The original 'Attention is All You Need' Transformer used sinusoidal positional encoding added to input embeddings before the encoder/decoder stacks; subsequent research (and the move to RoPE in LLaMA, GPT-NeoX, etc.) showed that encoding relative position directly within the attention score computation (rather than as an additive input bias) produces models that handle longer contexts and position-sensitive tasks more robustly.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: Learned positional encoding represents each position (0, 1, 2, ..., max_len-1) with its own trainable embedding vector, looked up from an embedding table and added to the token embedding — analogous to word embeddings but indexed by position instead of word identity.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Rather than committing to a fixed mathematical function (sinusoidal) for position representations, learned positional embeddings let the model discover whatever position representation works best for the data via gradient descent — simple to implement (just another embedding table) and used by models like BERT and GPT-2.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: A position embedding matrix of shape (max_seq_len, d_model) is initialised (often randomly) and trained jointly with all other model parameters. For an input sequence, position i's embedding (row i of this matrix) is added to token i's word embedding before the first Transformer layer. The model learns through training which position-dependent adjustments help the task.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: When the maximum sequence length is known and fixed in advance (BERT: 512, GPT-2: 1024), and training data is sufficient to learn good position representations across that full range.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Avoid when you need to handle sequences longer than the maximum length seen during training — learned positional embeddings have no representation for positions beyond max_seq_len (a hard architectural limit), unlike relative encodings (RoPE/ALiBi) which can extrapolate or be designed for length generalisation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: The model cannot process any sequence longer than the positional embedding table's size — position max_seq_len+1 simply has no embedding, causing an index error or requiring truncation. Positions near the maximum length may be seen less frequently during training (if most training examples are shorter), leading to poorly-trained embeddings for those positions and degraded performance near the context limit. Extending context length later (e.g. via fine-tuning with interpolated position embeddings) requires careful handling.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: BERT-base has a learned position embedding table of shape (512, 768) — any input longer than 512 tokens must be truncated or chunked, because position 513 has no corresponding learned embedding; this hard 512-token limit was a long-standing practical constraint for applying BERT to long documents, motivating later models (Longformer, BigBird) that use sparse attention plus different position encoding schemes to handle longer contexts.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) encodes positional information by rotating the Query and Key vectors in 2D subspaces by an angle proportional to their position, such that the dot product between a query at position m and a key at position n depends only on their relative distance (m-n), not their absolute positions.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Absolute positional encodings (sinusoidal or learned) get added once at the input and must be 'remembered' through all subsequent layers, and don't generalise well to sequence lengths beyond training. RoPE instead bakes relative position directly into every attention computation via rotation, giving better length generalisation and is the dominant choice in modern open-weight LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, etc.).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: Each Q and K vector is split into pairs of dimensions, and each pair is treated as a 2D coordinate that gets rotated by an angle theta * position, where theta differs across dimension-pairs (similar frequency-spectrum idea to sinusoidal encoding — different pairs rotate at different rates). When computing Q_m . K_n (dot product for attention), the rotation by position m and position n combine such that the result depends only on (m-n) — the relative offset — due to the rotation matrices' composition properties (rotating by m then by -n is equivalent to rotating by m-n). No extra parameters or additive terms — position information is applied via the Q/K projections themselves.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Default choice for modern decoder-only LLMs (LLaMA family, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, GPT-NeoX) — gives good relative-position modelling and is compatible with techniques for context-length extension (RoPE scaling/interpolation methods like YaRN, NTK-aware scaling) that let pretrained models handle longer contexts than they were trained on.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Not generally avoided in modern LLM design — it's close to a default. Encoder models with fixed, known sequence lengths and no need for length extrapolation (classic BERT-style use cases) may stick with learned absolute embeddings for simplicity/legacy compatibility, but new architectures broadly favour RoPE or ALiBi.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: RoPE's relative-position property degrades for positions much larger than seen during training (the rotation angles for very large position indices weren't well-represented during training), causing a documented 'context length extrapolation' problem — directly running a model far beyond its trained context length produces degraded outputs unless RoPE-scaling techniques (linear interpolation, NTK-aware/YaRN scaling) are applied. Implementation bugs in the rotation (wrong dimension pairing, wrong theta base) silently corrupt position information without an obvious error.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: LLaMA-2 was trained with RoPE at a 4096-token context length; extending it to 32K+ tokens (as done in LLaMA-2-Long and similar fine-tunes) required RoPE-scaling techniques that adjust the rotation frequencies (theta base) so that relative positions within the extended range fall into a similar numerical regime as during original training — a direct practical application of understanding RoPE's mechanics for context extension.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) encodes position information by adding a penalty to attention scores that grows linearly with the distance between query and key positions, with no positional embeddings added to the input at all.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: ALiBi was designed specifically to enable training on shorter sequences while generalising well to much longer sequences at inference ('train short, test long') — a property that both sinusoidal and learned absolute positional encodings, and even RoPE to a lesser extent, struggle with.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: For attention from query position i to key position j (where j <= i due to causal masking), ALiBi subtracts a penalty m * (i - j) from the raw attention score before softmax, where m is a head-specific slope (different heads get different fixed slopes, geometrically spaced, e.g. 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... so different heads have different 'effective ranges'). This means tokens further away are always penalised more, with no learned parameters for position at all — just a fixed linear bias added to QK^T before softmax.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Models needing strong length extrapolation — train on shorter sequences (cheaper) and deploy on longer ones at inference with minimal quality degradation. Used in models like BLOOM and MPT.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: If extreme length extrapolation isn't a requirement and the application always operates within the training context length, the simplicity benefit of ALiBi is less critical, and RoPE (now more widely supported in tooling/kernels) may be preferred for compatibility with the broader ecosystem.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: The fixed linear distance penalty is a strong inductive bias toward 'recency' (nearby tokens matter more), which may not always be appropriate for tasks where a distant token (e.g. a definition at the start of a long document) is critically important regardless of distance — ALiBi's bias works well empirically but is a hard constraint baked into the architecture, less flexible than fully learned relative position schemes for tasks that violate the recency assumption.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: A model trained with ALiBi on 2048-token sequences can be evaluated on 8192-token sequences with substantially better perplexity retention than an equivalent model trained with learned absolute position embeddings (which simply has no representation for positions beyond 2048) — this 'train short, test long' property was the key empirical result motivating ALiBi's adoption in models like BLOOM (176B parameters, trained partly to keep compute costs manageable while supporting longer contexts at inference).

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: FlashAttention is an algorithm that computes exact (mathematically identical) scaled dot-product attention faster and with much less memory by reordering computation to minimise reads/writes between GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and fast on-chip SRAM, rather than approximating attention.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Standard attention implementations materialise the full (seq_len x seq_len) attention score matrix in GPU HBM, which is both memory-intensive (O(n^2)) and slow because moving data between HBM and the GPU's compute units (SRAM) is the actual bottleneck — not the FLOPs themselves. FlashAttention was designed to be 'IO-aware': minimise memory movement while computing the exact same result.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: FlashAttention uses tiling/blocking: it processes the attention computation in blocks small enough to fit in fast SRAM, computing partial softmax statistics incrementally using the 'online softmax' technique (maintaining running max and sum to avoid needing the full row before normalising), and never materialises the full n x n attention matrix in HBM. The backward pass similarly avoids storing the full attention matrix by recomputing necessary values from saved statistics, trading a small amount of extra compute for a large reduction in memory traffic.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Essentially always, when training or running inference with Transformers on GPUs that support it — it's a drop-in replacement for standard attention that produces numerically identical (or near-identical) results with 2-4x speedup and dramatically reduced memory usage, enabling longer context lengths and larger batch sizes.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Only relevant constraint is hardware/kernel support — older GPUs or certain hardware/software combinations may not have optimised FlashAttention kernels available, and some custom attention variants (heavily modified attention patterns) may not have a corresponding FlashAttention implementation yet, requiring fallback to standard attention.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: Because FlashAttention changes the low-level computation order (though mathematically equivalent), bugs in custom attention-masking logic that worked with naive attention can behave unexpectedly if not correctly adapted to FlashAttention's API (e.g. custom mask formats). Numerical results can differ in the last few bits of precision due to different summation orders (generally not an issue, but can occasionally cause test flakiness in exact-reproduction checks).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: Training a Transformer with a 2048-token context using standard attention might require ~16x more memory for the attention matrices than FlashAttention for the same batch size — in practice, switching to FlashAttention (e.g. via PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention with the flash backend, or the flash-attn library) lets practitioners either train with 2-4x larger batch sizes/longer sequences on the same GPU, or simply get a 2-4x wall-clock speedup with no change to model quality, which is why it's now the default in virtually all modern LLM training/inference stacks.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: The KV cache stores the Key and Value vectors computed for all previously generated tokens during autoregressive decoding, so that generating each new token only requires computing Q/K/V for that one new token rather than recomputing K/V for the entire sequence so far.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: In autoregressive generation, each new token's causal self-attention needs K and V from all previous positions. Without caching, generating token t would require recomputing K and V for tokens 1..t-1 (which haven't changed) every single step — wasting enormous amounts of redundant computation for long generations.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: After computing K and V for a token during generation, they're stored in a cache (per layer, per attention head). When generating the next token, only the new token's Q, K, V are computed; the new K and V are appended to the cache; attention for the new token's Q is computed against the full cached K/V (old + new). This turns each generation step's attention cost from O(t^2) (recompute everything) to O(t) (attend to cached history with one new query), making the total generation cost O(n^2) instead of O(n^3) for an n-token sequence.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: Universal for autoregressive decoder inference — virtually all LLM serving systems (vLLM, TGI, llama.cpp, transformers' generate()) use KV caching by default for any multi-token generation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Not applicable during training (where the full sequence is processed in parallel with teacher forcing, so there's no sequential generation to cache for) — KV caching is purely an inference-time optimisation for autoregressive generation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: KV cache memory grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, and for large models/long contexts can exceed the model weights' memory footprint itself — this is the primary memory bottleneck for serving long-context LLMs at scale, motivating techniques like Multi-Query Attention/Grouped-Query Attention (shrink the cache by sharing K/V across heads) and PagedAttention (manage cache memory more efficiently). A naive implementation that doesn't properly cache (recomputing from scratch each step) makes generation prohibitively slow for anything beyond short outputs — O(n^3) vs O(n^2) total cost is a massive practical difference for n in the thousands.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: Generating a 1000-token response with a 7B-parameter model: with KV caching, each new token requires one forward pass through the new token only (~constant work per step, attending to the growing cache); without caching, generating token 1000 would require reprocessing all 999 previous tokens through every layer — a ~1000x difference in redundant computation by the final tokens, which is why KV caching is considered non-negotiable for practical LLM serving.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_it_is: PagedAttention is a memory management technique (introduced by the vLLM serving system) that manages the KV cache using fixed-size blocks ('pages'), similar to how operating systems manage virtual memory with paging — avoiding memory fragmentation and enabling efficient sharing of KV cache across requests.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.why_it_exists: Naive KV cache allocation reserves a contiguous memory buffer for each request sized for the maximum possible sequence length, but actual generation lengths vary widely and aren't known in advance — this causes massive memory waste (internal fragmentation) and prevents memory sharing between requests (e.g. for shared prompt prefixes in batch serving), severely limiting the number of concurrent requests a GPU can serve.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.how_it_works: Instead of one contiguous buffer per sequence, the KV cache for each sequence is stored as a list of fixed-size blocks (pages), which can be allocated non-contiguously in GPU memory — analogous to OS virtual memory pages. A block table (like a page table) maps logical positions to physical blocks. This allows: (1) near-zero internal fragmentation since blocks are allocated on demand as generation proceeds, (2) memory sharing — multiple sequences with identical prefixes (e.g. the same system prompt across many requests, or parallel sampling/beam search branches from a shared prefix) can share the same physical blocks via copy-on-write, drastically reducing memory for high-throughput serving.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.use_when: High-throughput LLM serving systems handling many concurrent requests with variable output lengths and/or shared prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples, beam search/parallel sampling) — this is the core innovation behind vLLM's throughput advantages.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.avoid_when: Less relevant for single-request, offline batch-of-one inference where memory fragmentation/sharing across requests isn't a concern — the added complexity of block management provides little benefit if there's no multi-request memory contention to manage.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.what_goes_wrong: Implementing custom attention kernels that work with the non-contiguous, block-based KV cache layout (rather than a simple contiguous tensor) is significantly more complex than standard attention — vLLM had to write custom CUDA kernels for PagedAttention specifically. Block size choice trades off fragmentation (smaller blocks = less waste but more management overhead) against kernel efficiency (larger blocks = better memory throughput per access).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Attention Mechanism|.real_example: Serving many concurrent chat requests that all share the same long system prompt (e.g. a 1000-token instruction prefix): with PagedAttention, the KV cache blocks for that shared prefix are computed once and referenced (copy-on-write) by all requests' block tables, rather than each request storing its own redundant copy of the same 1000 tokens' KV cache — this sharing, combined with reduced fragmentation, is a major reason vLLM achieves substantially higher serving throughput than naive HuggingFace transformers.generate() in production deployments.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.what_it_is: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is pretrained on two self-supervised objectives: Masked Language Modelling (MLM) — randomly mask 15% of input tokens and predict them from bidirectional context — and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) — predict whether two given sentences are consecutive in the original text.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.why_it_exists: Standard left-to-right language modelling (GPT-style) only lets each token see leftward context, but many NLP tasks (classification, NER, QA) benefit from understanding a token's full bidirectional context. MLM enables bidirectional pretraining by hiding tokens and forcing the model to use both left and right context to predict them. NSP was added to give the model some notion of inter-sentence relationships, useful for tasks like QA and NLI that involve sentence pairs.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.how_it_works: For MLM: 15% of input tokens are selected; of those, 80% are replaced with a [MASK] token, 10% with a random token, and 10% left unchanged — this mixture prevents the model from only learning to predict [MASK] tokens specifically (since at fine-tuning time there's no [MASK] token) and forces it to maintain good representations for all tokens, not just ones it expects to be masked. The model predicts the original token at each masked position via a softmax over the vocabulary, using bidirectional self-attention (no causal mask) so every position can attend to all others. For NSP: training examples are pairs of sentences A and B, where 50% of the time B truly follows A and 50% of the time B is a random sentence; the [CLS] token's final representation is fed to a binary classifier predicting IsNext/NotNext.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.use_when: Conceptually relevant for understanding how to pretrain bidirectional encoder representations from unlabelled text, and as the historical foundation that RoBERTa, ALBERT, DeBERTa, etc. all build on and modify.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.avoid_when: Don't use BERT's exact pretraining recipe for new models — RoBERTa demonstrated NSP contributes little/nothing and removing it (with better-tuned MLM and more data) improves downstream performance; new pretraining should follow more modern recipes (RoBERTa-style or ELECTRA-style).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.what_goes_wrong: The 15% masking rate creates a train/inference mismatch: during pretraining the model constantly sees [MASK] tokens, but at fine-tuning/inference time there's no masking, so the 80/10/10 corruption scheme exists specifically to mitigate (but not fully eliminate) this discrepancy. NSP's negative examples (random sentence pairs) are 'too easy' — the model can often distinguish them via topic/style alone rather than genuine coherence understanding, making NSP a weak training signal (this is exactly RoBERTa's finding).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|BERT pre.real_example: For the input 'The [MASK] sat on the mat', BERT's bidirectional self-attention lets the masked position attend to both 'The' (left context) and 'sat on the mat' (right context) simultaneously when predicting the masked word ('cat'), something a left-to-right GPT-style model fundamentally cannot do for that position — this bidirectionality is precisely why BERT excels at understanding-focused tasks like classification and NER, while GPT excels at generation.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.what_it_is: BERT's encoder architecture applies self-attention without any causal mask, so every token's representation is computed using context from both preceding AND following tokens in the sequence — the entire input is processed bidirectionally/non-causally.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.why_it_exists: For understanding-focused tasks (is this review positive? what entity type is this word? what's the answer to this question given this passage?), the model benefits from seeing the full context of a word — both what comes before and after — rather than being artificially restricted to only leftward context as autoregressive models are.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.how_it_works: Each Transformer encoder layer's self-attention computes QK^T over the full sequence with no masking — position i's attention can include positions j < i, j = i, and j > i. Stacking multiple such layers means each token's final representation is influenced by the entire input sequence, with information flowing in both directions through the network. This is fundamentally different from causal self-attention (used in GPT decoders), where position i can only attend to positions <= i.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.use_when: Any task where the full input is available at once and the goal is to produce a representation/classification/labelling based on the complete context: text classification, NER, extractive QA, sentence-pair tasks (NLI, similarity).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.avoid_when: Avoid for autoregressive generation tasks — a bidirectional encoder cannot generate text token-by-token (it has no notion of 'what comes next' since it assumes the whole sequence is given), which is why BERT is not used as a standalone text generator (encoder-decoder or decoder-only architectures are needed for generation).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.what_goes_wrong: Using a bidirectional encoder for a generation task by naively removing the causal mask during 'generation' breaks the autoregressive factorisation — the model would need the future tokens it's supposed to be predicting as input, which is circular/impossible at inference. This is a common conceptual confusion for newcomers: 'why can't I just use BERT to write text?' — the answer is that BERT's training and architecture fundamentally assume the full sequence is observed.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Bidirect.real_example: For sentiment classification of 'The film started slow but the ending was incredible', BERT's [CLS] token representation is computed via bidirectional attention that incorporates 'incredible' (near the end) when forming the representation used for classification — even though [CLS] is the first token, bidirectional self-attention lets it 'see' the entire sentence including later tokens, which is essential for correctly weighing the overall (positive) sentiment despite the early negative cue ('slow').

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.what_it_is: The standard way to adapt a pretrained BERT model to a downstream classification task: add a small task-specific layer (typically a single linear layer + softmax/sigmoid) on top of the [CLS] token's final hidden representation, then fine-tune the entire model (pretrained weights + new head) end-to-end on labelled task data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.why_it_exists: BERT's pretraining produces general-purpose contextual representations, but doesn't itself produce task-specific outputs (e.g. a sentiment label). The [CLS] token (prepended to every input during pretraining, originally for NSP) acts as an aggregate representation of the whole input, making it a natural 'summary vector' to feed into a small classifier head for sentence/sentence-pair classification tasks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.how_it_works: Input is tokenised as [CLS] token1 token2 ... [SEP] (and for pair tasks, [SEP] token1' token2' ... [SEP]). After passing through all Transformer layers, the [CLS] position's final hidden vector (size d_model, e.g. 768 for BERT-base) is fed into a new linear layer mapping to num_labels logits, followed by softmax (multi-class) or sigmoid (multi-label/binary). During fine-tuning, gradients flow back through this new head AND all of BERT's pretrained parameters, typically with a small learning rate (e.g. 2e-5) for a few epochs (2-4) to avoid catastrophic forgetting of pretrained knowledge.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.use_when: Sentence/document classification (sentiment, topic), sentence-pair tasks (NLI, paraphrase detection, semantic similarity classification) — any task with a single fixed-size output per input that can be derived from one summary vector.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.avoid_when: Avoid [CLS]-based heads for token-level tasks (NER, POS tagging) — those need a classification head applied to EVERY token's representation, not just [CLS]. Avoid for extractive QA — that needs start/end span prediction heads over all token positions, not a single [CLS] vector.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.what_goes_wrong: Using too high a learning rate or too many epochs causes catastrophic forgetting — the pretrained representations degrade toward overfitting the small fine-tuning dataset, losing general language understanding (a phenomenon sometimes visible as good training loss but poor generalisation). For very small fine-tuning datasets, the new head's random initialisation combined with full fine-tuning can be unstable across random seeds (a well-documented issue — BERT fine-tuning results can vary significantly run-to-run on small datasets like RTE in GLUE).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.real_example: For sentiment classification on SST-2 (binary positive/negative), bert-base-uncased + a new nn.Linear(768, 2) head on [CLS], fine-tuned for 3 epochs at learning rate 2e-5 with the AutoModelForSequenceClassification API, typically reaches ~92-93% accuracy — the [CLS] representation, having been refined through fine-tuning to encode sentiment-relevant information (not just NSP-relevant information from pretraining), becomes a good summary vector for the binary classifier.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.what_it_is: RoBERTa (Robustly optimised BERT approach) is a re-examination and re-training of BERT's pretraining recipe: same architecture, but removes the Next Sentence Prediction objective, trains with much larger batches and more data for longer, uses dynamic masking, and tunes other hyperparameters — yielding substantially better downstream performance with the same architecture.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.why_it_exists: BERT's original training recipe was under-tuned — RoBERTa's authors showed that BERT was significantly undertrained, and that several design choices (NSP, static masking, small batches, limited data) were either unhelpful or actively suboptimal. RoBERTa demonstrates that pretraining recipe/scale matters as much as architecture.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.how_it_works: Key changes from BERT: (1) Remove NSP entirely — train only on MLM, using full sentences/documents packed into the input rather than sentence-pairs with the artificial NSP framing. (2) Dynamic masking — generate a new random mask each time a sequence is seen during training (BERT used a fixed mask precomputed once), giving more diverse training signal. (3) Much larger batch sizes (8K sequences) and more training data (160GB vs BERT's 16GB) and longer training. (4) Byte-level BPE tokenizer instead of WordPiece. All other architectural details (Transformer encoder, MLM objective itself) remain the same as BERT.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.use_when: As a drop-in upgrade for BERT in virtually any encoder-based application — roberta-base/roberta-large consistently outperform bert-base/bert-large on GLUE and most downstream tasks with the same fine-tuning procedure, for the same or similar compute cost at inference.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.avoid_when: If you specifically need BERT's exact tokenizer/vocabulary for compatibility with existing BERT-based tooling or pretrained checkpoints in a pipeline, switching to RoBERTa requires retokenising/reprocessing data (different vocab). For extremely resource-constrained settings, RoBERTa-large's increased training data requirements (if pretraining from scratch) are a consideration, though using pretrained checkpoints sidesteps this.
