4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.what_goes_wrong: RoBERTa's findings ('NSP doesn't help, dynamic masking and more data/compute do') are sometimes mis-cited as 'NSP is always useless' — for very specific sentence-pair-relationship tasks, some inter-sentence pretraining signal could in principle help, though RoBERTa's specific NSP formulation wasn't the right way to provide it (later models like ALBERT use Sentence Order Prediction instead, which proved more useful). Fine-tuning RoBERTa requires care with its byte-level BPE tokenizer's whitespace handling, which differs subtly from BERT's WordPiece.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|RoBERTa.real_example: On the GLUE benchmark, roberta-large outperforms bert-large by several points on average despite using the exact same Transformer encoder architecture — the entire improvement comes from pretraining recipe changes (more data, longer training, dynamic masking, no NSP), a result that significantly influenced subsequent pretraining research to focus heavily on data scale and training recipe rather than just architectural novelty.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.what_it_is: DistilBERT is a compressed version of BERT produced via knowledge distillation: a smaller 'student' model (6 layers vs BERT's 12) is trained to mimic the behaviour of the full BERT 'teacher' model, achieving ~40% fewer parameters and ~60% faster inference while retaining ~97% of BERT's performance on language understanding benchmarks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.why_it_exists: Full-size BERT models are expensive to run in production (latency, memory, cost), especially at scale or on edge devices. Knowledge distillation provides a way to compress a large pretrained model into a smaller one that retains most of its capability, by training the small model to match the large model's output distributions rather than training from scratch on raw data alone.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.how_it_works: DistilBERT is initialised by taking every other layer from BERT-base (6 of 12 layers) and pretrained using a distillation loss that combines: (1) a soft-label cross-entropy between the student's and teacher's MLM output distributions (matching the teacher's full probability distribution over the vocabulary, not just the single correct answer — this 'soft target' carries more information than a one-hot label), (2) the standard MLM loss on the true labels, and (3) a cosine-embedding loss aligning the student's and teacher's hidden state directions. The student is trained on the same unlabelled corpus as BERT, learning to replicate the teacher's behaviour.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.use_when: Production deployments where inference latency/cost/memory matters and a small accuracy trade-off (typically 1-3 points on benchmarks) is acceptable — mobile/edge deployment, high-throughput services, or as a faster baseline during development/experimentation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.avoid_when: Avoid when maximum accuracy is required and compute/latency is not the binding constraint — the full teacher model (or an even larger one) will outperform the distilled student. Avoid distillation as a substitute for proper task-specific fine-tuning data — distillation transfers the teacher's general language understanding, but task performance still depends on fine-tuning quality.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.what_goes_wrong: The distilled model inherits any biases or blind spots present in the teacher model — distillation doesn't 'fix' the teacher's weaknesses, only compresses its overall behaviour (including weaknesses). Performance gaps between teacher and student can widen on harder/out-of-distribution tasks even if average benchmark scores look close. Choosing which layers to retain from the teacher (every other layer) is itself a design choice that affects which 'capabilities' transfer best.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DistilBE.real_example: distilbert-base-uncased retains 97% of bert-base-uncased's performance on the GLUE benchmark while being 40% smaller (66M vs 110M parameters) and running about 60% faster on CPU — making it a popular choice for production sentiment analysis, text classification APIs, and other latency-sensitive services where the small accuracy trade-off is worth the substantial efficiency gain.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.what_it_is: ALBERT (A Lite BERT) reduces BERT's parameter count dramatically through two techniques — factorised embedding parameterisation and cross-layer parameter sharing — while replacing NSP with Sentence Order Prediction (SOP), a harder and more useful pretraining task.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.why_it_exists: Larger BERT models (BERT-large) hit diminishing returns and become unwieldy to train (memory, communication overhead for distributed training) primarily due to parameter count growth from embedding size and per-layer parameters. ALBERT shows that most of BERT's parameters can be shared/factorised with minimal performance loss, enabling much larger effective depth/width within a fixed parameter budget.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.how_it_works: Factorised embedding parameterisation: instead of tying the vocabulary embedding size to the hidden size (both = H in BERT, where vocabulary embeddings are huge: V x H), ALBERT projects vocabulary embeddings into a smaller dimension E first, then projects up to H — reducing embedding parameters from O(V x H) to O(V x E + E x H). Cross-layer parameter sharing: all Transformer layers share the same parameters (instead of each of the 12/24 layers having distinct weights), drastically cutting total parameter count — ALBERT-large has 18M parameters vs BERT-large's 334M. Sentence Order Prediction (SOP) replaces NSP: both training examples are two consecutive segments from the same document, but the model must predict whether they're in the correct order or swapped — this is harder than NSP's topic-based discrimination and forces genuine coherence/discourse understanding.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.use_when: When parameter-efficiency is critical (model storage/distribution constraints) and you can tolerate the computational cost of sharing layers (since sharing parameters doesn't reduce compute/FLOPs — only storage — each layer still does a full forward pass).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.avoid_when: Avoid when inference speed/latency is the primary concern — ALBERT's parameter sharing doesn't reduce the number of layer computations, so it's not faster than an equivalently-deep BERT (unlike DistilBERT, which actually has fewer layers). Avoid when fine-tuning stability matters and you have limited experimentation budget — shared-parameter models can have different fine-tuning dynamics than standard architectures.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.what_goes_wrong: Cross-layer parameter sharing means ALBERT-large has far fewer total parameters than BERT-large but similar or greater compute cost per forward pass (same number of layer computations) — so it doesn't speed up inference the way DistilBERT does; the benefit is purely in model size/storage. SOP, while better than NSP, still doesn't capture all useful discourse-level signal, and subsequent models have moved past both NSP and SOP entirely (RoBERTa-style MLM-only).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ALBERT —.real_example: ALBERT-xxlarge achieves better GLUE/SQuAD scores than BERT-large while having fewer total parameters (due to embedding factorisation and layer sharing) — but because it shares the same set of weights across many layers (effectively running the same Transformer block repeatedly), its training and inference compute (FLOPs) per example is comparable to or greater than BERT-large's, illustrating the parameters-vs-compute distinction that's easy to overlook when comparing model 'sizes'.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.what_it_is: ELECTRA (Efficiently Learning an Encoder that Classifies Token Replacements Accurately) replaces BERT's MLM pretraining with a more sample-efficient task: a small 'generator' model replaces some tokens with plausible alternatives, and the main 'discriminator' model (the one actually used downstream) predicts, for every token, whether it was replaced or is original.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.why_it_exists: MLM only provides a training signal for the ~15% of tokens that were masked — the other 85% contribute nothing to the loss, making pretraining sample-inefficient (most of the compute on each example is 'wasted' on tokens that don't directly contribute gradients for the prediction task). ELECTRA's replaced-token-detection task provides a training signal for EVERY token in the input, making pretraining dramatically more compute-efficient.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.how_it_works: A small generator network (typically a small MLM model) is trained jointly to predict masked tokens, similar to standard MLM. Its predictions (sampled, not necessarily the ground truth) are used to replace the masked tokens, producing a 'corrupted' sequence where some tokens are original and some are generator-sampled replacements (which may or may not coincidentally equal the original). The discriminator (the main model, same size as a BERT of that scale) then performs binary classification at every token position: 'original' or 'replaced'. Because every position has a label (not just masked ones), the discriminator gets dense training signal from the entire sequence. After pretraining, the generator is discarded and the discriminator is used for downstream fine-tuning, just like BERT.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.use_when: When pretraining compute budget is limited and you want BERT-level or better downstream performance — ELECTRA-small/base substantially outperform BERT models of the same size trained with the same compute budget, making it attractive for efficient pretraining research or resource-constrained pretraining.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.avoid_when: If using existing pretrained checkpoints rather than pretraining from scratch, the choice between ELECTRA and other encoders mainly comes down to available checkpoint quality for your task/language — ELECTRA's efficiency advantage is primarily a pretraining-time benefit, less relevant if you're just fine-tuning an already-pretrained model.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.what_goes_wrong: The adversarial-flavoured setup (generator produces replacements, discriminator detects them) is reminiscent of GANs but is NOT trained adversarially (the generator is trained with its own MLM loss, not to fool the discriminator) — a common point of confusion. The generator and discriminator share embeddings in some configurations, requiring care in implementation to avoid instability. Discriminator output (real/replaced classification) must still be adapted with a task head for downstream use, same as BERT.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|ELECTRA.real_example: ELECTRA-small (14M parameters) trained on a single GPU for a few days achieves GLUE scores competitive with much larger BERT models trained with far more compute — demonstrating that the replaced-token-detection objective extracts more learning signal per unit of compute than MLM, which was a significant result for making strong pretrained encoders accessible without massive compute budgets.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.what_it_is: DeBERTa (Decoding-enhanced BERT with disentangled attention) v3 is an encoder model that improves on BERT/RoBERTa via 'disentangled attention' (separating content and position representations) and an ELECTRA-style replaced-token-detection pretraining objective with gradient-disentangled embedding sharing, achieving state-of-the-art results on GLUE and SuperGLUE among encoder models.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.why_it_exists: Standard Transformers add positional information to content embeddings and compute attention on the combined representation, which entangles 'what the token is' with 'where it is'. DeBERTa's disentangled attention represents content and relative position separately, computing attention scores as a sum of content-to-content, content-to-position, and position-to-content terms — giving the model more explicit control over how position and content interact, which empirically improves performance, especially on tasks sensitive to word order and relative position (e.g. natural language inference).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.how_it_works: Each token is represented by two vectors: a content embedding and a relative position embedding. Attention scores between tokens i and j are computed as a sum of multiple terms involving content_i, content_j, and the relative position embedding for (i-j) — rather than a single combined embedding's dot product. DeBERTa v3 additionally replaces MLM with ELECTRA-style replaced-token-detection for pretraining, and introduces 'gradient-disentangled embedding sharing' (GDES) to stabilise the generator/discriminator embedding sharing that plain ELECTRA's sharing can destabilise at scale.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.use_when: When you need the strongest possible encoder-only model for classification/NER/QA-style tasks and can afford somewhat higher compute than BERT/RoBERTa of comparable size — DeBERTa-v3 models are frequently top performers on GLUE/SuperGLUE leaderboards among open encoder models, making them a strong default for fine-tuning-based NLU tasks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.avoid_when: Avoid if you need a generative model — DeBERTa is encoder-only, same generation limitations as BERT/RoBERTa apply. Avoid if working with tooling/ecosystems that have less mature support for DeBERTa's architecture-specific details (disentangled attention requires custom implementation, not just a standard Transformer layer) compared to the very widely supported BERT/RoBERTa.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.what_goes_wrong: The disentangled attention mechanism is more complex to implement and slightly more compute-intensive per layer than standard attention (multiple score terms instead of one), so DeBERTa models can be slower at the same parameter count compared to BERT/RoBERTa. The ELECTRA-style pretraining with generator/discriminator requires more careful setup (and the GDES technique specifically) to avoid the training instabilities that plain shared-embedding ELECTRA can exhibit at larger scales.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|DeBERTa.real_example: microsoft/deberta-v3-base fine-tuned on GLUE tasks consistently scores higher than roberta-base and bert-base-uncased at similar parameter counts, making it a common 'best small encoder' choice for production NLU systems (intent classification, NLI-based zero-shot classification pipelines) where encoder-only models remain preferred over decoder-only LLMs for cost/latency reasons.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.what_it_is: The general pattern for adapting a pretrained encoder (BERT/RoBERTa/DeBERTa) to different downstream task types by attaching different task-specific heads to the same pretrained backbone: a single linear layer on [CLS] for classification, a per-token linear layer for NER, two linear layers (start/end span) for extractive QA, and a single linear output (no softmax) for regression.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.why_it_exists: A single pretrained encoder backbone learns general contextual language representations; the same backbone can serve many different task types simply by changing the small output head and the loss function — this 'one backbone, many heads' pattern is the foundation of transfer learning's efficiency, avoiding the need to pretrain separate models for each task type.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.how_it_works: Classification: [CLS] hidden state -> Linear(H, num_classes) -> softmax -> cross-entropy loss against a single label. NER (token classification): every token's hidden state -> Linear(H, num_tags) -> softmax -> cross-entropy loss against per-token BIO tags, summed/averaged over all tokens. Extractive QA: every token's hidden state -> two separate Linear(H,1) layers producing start-logit and end-logit per token -> softmax over positions for each -> cross-entropy loss against the gold start/end positions. Regression: [CLS] hidden state -> Linear(H,1) with no activation -> MSE (or similar) loss against a continuous target value (e.g. similarity score 0-5 in STS-B).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.use_when: Whenever you have a pretrained encoder and labelled task data — this is the default transfer-learning workflow for encoder-based NLU: pick the head matching your task's output structure (single label, per-token labels, span, or scalar), attach it, and fine-tune end-to-end.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.avoid_when: Avoid for generation tasks (summarisation, translation, open-ended dialogue) — encoder-only models with these heads can't generate variable-length free text; use encoder-decoder or decoder-only models instead. Avoid building custom heads from scratch when a library (HuggingFace AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoModelForTokenClassification, AutoModelForQuestionAnswering) already provides the correct head architecture for your task type.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.what_goes_wrong: Mismatched loss functions for the task type (e.g. using cross-entropy for a regression task, or MSE for classification) silently produces a model that 'trains' but optimises the wrong objective — predictions won't be calibrated probabilities/correct labels. For NER, subword tokenisation means one word can split into multiple tokens, requiring a labelling strategy (label only the first subtoken, or all subtokens) — getting this wrong corrupts the BIO tag alignment. For QA, if the gold answer span doesn't align cleanly with tokenizer boundaries (partial token overlap), the start/end position labels must be carefully computed via offset mapping.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|BERT Family|Fine-tun.real_example: Using AutoModelForSequenceClassification with num_labels=1 and a regression loss (MSELoss) on the STS-B task (predict a 0-5 similarity score for a sentence pair) reuses the exact same bert-base-uncased backbone as AutoModelForSequenceClassification with num_labels=2 for SST-2 sentiment (cross-entropy loss) — same pretrained weights, same backbone code path, only the final linear layer's output dimension and the loss function differ, demonstrating the 'one backbone, many heads' transfer-learning pattern in practice.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.what_it_is: GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) uses a decoder-only Transformer architecture: a stack of Transformer blocks with causal (masked) self-attention only — no encoder, no cross-attention — trained to predict the next token given all previous tokens.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.why_it_exists: For pure text generation, an encoder-decoder architecture is unnecessary overhead — there's no separate 'source' sequence to encode. A decoder-only architecture, where the same sequence serves as both input and the thing being predicted (shifted by one position), is simpler, scales well, and naturally supports both understanding (via in-context processing) and generation (via autoregressive sampling) within one unified architecture.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.how_it_works: Each GPT block consists of causal self-attention followed by a feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalisation (GPT uses pre-layer-norm, applying LayerNorm before each sub-layer rather than after, which improves training stability at scale). The causal mask ensures position i only attends to positions <= i. The model is trained on raw text by shifting the input by one position to create targets — input 'The cat sat' / target 'cat sat on' — and computing cross-entropy loss between predicted and actual next tokens at every position simultaneously (parallelisable during training despite the sequential nature of generation).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.use_when: Default architecture for general-purpose language models (chat assistants, code generation, few-shot in-context learning) — virtually all modern frontier LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, Gemini) are decoder-only Transformers.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.avoid_when: Avoid decoder-only architectures for tasks that are naturally encoder-decoder shaped with a clear separate 'input to be transformed' (e.g. some translation/summarisation setups historically favoured encoder-decoder for efficiency) — though in practice, modern decoder-only LLMs handle these tasks well via prompting, so this distinction matters less than it used to.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.what_goes_wrong: Decoder-only models process the entire prompt with causal masking even though the prompt is fully known upfront — this means prompt tokens can't benefit from bidirectional context the way an encoder could provide, a theoretical inefficiency that in practice doesn't seem to meaningfully limit capability at scale. Very long prompts still incur the full causal self-attention cost (though KV caching amortises generation cost).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.real_example: GPT-2 (124M to 1.5B parameters) demonstrated that a decoder-only Transformer trained purely on next-token prediction over diverse web text could perform zero-shot task transfer (e.g. answering questions, summarising) just by being prompted appropriately — without any task-specific architecture changes, foreshadowing the in-context learning paradigm that GPT-3 and later models scaled up dramatically.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.what_it_is: Next-token prediction (also called causal/autoregressive language modelling) is the training objective where the model learns to predict the probability distribution over the next token given all preceding tokens, trained via cross-entropy loss against the actual next token at every position in a sequence.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.why_it_exists: This objective requires no labelled data — any text corpus automatically provides training signal (each token is a 'label' for predicting it from its prefix), making it possible to pretrain on essentially the entire internet's worth of text. It's also directly aligned with the generation task itself: a model that's good at predicting the next token IS a generative language model.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.how_it_works: For a sequence of tokens x_1, ..., x_n, the model computes P(x_t | x_1,...,x_{t-1}) for each position t via causal self-attention and a final softmax over the vocabulary. The training loss is the sum (or average) of -log P(x_t | x_<t) over all positions t in the sequence — this is exactly the cross-entropy between the predicted distribution and the one-hot true next token, summed across the whole sequence in a single forward pass (teacher forcing: the true previous tokens are used as input regardless of what the model would have predicted).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.use_when: The standard pretraining objective for all decoder-only LLMs — used at massive scale on web-text/book/code corpora to build general-purpose language models before any task-specific fine-tuning or instruction-tuning.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.avoid_when: Not directly applicable as a fine-tuning objective for tasks with a different output structure (classification, regression) — though instruction-tuning and RLHF still build on top of next-token prediction by framing the desired output as the 'next tokens' to predict given an instruction prompt.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.what_goes_wrong: Next-token prediction trains the model to be a good 'text continuer', which is not the same as being a good assistant — a raw pretrained model will often continue a question with more questions (mimicking forum/FAQ patterns) rather than answering it, which is why instruction-tuning and RLHF are needed on top of pretraining to align model behaviour with user intent. Perplexity (the standard metric derived from this objective) doesn't always correlate with downstream task usefulness or human-judged quality.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Nex.real_example: A base (non-instruction-tuned) GPT model given the prompt 'What is the capital of France?' might continue with 'What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Italy?' — because in its training data, lists of similar questions are a common pattern following such a question, and pure next-token prediction has no inherent notion that it should 'answer' rather than 'continue in a plausible way' — this gap is exactly what instruction-tuning (training on (instruction, response) pairs) addresses.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.what_it_is: GPT-2 (2019, up to 1.5B params), GPT-3 (2020, 175B params), and GPT-4 (2023, undisclosed but much larger, likely mixture-of-experts) represent successive scale-ups of the same fundamental decoder-only Transformer architecture, demonstrating that increasing model size, data, and compute predictably improves performance and unlocks qualitatively new capabilities.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.why_it_exists: Scaling laws research found that language model loss decreases predictably (as a power law) with increases in model parameters, dataset size, and compute, as long as these are scaled together appropriately — this gave the field a quantitative basis for deciding 'how much bigger should the next model be, and how much data/compute does that require', driving the rapid scale-up from GPT-2 to GPT-4.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.how_it_works: Each generation primarily scaled up parameters, training data, and compute while keeping the core architecture similar (decoder-only Transformer with causal self-attention). GPT-2 showed zero-shot task transfer was possible at modest scale. GPT-3 (100x larger) showed dramatically improved few-shot in-context learning — providing a handful of examples in the prompt let it perform new tasks without any weight updates. GPT-4 added further scale plus likely architectural changes (mixture-of-experts is widely speculated), multimodal input (images), and was trained with more extensive instruction-tuning/RLHF, showing further jumps in reasoning, coding, and multi-step task performance.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.use_when: Useful as a historical/conceptual framework for understanding why model scale matters and how capabilities have evolved — when discussing why larger models tend to perform better and what kinds of capability jumps to expect from scale increases.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.avoid_when: Don't assume scaling alone explains all capability differences between generations — training data quality/curation, instruction-tuning, RLHF, and architectural refinements (e.g. better tokenizers, longer context, MoE) all contribute substantially, especially in GPT-3 -> GPT-4. Avoid extrapolating scaling-law trends indefinitely without considering practical constraints (data availability, compute cost, diminishing returns) — see Chinchilla scaling laws for a more nuanced framing of optimal scaling.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.what_goes_wrong: Naively assuming 'bigger is always better regardless of data' led to early models that were undertrained relative to their parameter count for their compute budget (addressed by Chinchilla's findings on compute-optimal scaling). Public benchmarks can become saturated/contaminated (test data leaking into training corpora) across generations, making generation-over-generation benchmark comparisons less meaningful than they appear.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|GPT.real_example: GPT-3's paper title, 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', captured the key qualitative jump from GPT-2: GPT-2 needed fine-tuning to perform well on most tasks, while GPT-3 (175B params, ~100x GPT-2) could perform competitively on many tasks just from a few examples in the prompt (in-context learning), with no weight updates at all — a capability that simply wasn't present at GPT-2's scale, illustrating an 'emergent capability' from scaling.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.what_it_is: T5 (Text-To-Text Transfer Transformer) is an encoder-decoder Transformer that reframes every NLP task — classification, translation, summarisation, regression, QA — as a text-to-text problem: both input and output are always text strings, with the task specified via a text prefix.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.why_it_exists: Different NLP tasks traditionally required different model architectures/heads (classification head, span-extraction head, generation decoder). T5's insight was that if every task is framed as 'input text -> output text', a single architecture, training procedure, and loss function (sequence-to-sequence cross-entropy) can handle all of them — radically simplifying multi-task learning and transfer.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.how_it_works: T5 uses a standard encoder-decoder Transformer (encoder: bidirectional self-attention; decoder: causal self-attention + cross-attention to encoder output, same as the original Transformer). Tasks are specified by prefixing the input text with a task description, e.g. 'translate English to German: That is good.' -> 'Das ist gut.', or 'summarize: <article text>' -> '<summary>', or even 'cola sentence: <sentence>' -> 'acceptable'/'unacceptable' for grammaticality classification (framing classification labels as output text strings). T5 was pretrained on a 'span corruption' objective (similar in spirit to MLM but masking contiguous spans, replaced with sentinel tokens, which the decoder must reconstruct) on the large C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus) dataset.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.use_when: Multi-task setups where unifying diverse tasks under one model/training framework simplifies the system, or when a task's output is naturally textual (translation, summarisation) and you want one model that can also handle classification-like tasks by generating label strings.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks needing precise numeric outputs where 'generating a number as text' introduces unnecessary risk of malformed outputs (e.g. regression tasks where T5 must generate a string like '3.7' that must then be parsed back to a float — a dedicated regression head avoids this). Avoid when inference latency is critical and the task is a simple classification — an encoder-only model with a classification head is cheaper than running a full encoder-decoder generation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.what_goes_wrong: Framing classification as text generation means the model could in principle generate an invalid label string not in the expected label set (e.g. generating 'maybe' when only 'positive'/'negative' are valid) — requiring constrained decoding or output validation. Generation is inherently slower than a single forward pass through a classification head, since the decoder must generate token-by-token even for short categorical outputs.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|T5.real_example: T5 frames the CoLA grammaticality task as: input 'cola sentence: The cat sat on the mat.' -> output 'acceptable', and the STS-B similarity task as input 'stsb sentence1: ... sentence2: ...' -> output a string like '3.8' representing the similarity score — both handled by the exact same encoder-decoder architecture and generation procedure, demonstrating the 'everything is text-to-text' unification that influenced how later instruction-tuned LLMs frame diverse tasks via natural language prompts.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.what_it_is: BART (Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers) is an encoder-decoder Transformer pretrained by corrupting text with an arbitrary noising function and training the model to reconstruct the original, uncorrupted text — combining BERT's bidirectional encoder with GPT's autoregressive decoder.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.why_it_exists: BERT's MLM objective is well-suited to encoder-only understanding tasks but doesn't directly produce a generative model. GPT's left-to-right objective produces a strong generator but lacks bidirectional encoding. BART combines both: a bidirectional encoder (like BERT) processes corrupted input, and an autoregressive decoder (like GPT) reconstructs the original text — giving a model strong at both understanding (via the encoder) and generation (via the decoder), well-suited to tasks like summarisation and translation that require both.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.how_it_works: During pretraining, input text is corrupted using a combination of noising transformations: token masking (like BERT), token deletion, sentence permutation (shuffle sentence order), document rotation (start the document at a random token), and especially text infilling (replace spans of varying length with a single mask token — the model must determine how many tokens to generate to fill the span, not just predict the masked content, which is a harder and more useful task than BERT's single-token masking). The encoder processes this corrupted document bidirectionally; the decoder autoregressively generates the original, uncorrupted document, with cross-attention to the encoder's representations.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.use_when: Sequence-to-sequence generation tasks where both understanding the (possibly noisy/incomplete) input and generating fluent output matter — summarisation, translation, and other text-to-text generation tasks, particularly when fine-tuning on a moderate amount of task-specific data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.avoid_when: Avoid for pure classification/NER/extractive tasks where an encoder-only model (BERT/RoBERTa) is simpler and cheaper — BART's decoder adds generation overhead unnecessary for tasks that don't require generating text. Avoid for tasks needing very long-context generation without chunking — like other Transformer-based models of its era, BART has fixed context length limits.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.what_goes_wrong: The variety of noising functions used in pretraining (token masking, deletion, permutation, rotation, infilling) means BART's pretraining is more complex to implement/reproduce than BERT's simple MLM or GPT's simple next-token prediction. Like other seq2seq models, BART can hallucinate during generation (produce fluent text not faithful to the input), an important consideration for summarisation where factual accuracy matters.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.real_example: BART's text-infilling pretraining — where a span of arbitrary length is replaced by a single mask token, and the model must generate the correct number and content of replacement tokens — directly mirrors the summarisation task structure (input: full document; output: a condensed version), which is part of why facebook/bart-large-cnn (BART fine-tuned on the CNN/DailyMail summarisation dataset) became one of the most widely used pretrained summarisation models before being further surpassed by larger instruction-tuned LLMs.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.what_it_is: BART's encoder-decoder architecture and corrupt-and-reconstruct pretraining make it particularly effective when fine-tuned on summarisation (compress a document into key points) and translation (rewrite text in another language) — two tasks that, like BART's pretraining, require mapping a longer/different input to a related but shorter/transformed output.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.why_it_exists: Summarisation and translation are both seq2seq tasks requiring (1) deep understanding of the full input (BART's bidirectional encoder) and (2) fluent generation of a related but distinct output sequence (BART's autoregressive decoder with cross-attention) — BART's architecture and pretraining objective are directly aligned with this input-transformation pattern, giving it a head start (better initialisation) for fine-tuning on these tasks compared to encoder-only or decoder-only models.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.how_it_works: For summarisation fine-tuning: (document, reference summary) pairs are used, with the encoder processing the full document and the decoder trained (via cross-entropy / teacher forcing) to generate the reference summary, attending to encoder representations via cross-attention. For translation: (source sentence, target sentence) pairs are used similarly — BART can be fine-tuned for translation, though multilingual variants (mBART) pretrained on multiple languages are typically used for translation rather than the original English-only BART.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.use_when: Fine-tuning for abstractive summarisation on a moderate-sized labelled dataset (news articles + reference summaries, e.g. CNN/DailyMail or XSum), or as a strong encoder-decoder baseline for translation tasks (especially with mBART for multilingual settings) before considering larger general-purpose LLMs.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.avoid_when: Avoid for zero-shot or few-shot summarisation/translation without fine-tuning — BART's pretraining objective (reconstruct corrupted text) is related to but not the same as summarisation/translation, so without task-specific fine-tuning, output quality is poor compared to instruction-tuned LLMs that can perform these tasks zero-shot via prompting.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.what_goes_wrong: Fine-tuned BART summarisers can produce summaries with factual inconsistencies relative to the source document (hallucination), a well-documented issue for abstractive summarisation models in general. Translation quality with (non-multilingual) BART for language pairs not well-represented in its English-centric pretraining data will be poor — mBART or dedicated multilingual NMT models are needed for genuinely multilingual translation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|BAR.real_example: facebook/bart-large-xsum, fine-tuned on the XSum dataset (highly abstractive single-sentence summaries of BBC articles), generates concise one-sentence summaries that often paraphrase rather than extract — e.g. summarising a long article about a sports match result into a single sentence capturing the outcome, demonstrating BART's strength at genuinely abstractive (not just extractive) summarisation due to its generative decoder.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.what_it_is: Chinchilla scaling laws (from DeepMind's 2022 paper) established that for a given compute budget, there's an optimal balance between model size (parameters) and training data size (tokens) — and that many large models of that era (like GPT-3) were oversized relative to the amount of training data, i.e. 'undertrained'. The commonly cited rule of thumb is that the optimal number of training tokens is roughly 20x the number of parameters.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.why_it_exists: Before Chinchilla, the trend was 'bigger models = better', often scaling parameter count aggressively while keeping training data roughly fixed or under-scaled. Chinchilla's controlled experiments (training many models of varying size on varying amounts of data, all at fixed compute budgets) found that for a fixed compute budget, a smaller model trained on more data often outperforms a larger model trained on less data — providing a principled basis for allocating compute between model size and data size.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.how_it_works: Chinchilla trained ~400 models of varying sizes (70M to 16B parameters) on varying numbers of tokens, all at different fixed FLOP budgets, and fit power-law curves relating final loss to (parameters, tokens, compute). The key finding: for compute-optimal training, both model size N and training tokens D should scale roughly equally with compute C (N ~ C^0.5, D ~ C^0.5), implying a roughly constant ratio of tokens to parameters at the optimum — empirically around 20 tokens per parameter. The Chinchilla model itself (70B parameters, trained on 1.4T tokens — about 20x) outperformed the much larger Gopher (280B parameters, trained on ~300B tokens, only ~1x) at the same training compute budget.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.use_when: Planning pretraining runs: given a fixed compute budget, use Chinchilla-derived ratios to decide the model-size/data-size split rather than maximising model size alone. Also useful for interpreting why some smaller, more-heavily-trained models (Chinchilla, LLaMA) outperform larger but less-trained predecessors (Gopher, GPT-3) on many benchmarks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.avoid_when: Don't treat the 20x ratio as a universal constant for all scenarios — the optimal ratio depends on data quality/diversity and the specific compute-cost model (training vs inference costs). For models intended for heavy inference deployment, 'overtraining' a smaller model beyond its Chinchilla-optimal point (using more tokens than 20x parameters) can be worth it because it reduces inference cost for a given quality level — this is part of why later models (LLaMA, etc.) are often trained well beyond the strict Chinchilla-optimal point for their size.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.what_goes_wrong: Applying Chinchilla's ratios naively without considering data availability/quality can be misleading — if high-quality training data is limited (a real constraint for some domains/languages), you can't simply scale tokens to match the Chinchilla-optimal ratio for a larger model. Also, Chinchilla's analysis focused on training-compute optimality and didn't account for inference costs at all — a model used by millions of users has inference costs that dwarf training costs, changing the optimal trade-off toward smaller, more-trained models.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Chi.real_example: LLaMA (Meta, 2023) explicitly cited Chinchilla-style reasoning: rather than building the largest possible model, Meta trained relatively smaller models (7B-65B) on very large amounts of data (1-1.4T tokens, well beyond the ~20x ratio for the smaller models) — producing models that, despite being smaller than GPT-3 (175B), matched or exceeded its performance on many benchmarks while being far cheaper to run at inference, directly leveraging the insight that training-data quantity/quality matters as much as raw parameter count.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.what_it_is: Emergent capabilities are abilities that appear abruptly and unpredictably in large language models once they cross a certain scale threshold, despite being absent (near-random performance) in smaller models trained the same way — e.g. multi-step arithmetic, chain-of-thought reasoning, or in-context learning of novel tasks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.why_it_exists: This phenomenon was observed empirically when researchers evaluated models of varying sizes on the same benchmarks: many tasks showed flat, near-chance performance across a wide range of smaller model sizes, then a sharp jump to substantially-above-chance performance once models crossed a certain parameter/compute threshold — a discontinuity not predicted by smooth extrapolation of smaller models' performance.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.how_it_works: The exact mechanism isn't fully understood, but a few contributing factors are discussed: (1) some tasks require composing multiple sub-skills, each individually improving smoothly with scale, but the TASK's success metric (e.g. exact-match accuracy) only registers success once ALL sub-skills cross a usability threshold simultaneously, creating an apparently sudden jump in the aggregate metric even if underlying capabilities improved smoothly; (2) some researchers have argued that 'emergence' is partly an artifact of using discontinuous evaluation metrics (exact match) rather than continuous ones (e.g. token-level log-likelihood, which often DOES show smooth improvement even when exact-match doesn't).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.use_when: Useful for framing discussions about why capability evaluations of smaller models may not predict larger models' capabilities on certain tasks — relevant when deciding whether a smaller/cheaper model can substitute for a larger one on tasks suspected to be 'emergent'.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.avoid_when: Avoid treating 'emergence' as evidence for unbounded or unpredictable future capability jumps without scrutiny — the metric-discontinuity explanation suggests at least some apparent emergence reflects evaluation methodology rather than a fundamental discontinuity in the underlying model's competence, and this remains an active area of research/debate.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.what_goes_wrong: Relying on a smaller model for a task believed to require an 'emergent' capability (e.g. multi-step reasoning) can lead to silent failures — the smaller model doesn't gracefully degrade, it simply fails the task entirely (near-chance performance) while perhaps appearing competent on superficially similar simpler tasks, making capability gaps hard to anticipate without direct evaluation on the exact task of interest.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|GPT & Generative|Eme.real_example: In the GSM8K grade-school math word problem benchmark, models below a certain scale perform near 0% (essentially random/no meaningful arithmetic reasoning), while models above that scale threshold (combined with chain-of-thought prompting) jump to substantially higher accuracy — this kind of result, widely cited in early discussions of emergent capabilities, illustrates why capability planning for LLM-based products often requires empirical testing at the target model scale rather than extrapolating from smaller/cheaper models' performance.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: ViT (Vision Transformer) applies the standard Transformer encoder architecture to images by splitting an image into fixed-size patches (e.g. 16x16 pixels), linearly embedding each patch as a 'token', and processing the resulting sequence of patch embeddings (plus a learnable [CLS] token) exactly like a sequence of word embeddings in NLP.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: CNNs had been the dominant architecture for vision, with built-in inductive biases (locality, translation invariance via convolution/pooling). ViT explored whether a generic Transformer, with minimal vision-specific inductive bias, could match or exceed CNNs given sufficient training data — testing the hypothesis that attention-based global reasoning over patches could learn useful visual representations without hand-coded locality assumptions.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: An image of size HxW is divided into N non-overlapping patches of size PxP (e.g. 16x16), each patch is flattened into a vector and linearly projected to dimension D, producing N patch embeddings. A learnable [CLS] token embedding is prepended. Learnable position embeddings are added to all N+1 embeddings (since attention is permutation-invariant, position info is needed to encode patch location). This sequence is fed through a standard Transformer encoder (multi-head self-attention + MLP blocks). The final [CLS] token representation is passed through a classification head (linear layer) to produce class logits.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Large-scale image classification when sufficient pretraining data is available (ViT was shown to underperform CNNs when trained from scratch on smaller datasets like ImageNet alone, but to match/exceed CNNs when pretrained on much larger datasets like JFT-300M). Also the foundation for vision-language models (CLIP's image encoder, LLaVA's vision tower) where a unified Transformer architecture across modalities simplifies multimodal fusion.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid for small datasets without strong pretraining or data augmentation/regularisation — ViT lacks CNN's built-in spatial inductive biases (locality, translation equivariance), so it needs more data or careful training tricks (heavy augmentation, distillation) to reach CNN-level performance from scratch. Avoid when fine-grained spatial/local detail is critical and patch granularity (16x16) is too coarse for the task without architectural modifications.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Quadratic attention cost in the number of patches means high-resolution images produce very long token sequences (e.g. a 224x224 image with 16x16 patches = 196 patches, but a 1024x1024 image = 4096 patches, making attention 400x more expensive) — this motivated hierarchical architectures like Swin Transformer for high-resolution tasks. Training ViT from scratch on small datasets without proper regularisation/augmentation underperforms equivalent CNNs significantly, a common pitfall for practitioners expecting 'just swap the architecture' to work.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: google/vit-base-patch16-224, pretrained on ImageNet-21k and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, splits each 224x224 input image into 196 (14x14 grid) patches of 16x16 pixels, processes them through 12 Transformer encoder layers, and uses the [CLS] token's final representation for 1000-way classification — achieving competitive accuracy with ResNet-based CNNs of similar size, the first strong evidence that 'images are just sequences of patches' is a viable alternative to convolution-based vision.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: Positional encoding for 2D patches adapts the Transformer's position-encoding concept to image patches arranged in a 2D grid, so the model knows each patch's spatial location (row, column) within the image — since self-attention over a flattened sequence of patches would otherwise be unaware of the original 2D spatial arrangement.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: When an image is split into patches and flattened into a 1D sequence for the Transformer, the spatial relationships between patches (which patch is above/below/left/right of another) are lost unless explicitly encoded — without this, a patch in the top-left corner and a patch in the bottom-right would be indistinguishable in terms of 'position' to the attention mechanism.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: The simplest and most common approach (used in the original ViT) is to use standard 1D learnable position embeddings — one embedding per position in the flattened sequence (position 0, 1, 2, ..., N-1 for N patches), exactly like BERT's learned position embeddings, letting the model implicitly learn 2D spatial relationships from the 1D positional indices through training. More explicit 2D-aware schemes assign separate learnable embeddings for row index and column index (and combine/add them), or use 2D sinusoidal encodings (extending the 1D sinusoidal formula to separate x and y coordinates). ViT's ablations found that 1D learned position embeddings work nearly as well as more complex 2D-aware schemes, likely because the model can learn the implicit 2D structure from data given enough training.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Required for any patch-based vision Transformer (ViT, Swin, CvT, etc.) — some form of positional encoding for patches is always necessary, since self-attention has no inherent notion of spatial arrangement.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Not avoidable in patch-based Transformers, but the CHOICE of scheme (1D learned vs 2D-aware vs relative) matters less in practice than one might expect for standard image sizes — ViT's findings suggest simpler 1D learned embeddings often suffice, so added complexity of 2D-specific schemes should be justified by measured improvement for the specific task.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Position embeddings are tied to the training resolution/patch grid size — if the model is fine-tuned or used at a different image resolution (different number of patches), the position embedding table size mismatches, requiring interpolation of the position embeddings to the new grid size (a common practical step when fine-tuning ViT at higher resolution than pretraining). Getting this interpolation wrong silently degrades spatial understanding without an obvious error.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: When fine-tuning a ViT pretrained at 224x224 resolution (196 patches, 14x14 grid) on images at 384x384 resolution (576 patches, 24x24 grid), the original 196 learned position embeddings must be reshaped to a 14x14 grid and bicubically interpolated up to a 24x24 grid to produce 576 position embeddings — a technique used in practice to adapt pretrained ViTs to higher-resolution fine-tuning without retraining position embeddings from scratch.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: CvT (Convolutional vision Transformer) is a hybrid architecture that introduces convolutional operations into the Vision Transformer pipeline — specifically, using convolutional projections for generating Query/Key/Value in attention and a hierarchical multi-stage design with convolutional token embedding — combining CNN inductive biases with Transformer's global modelling.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Pure ViT lacks the locality and translation-equivariance inductive biases that make CNNs data-efficient, requiring large-scale pretraining to compensate. CvT was designed to inject convolutional inductive biases directly into the Transformer architecture, aiming to get CNN-like data efficiency (good performance even without massive pretraining datasets) while retaining the Transformer's global self-attention for long-range dependencies.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: CvT introduces a 'Convolutional Token Embedding' that uses convolutional layers (with overlapping patches via stride) instead of ViT's non-overlapping linear patch projection — this provides local spatial context to each token from the start. It also introduces 'Convolutional Projection' for attention: instead of computing Q, K, V via simple linear projections of token embeddings, CvT applies depth-wise separable convolutions before the linear projections, giving the attention mechanism access to local spatial structure. The architecture is organised in multiple stages with progressively reduced spatial resolution and increased channel dimension (similar to CNN hierarchies like ResNet), removing the need for explicit position embeddings since convolutions inherently encode some positional information.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: When training vision Transformers on moderate-sized datasets without access to massive pretraining corpora, where CNN-like inductive biases improve sample efficiency, or when you want a single architecture that performs well across a range of dataset sizes without ViT's heavy dependence on large-scale pretraining.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid when working in an ecosystem heavily standardised around pure ViT (e.g. for compatibility with CLIP/vision-language model conventions that expect a standard ViT image encoder) — hybrid architectures may have less plug-and-play compatibility with multimodal frameworks built around plain ViT.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Adding convolutional operations increases architectural complexity compared to 'pure' Transformer designs, and some of the simplicity/uniformity benefits that made Transformers attractive (same architecture across modalities) are reduced by introducing vision-specific convolutional components. Hybrid architectures can be harder to scale/transfer to non-image modalities compared to pure attention-based designs.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: CvT-13 (13M parameters) achieves higher ImageNet top-1 accuracy than a similarly-sized ViT trained from scratch on ImageNet-1k alone (without large-scale extra pretraining), demonstrating that injecting convolutional inductive biases closes much of the data-efficiency gap between pure Transformers and CNNs — relevant for practitioners who don't have access to JFT-300M-scale pretraining data that the original ViT relied on.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: BLIP (Bootstrapping Language-Image Pretraining) and BLIP-2 are vision-language pretraining frameworks whose key innovation is in HOW training data is improved: BLIP uses a 'CapFilt' bootstrapping process to clean noisy web image-text pairs by generating new captions and filtering out poor ones; BLIP-2 instead focuses on efficiently bridging frozen pretrained image encoders and frozen LLMs via a lightweight trainable 'Querying Transformer' (Q-Former).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Web-scraped image-caption datasets are extremely noisy (alt-text is often irrelevant, generic, or missing context) — training directly on this noise limits vision-language model quality. BLIP's CapFilt addresses data quality directly. Separately, training large vision-language models end-to-end from scratch is extremely expensive — BLIP-2 addresses this by reusing existing frozen pretrained unimodal models (an image encoder and an LLM) and training only a small bridging module, dramatically reducing the trainable parameter count and compute needed.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: BLIP's CapFilt: a 'captioner' model (fine-tuned on a small set of clean human-annotated captions) generates synthetic captions for web images; a 'filter' model (also fine-tuned on clean data) scores both original web captions and synthetic captions for image-text relevance, discarding low-quality pairs — producing a cleaner, bootstrapped dataset for pretraining the main vision-language model. BLIP-2's Q-Former is a small Transformer with a fixed number of learnable 'query' tokens that attend to a frozen image encoder's outputs (extracting a compact set of visual features) and is trained in two stages: first to align these visual features with text representations (contrastive + matching + captioning losses against a frozen image encoder), then to make these features digestible by a frozen LLM (training the Q-Former's output projection so the frozen LLM can use the visual queries as a 'soft prompt' prefix for generation).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: BLIP-style data bootstrapping is useful conceptually whenever training on noisy web-scraped multimodal data and data quality is a bottleneck. BLIP-2's frozen-encoder + lightweight-bridge approach is the template for efficiently building new vision-language capabilities on top of existing strong unimodal models without expensive end-to-end retraining — directly influential on subsequent VLM designs.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid BLIP-2's frozen-backbone approach if your downstream task requires the image encoder or LLM itself to adapt significantly to a new domain (frozen backbones limit how much the underlying representations can shift — only the small bridge module is trained). Avoid CapFilt-style bootstrapping without careful validation — the captioner/filter models themselves have biases that get amplified/propagated into the bootstrapped dataset.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: BLIP-2's frozen components mean the overall system's capability is bounded by what the frozen image encoder and frozen LLM can represent — the Q-Former can only 'translate' between their representation spaces, not add fundamentally new visual or linguistic capabilities. CapFilt's quality depends on the captioner/filter models' own training data and biases — systematic biases in what they consider 'good' captions propagate into the final pretraining dataset, potentially narrowing diversity.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: BLIP-2 connects a frozen ViT-based image encoder (e.g. from CLIP or EVA-CLIP) to a frozen large language model (e.g. OPT or FlanT5) via a Q-Former with only ~188M trainable parameters — orders of magnitude fewer than training a comparable vision-language model end-to-end — yet achieves strong zero-shot image captioning and VQA performance, demonstrating that most of the needed 'knowledge' already exists in the frozen unimodal models and only a small bridge is needed to connect them.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: ALIGN (A Large-scale ImaGe and Noisy-text embedding) is a vision-language model from Google that trains a dual-encoder (image encoder + text encoder) using contrastive learning on over a billion noisy image-alt-text pairs scraped from the web — without any data cleaning/filtering, in contrast to approaches like BLIP that explicitly clean their training data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Curating clean image-text datasets is expensive and limits scale. ALIGN demonstrated that simply scaling up the amount of (noisy) data far enough could compensate for per-example noise — showing that data scale can substitute for data cleanliness in contrastive vision-language pretraining, an important data-strategy finding alongside CLIP's similar but smaller-scale approach.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: ALIGN uses a standard dual-encoder contrastive setup (architecturally similar to CLIP): an image encoder (EfficientNet in the original ALIGN paper) and a text encoder (BERT) independently embed images and their associated alt-text into a shared embedding space. The training objective (normalised softmax / contrastive loss, similar to InfoNCE) pulls matching image-text pairs' embeddings together and pushes non-matching pairs apart within each training batch. Crucially, the ~1.8 billion image-alt-text pairs used were NOT manually filtered or cleaned — the sheer scale of data was relied upon to average out noise.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Conceptually relevant when considering data strategy trade-offs for contrastive vision-language pretraining: ALIGN demonstrates that at sufficient scale, raw noisy web data can produce strong zero-shot image-text retrieval and classification performance, an alternative philosophy to heavily-curated-but-smaller datasets.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid assuming 'more noisy data is always better' for smaller-scale or domain-specific projects — ALIGN's result holds at billion-pair scale; at smaller scales (millions of pairs), data quality/cleaning (BLIP-style) likely matters more since there's less redundancy to average out noise.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Models trained on uncurated web data inherit and can amplify biases and inappropriate content present in that data (a general concern for large-scale web-scraped multimodal datasets, applicable beyond just ALIGN). Without any filtering, a meaningful fraction of 'noisy' pairs may have essentially no real relationship between image and text, and while scale helps the model learn robust representations on average, individual noisy examples are still 'wasted'/misleading training signal.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: ALIGN's zero-shot ImageNet classification accuracy (computed via the same image-text similarity approach as CLIP — embedding class names as text and finding the closest image embedding) was competitive with CLIP despite ALIGN's training data being entirely unfiltered web alt-text versus CLIP's somewhat more curated 400M pairs — a result widely cited as evidence that scale can substitute for curation in contrastive pretraining, though both approaches remain far smaller than later vision-language datasets used in models like BLIP-2 or LAION-5B-trained models.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: Swin Transformer (Shifted WINdow Transformer) is a hierarchical vision Transformer that computes self-attention within local non-overlapping windows (rather than globally across all patches), and shifts the window partitioning between consecutive layers to enable cross-window connections — producing a CNN-like hierarchical feature pyramid suitable for dense prediction tasks (detection, segmentation).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: ViT's global self-attention over all patches has O(n^2) cost in the number of patches, making it impractical for high-resolution images or dense prediction tasks (object detection, segmentation) that need multi-scale feature maps like CNNs produce (via downsampling stages). Swin was designed to give vision Transformers a CNN-like hierarchical structure (features at multiple resolutions) with linear (rather than quadratic) computational complexity relative to image size.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: The image is divided into small windows (e.g. 7x7 patches each); self-attention is computed independently within each window (local attention, much cheaper than global attention). To allow information to flow across window boundaries (otherwise windows would be isolated), consecutive Transformer blocks alternate between a regular window partition and a 'shifted' window partition (offset by half a window size), so that the second layer's windows straddle the boundaries of the first layer's windows, connecting previously-separate windows over successive layers. The architecture is organised in stages, with patch merging operations between stages that reduce spatial resolution and increase channel depth (analogous to CNN downsampling), producing a hierarchical pyramid of feature maps at multiple scales — directly usable as a backbone for detection/segmentation frameworks designed for CNN feature pyramids (e.g. Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, UperNet).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Dense prediction vision tasks (object detection, semantic/instance segmentation) where multi-scale feature maps are needed, or any vision task with high-resolution images where global ViT attention would be computationally prohibitive, while still wanting Transformer-based global modelling capacity (via the shifted-window cross-connections).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid when the task is simple image classification at standard resolutions and a plain ViT (or even a CNN) is simpler and sufficient — Swin's added complexity (window partitioning, shifting, patch merging) is primarily justified by dense-prediction use cases and high-resolution efficiency requirements.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: The shifted-window mechanism, while clever, means information takes multiple layers to propagate across distant parts of the image (each layer's window only directly connects to immediately adjacent windows via the shift) — for tasks requiring very long-range global reasoning in a single step, this is less direct than ViT's full global attention. Implementing the cyclic shift and window partitioning correctly (especially at image boundaries, requiring masking) is more complex than plain ViT's straightforward patch sequence.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: Swin Transformer backbones plugged into Mask R-CNN or UperNet for COCO object detection/segmentation achieved state-of-the-art results at the time of publication, outperforming comparable CNN (ResNet/ResNeXt) backbones — demonstrating that the hierarchical, linear-complexity design successfully adapted Transformer-based vision models to dense prediction tasks where plain ViT (quadratic cost, single-scale output) was impractical.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: A comparison of Vision Transformers (ViT and variants) versus Convolutional Neural Networks (ResNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, etc.) along dimensions of data efficiency, inductive bias, computational characteristics, and suitability for different vision tasks/deployment constraints.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Both architecture families remain viable choices for vision tasks in 2024-2025, and understanding their trade-offs (rather than assuming one strictly dominates) is essential for making sound architecture decisions — particularly because the 'CNNs are obsolete, use Transformers' narrative oversimplifies a more nuanced reality where dataset size, task type, and deployment constraints all matter.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: CNNs have built-in inductive biases — locality (each filter only looks at a local neighbourhood) and translation equivariance (the same filter applies everywhere) — that make them data-efficient: they perform well even on smaller datasets because these biases match natural image statistics well. ViTs have minimal inductive bias and must learn spatial relationships from data via attention and position embeddings — this gives them more flexibility (can learn non-local relationships directly) but requires more data/compute to reach the same performance, UNLESS heavily pretrained on massive datasets (where ViTs can match or exceed CNNs) or hybridised with convolutional elements (CvT, Swin). For deployment, CNNs often have more mature hardware-optimised kernels and lower memory overhead at high resolutions (due to linear-complexity convolutions vs quadratic attention in plain ViT).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Use CNNs (or hybrid/hierarchical Transformers like Swin/ConvNeXt) when: training data is limited, deployment is on resource-constrained hardware with mature CNN kernel support, or the task is dense prediction at high resolution. Use ViT (or ViT-based encoders) when: large-scale pretraining data/compute is available, the task benefits from global attention from the start (classification on large pretraining corpora), or — most commonly today — when building multimodal models (CLIP, LLaVA) where a Transformer image encoder integrates naturally with a Transformer language model.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid choosing ViT purely because it's 'newer'/'more modern' for a small-dataset task without large-scale pretraining available — a well-tuned CNN (or ConvNeXt, a modernised CNN incorporating some Transformer-inspired design choices) may outperform a from-scratch ViT on the same data. Avoid choosing CNNs when building multimodal systems where Transformer-Transformer integration (shared attention patterns, easier cross-modal fusion) provides architectural simplicity benefits that outweigh raw efficiency considerations.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Teams sometimes swap a CNN backbone for ViT in an existing pipeline without adjusting training recipe (augmentation, regularisation, learning rate schedule, training duration) — ViT's training recipe requirements differ substantially from CNN conventions, and a naive swap often underperforms the original CNN, leading to incorrect conclusions about architecture superiority when the real issue is training recipe mismatch.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: For a medical imaging classification task with only a few thousand labelled images and no access to large-scale pretrained ViT checkpoints in that domain, a fine-tuned ResNet-50 (or EfficientNet) pretrained on ImageNet often outperforms a ViT trained from scratch or fine-tuned from a general-domain ViT checkpoint — but for a multimodal medical report-generation system (image + text), a ViT-based image encoder (compatible with CLIP-style or LLaVA-style architectures) is the practical choice despite potentially needing more careful fine-tuning, because of the downstream integration benefits with the language model.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) trains a dual-encoder model — one image encoder (ViT or ResNet) and one text encoder (Transformer) — using contrastive learning on 400 million (image, caption) pairs from the web, learning a shared embedding space where matching images and captions have high cosine similarity.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Traditional image classifiers are trained on a fixed, predefined set of labels (e.g. 1000 ImageNet classes) and can't recognise new categories without retraining. CLIP was designed to learn visual concepts directly from natural language supervision at scale, producing a model that can perform 'zero-shot' classification on arbitrary categories by comparing an image's embedding to text embeddings of candidate class descriptions — no task-specific training data needed.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: For a batch of N (image, text) pairs, both encoders produce embeddings; CLIP computes the cosine similarity between every image embedding and every text embedding in the batch (an NxN similarity matrix), and trains with a contrastive loss (symmetric cross-entropy / InfoNCE) that maximises similarity for the N true (matched) pairs on the diagonal while minimising similarity for the N^2-N mismatched off-diagonal pairs. After training, zero-shot classification works by embedding the image and embedding text prompts for each candidate class (e.g. 'a photo of a {class}'), then picking the class whose text embedding has highest cosine similarity to the image embedding.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Zero-shot image classification/retrieval where the label set isn't known in advance or changes frequently, as the foundational image encoder for vision-language models (LLaVA, Stable Diffusion's text conditioning), or for image-text similarity/search applications (semantic image search by text query).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks requiring fine-grained visual discrimination beyond what's captured by natural-language image descriptions on the web (e.g. distinguishing very similar-looking fine-grained categories that aren't typically distinguished in captions) — CLIP's zero-shot performance on such fine-grained tasks is often weaker than a supervised classifier trained specifically for that distinction. Avoid for dense prediction tasks (segmentation, detection) without adaptation — CLIP produces a single global image embedding, not per-pixel/per-region features (though extensions exist).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: CLIP's zero-shot performance is sensitive to prompt phrasing (the exact text used for 'a photo of a {class}' vs other templates can shift accuracy by several points) — prompt engineering matters even for embedding-based zero-shot classification. CLIP inherits biases from its web-scraped training data (400M pairs scraped without careful curation), which can manifest as biased associations between images and text. CLIP's image-text similarity captures broad semantic alignment but isn't necessarily well-calibrated for tasks requiring precise counting, spatial relationships, or compositional reasoning ('a red cube on top of a blue sphere' vs 'a blue cube on top of a red sphere' may get similar CLIP scores despite being visually and semantically distinct).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: CLIP's image encoder (a ViT) is the standard image encoder used in LLaVA and many other vision-language models — the visual features it produces, having been trained to align with natural language descriptions, transfer well as input to an LLM's 'visual understanding' pathway; similarly, Stable Diffusion uses CLIP's text encoder to condition image generation on text prompts, leveraging CLIP's learned image-text alignment in the opposite direction (text -> guidance for image generation).

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: Beyond their pretraining/bootstrapping innovations, BLIP and BLIP-2 are vision-language models that support a unified set of vision-language UNDERSTANDING and generation tasks — image captioning, visual question answering (VQA), and image-text retrieval — from a single pretrained model, adaptable to each task with light fine-tuning or even zero-shot.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Different vision-language tasks (captioning = generate text from image; VQA = generate/select an answer given image+question; retrieval = match images and texts) were historically handled by separate specialised architectures. BLIP/BLIP-2's unified encoder-decoder-style design (BLIP) or modular Q-Former bridge (BLIP-2) supports all these tasks from one pretrained backbone, simplifying deployment and enabling transfer across tasks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: BLIP uses a multimodal mixture-of-encoder-decoder architecture with three functional modes sharing parameters: a unimodal encoder (for image-text contrastive matching/retrieval, similar to CLIP), an image-grounded text encoder (for image-text matching with cross-attention, used in retrieval reranking), and an image-grounded text decoder (for captioning/VQA-style generation, with causal self-attention and cross-attention to image features). For BLIP-2, the same frozen-image-encoder + Q-Former + frozen-LLM pipeline supports VQA and captioning by feeding the Q-Former's visual query outputs as a prefix to the LLM, which then generates the answer/caption conditioned on this visual context plus an optional text prompt/question.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Building applications needing multiple vision-language capabilities (e.g. an image search/captioning/QA system) from one model family, or as a strong pretrained starting point for fine-tuning on a specific vision-language task with limited labelled data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks requiring open-ended conversational visual reasoning with strong general-purpose language ability — later instruction-tuned multimodal LLMs (LLaVA, GPT-4V-class models) generally provide more fluent, flexible interaction than BLIP/BLIP-2's more task-templated outputs, especially BLIP-2's reliance on the frozen LLM's base (often non-chat-tuned) capabilities.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Zero-shot VQA performance with BLIP-2 depends heavily on the frozen LLM's pretraining — if the frozen LLM wasn't instruction-tuned, answers may be poorly formatted (e.g. continuing the question rather than answering it) even if the visual understanding (via Q-Former) is accurate, illustrating that visual grounding and language generation quality are somewhat separable failure modes in this modular architecture. Captioning models trained primarily on web alt-text style data can produce generic, low-detail captions ('a photo of a dog') that miss task-relevant specifics.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: BLIP-2 with a frozen FlanT5 LLM, given an image of a kitchen and the question 'What appliance is on the counter?', uses the Q-Former to extract visual features relevant to the question (via the Q-Former's learned queries attending to the frozen image encoder's output), prefixes these to the question text, and the frozen FlanT5 generates 'A toaster' (or similar) — demonstrating zero-shot VQA without any VQA-specific fine-tuning of the LLM itself, purely through the Q-Former bridge having been trained to produce LLM-digestible visual representations.
