4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: LLaVA (Large Language and Vision Assistant) connects a pretrained vision encoder (CLIP's ViT) to a pretrained LLM (e.g. Vicuna/LLaMA) via a simple projection layer, then applies instruction tuning on a dataset of (image, instruction, response) triples — generated using GPT-4 to create rich visual instruction-following data — to produce a multimodal chat assistant.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: Earlier vision-language models (BLIP-2, etc.) were good at specific tasks (captioning, VQA) but not at open-ended, instruction-following multimodal conversation in the style of ChatGPT. LLaVA's goal was to extend the instruction-tuning paradigm (which made text-only LLMs into helpful chat assistants) to the multimodal setting, using a simple architecture and a novel data-generation approach to create training data for visual instruction-following.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: Architecture: a frozen (or later, fine-tuned) CLIP ViT image encoder produces visual features; a simple linear (or small MLP) projection layer maps these visual features into the same embedding space as the LLM's token embeddings; these projected visual tokens are prepended to the text instruction tokens and fed into the LLM, which generates a response autoregressively (causal self-attention over both visual and text tokens). Training data generation: existing image-caption/bounding-box datasets are converted into rich (instruction, response) conversational data by prompting GPT-4 (text-only, given detailed textual descriptions of the image's content) to generate plausible multi-turn conversations, detailed descriptions, and complex reasoning Q&A about the image — producing diverse visual instruction data without manual annotation. Training proceeds in stages: first align the projection layer (keeping vision encoder and LLM frozen), then end-to-end instruction-tune (often unfreezing the LLM too).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Building open-ended visual chat assistants (answer questions about images, follow visual instructions, multi-turn visual dialogue), or as a base architecture/recipe for creating domain-specific visual assistants by fine-tuning on domain-specific visual instruction data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks needing precise pixel-level/spatial outputs (segmentation masks, exact bounding box coordinates) without architectural extensions — LLaVA's projection-based visual tokens provide global/regional semantic information well-suited to language-based reasoning but aren't designed for precise spatial localisation outputs.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: The simple linear projection layer is a relatively narrow 'bottleneck' between vision and language — very fine-grained visual details (small text in images, precise counting, exact spatial layouts) may not survive this projection well, leading to hallucinated or imprecise responses about fine details. Because training data is partly GPT-4-generated (text-only, from image descriptions/annotations, not the actual images), any errors or biases in the source annotations or in GPT-4's text-based 'imagination' of the image propagate into the visual instruction-tuning data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: Given a photo of a refrigerator's interior and the instruction 'What ingredients do I have for making a sandwich?', LLaVA's projected visual tokens (derived from CLIP's representation of the image) combined with the LLM's reasoning ability let it generate a conversational response identifying relevant items (bread, cheese, lettuce) visible in the image and reasoning about sandwich-making — a flexible, open-ended interaction that earlier task-specific VQA models (constrained to short factual answers) couldn't provide.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_it_is: Flamingo (DeepMind) is a vision-language model architecture designed for few-shot learning on multimodal tasks — given a few examples of (image/video, text) pairs in the prompt, it can perform new vision-language tasks (VQA, captioning, classification) without any gradient updates, analogous to GPT-3's text-only few-shot in-context learning but extended to interleaved sequences of images/videos and text.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.why_it_exists: GPT-3 showed that large language models could perform new tasks from a few in-context examples without fine-tuning. Flamingo extended this in-context few-shot paradigm to multimodal inputs — enabling a single pretrained model to be 'prompted' with a handful of example (image, caption) or (image, question, answer) pairs and then generalise to new images/questions, without task-specific fine-tuning, important for rapid adaptation to new visual tasks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.how_it_works: Flamingo combines a frozen pretrained vision encoder (processing images/video frames into feature maps) and a frozen pretrained LLM, bridged by two novel components trained from scratch: a 'Perceiver Resampler' that converts the vision encoder's variable-size spatial/temporal features into a fixed (small) number of visual tokens regardless of input image/video size, and 'gated cross-attention' layers interleaved within the frozen LLM's existing layers, which let the LLM attend to the visual tokens at each layer (the gating allows the model to learn how much to rely on visual information, initialised to preserve the frozen LLM's original text-only behaviour at the start of training). Training uses large-scale interleaved image-text web data (sequences where images and text are naturally interspersed, like web pages), teaching the model to process arbitrary interleavings of visual and textual content — directly enabling the few-shot prompting format (example1_image, example1_text, example2_image, example2_text, ..., query_image, ?).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.use_when: Tasks requiring rapid adaptation to new visual task formats via a few in-context examples rather than fine-tuning — useful when labelled fine-tuning data is scarce but a handful of demonstration examples can specify the desired task format (e.g. a specific VQA answer style, or a niche visual classification task).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.avoid_when: Avoid when fine-tuning data is plentiful and a task-specific fine-tuned model would be more accurate/efficient than relying on in-context examples at every inference call (few-shot prompting adds the example images/text to every prompt, increasing inference cost). Avoid for tasks needing precise spatial/pixel-level outputs — like other Perceiver-Resampler-based approaches, the fixed small number of visual tokens is a compressed summary, not preserving full spatial resolution.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.what_goes_wrong: Performance is sensitive to the choice and ordering of few-shot examples in the prompt (similar to text-only in-context learning's known sensitivity to example selection/order), so 'few-shot' results can vary significantly depending on which examples happen to be chosen. The Perceiver Resampler's fixed-size visual token bottleneck means very detailed or multi-object scenes must be compressed into the same number of tokens as simple scenes, potentially losing information for complex images.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Vision Transformers|.real_example: Given a Flamingo prompt containing two example pairs — (image of a cat, 'This is a cat'), (image of a dog, 'This is a dog') — followed by a new image of a rabbit and no text, Flamingo can generate 'This is a rabbit' by recognising the in-context pattern (image -> 'This is a {animal}') from the two examples and applying it to the new image, demonstrating few-shot task specification purely through the prompt, without any gradient updates to the model's weights.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.what_it_is: Greedy decoding generates text by, at each step, picking the single highest-probability token (argmax of the model's output distribution) and feeding it back as input for the next step — the simplest possible decoding strategy.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.why_it_exists: Generating text requires converting the model's probability distribution over the vocabulary at each step into an actual sequence of discrete tokens. Greedy decoding is the most straightforward way to do this: always take the locally optimal choice, requiring no extra hyperparameters and minimal computation.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.how_it_works: At step t, compute P(token | context) over the vocabulary, select token_t = argmax(P), append it to the context, and repeat until an end-of-sequence token is generated or a maximum length is reached. Each step is deterministic — given the same model and prompt, greedy decoding always produces the exact same output.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.use_when: Tasks where determinism/reproducibility matters and a single 'best guess' output is appropriate: factual short-answer QA, code completion where the most likely token is usually correct, or any setting where evaluation requires deterministic outputs (e.g. comparing model outputs across runs/checkpoints).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.avoid_when: Avoid for open-ended creative generation (stories, brainstorming) where diversity/creativity matters — greedy decoding tends to produce generic, repetitive, bland text. Avoid when locally-optimal choices lead to globally poor sequences — greedy decoding has no lookahead, so it can paint itself into a corner.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.what_goes_wrong: Greedy decoding is prone to repetition loops — once a phrase becomes likely to repeat (a known degenerate behaviour of language models), greedy decoding has no mechanism to escape it, producing text like 'I think I think I think...'. It also can't represent any uncertainty in the model's output — even when the model assigns similar probability to two very different continuations, greedy decoding commits to one with no signal of the alternative. Locally optimal token choices can lead to globally suboptimal sequences (the classic motivation for beam search).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|G.real_example: Asking a language model 'Once upon a time' with greedy decoding might produce a bland, generic continuation like 'there was a girl who lived in a small village. She was a kind and gentle girl who loved to help others.' — grammatically correct and locally plausible at every step, but lacking the creativity or surprising turns that sampling-based methods (top-p, temperature) would introduce.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.what_it_is: Beam search is a decoding strategy that maintains the top-B most probable partial sequences ('beams') at each step, expanding each by all possible next tokens and keeping only the overall top-B resulting sequences — a middle ground between greedy decoding (B=1) and exhaustive search.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.why_it_exists: Greedy decoding's locally-optimal choices can lead to globally suboptimal sequences — a slightly lower-probability first token might lead to a much higher-probability overall sequence. Beam search hedges against this by tracking multiple candidate sequences in parallel, increasing the chance of finding a higher total-probability sequence than greedy's single path, without the exponential cost of considering every possible sequence.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.how_it_works: At each step, for each of the current B beams, compute the probability distribution over the next token and consider all B x |vocabulary| extensions; keep only the B extensions with highest cumulative sequence log-probability (sum of log P for all tokens so far) to form the new set of B beams. Continue until all beams produce an end-of-sequence token or reach max length; return the beam with highest total (often length-normalised) log-probability.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.use_when: Tasks with a relatively 'correct' target output where higher overall sequence probability correlates with better quality: machine translation, summarisation (especially extractive-leaning abstractive summarisation), and other tasks evaluated by metrics like BLEU/ROUGE that reward closeness to a reference.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.avoid_when: Avoid for open-ended generation (chat, creative writing) — beam search tends to produce generic, repetitive output (even more so than greedy in some cases) because high-probability sequences in language models tend to be bland/common phrasings; it also lacks any notion of diversity across beams without additional techniques (diverse beam search).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.what_goes_wrong: Beam search famously favours shorter sequences without length normalisation (since each additional token multiplies cumulative probability by a value <1, longer sequences have lower raw probability) — practical implementations apply a length penalty to counteract this. Increasing beam size doesn't monotonically improve human-judged quality for many generation tasks beyond a certain point (and can even degrade BLEU/quality in some neural MT settings) — 'more search isn't always better' is a well-documented finding for neural sequence models. Beam search is computationally more expensive than greedy (B times the per-step cost) and incompatible with some sampling-based diversity techniques.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|B.real_example: Neural machine translation systems commonly use beam search with B=4 or 5 and a length penalty — for translating 'Das ist gut' to English, beam search might consider 'That is good', 'This is good', 'That's good', etc. in parallel and select the one with highest overall sequence probability (often 'That is good' or 'This is good' depending on the model), generally producing more fluent/accurate translations than greedy decoding for this kind of task with a well-defined 'correct' answer space.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.what_it_is: Top-k sampling restricts the next-token distribution to only the k highest-probability tokens, renormalises their probabilities to sum to 1, and samples randomly from this restricted distribution — introducing controlled randomness while excluding very-low-probability (likely nonsensical) tokens.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.why_it_exists: Pure random sampling from the full vocabulary distribution occasionally samples extremely low-probability tokens (the 'long tail'), which can derail generation into incoherent text. Top-k sampling caps the candidate pool to the k most plausible options, preserving diversity (unlike greedy/beam) while avoiding the long tail's incoherence risk.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.how_it_works: At each step, sort the vocabulary by P(token|context), keep only the top k tokens, renormalise their probabilities (divide each by the sum of the top-k probabilities so they sum to 1), and sample from this distribution. k is a fixed hyperparameter (common values: 40-100) chosen independent of how 'peaked' or 'flat' the actual distribution is at any given step.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.use_when: General-purpose text generation where some randomness/diversity is desired but you want to avoid the worst tail-risk tokens — often combined with temperature and/or top-p for finer control, as in most chat/completion APIs' default sampling configurations.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.avoid_when: Avoid using top-k alone (without top-p) when the model's distribution varies dramatically in 'peakiness' across steps — a fixed k can be too restrictive when the model is very confident (only 1-2 tokens are reasonable, but top-k forces consideration of k tokens including poor ones) or too permissive when the model is very uncertain (k tokens might still include implausible options if the distribution is very flat across many tokens).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.what_goes_wrong: A fixed k doesn't adapt to the shape of the distribution: for a very confident prediction (e.g. completing 'The capital of France is' where 'Paris' has 95% probability), top-k=40 still includes 39 other much-less-likely tokens as sampling candidates, introducing unnecessary risk of an odd token. For a very uncertain prediction (many plausible continuations with similar low probabilities), top-k=40 might exclude reasonable options ranked 41+. This adaptivity problem is exactly what top-p (nucleus) sampling addresses.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.real_example: With top-k=50, generating from the prompt 'My favorite food is' considers only the 50 most likely next tokens (e.g. 'pizza', 'sushi', 'pasta', 'tacos', ... down to less common but still food-related words), excluding the vast majority of the vocabulary (function words, unrelated nouns) that would have near-zero probability anyway — producing varied but generally sensible completions across multiple samples.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.what_it_is: Top-p (nucleus) sampling selects the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p (e.g. 0.9), renormalises probabilities over this 'nucleus' set, and samples from it — adapting the candidate pool size dynamically based on the model's confidence at each step.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.why_it_exists: Top-k's fixed candidate count doesn't adapt to how confident/uncertain the model is at each step. Top-p instead adapts: when the model is very confident (probability mass concentrated in few tokens), the nucleus is small; when uncertain (mass spread across many tokens), the nucleus is larger — directly addressing top-k's main weakness.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.how_it_works: Sort tokens by probability in descending order; accumulate probabilities until the cumulative sum first exceeds threshold p (e.g. 0.9); this set of tokens forms the 'nucleus'. Renormalise their probabilities to sum to 1 and sample from this distribution. The size of the nucleus varies per step: it might be just 1-2 tokens when the model is very confident, or dozens/hundreds of tokens when the distribution is flat.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.use_when: The most common default sampling method for general-purpose LLM text generation (chat assistants, creative writing, code generation with some variability) — typical values are p=0.9 to 0.95, often combined with a moderate temperature.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.avoid_when: Avoid when strict determinism is required (use greedy/argmax instead — set do_sample=False). For tasks with a single objectively correct output (precise factual lookups, code that must compile exactly), sampling-based methods including top-p introduce unnecessary risk of incorrect output compared to greedy/beam search.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.what_goes_wrong: Setting p too high (close to 1.0) approaches full random sampling, including the incoherent long tail. Setting p too low (e.g. 0.5) can make outputs nearly as repetitive/bland as greedy decoding. Combining top-p with top-k and temperature simultaneously (common in practice) creates a compound hyperparameter space where the individual effects of each parameter can be hard to disentangle when debugging generation quality issues.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.real_example: With top-p=0.9, if the model's distribution for the next token after 'The weather today is' is {sunny: 0.4, cloudy: 0.25, rainy: 0.15, windy: 0.1, ...long tail...}, the nucleus would include 'sunny', 'cloudy', 'rainy', 'windy' (cumulative ~0.9) and exclude the long tail of implausible words — but if instead the distribution after 'The capital of France is' were {Paris: 0.97, ...}, the nucleus might contain just 'Paris' alone (already exceeding p=0.9), effectively behaving like greedy decoding for that highly-confident step — this adaptivity is top-p's key advantage over fixed top-k.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.what_it_is: Temperature is a scalar hyperparameter (typically 0 to ~2) that divides the model's output logits before applying softmax, controlling how 'sharp' or 'flat' the resulting probability distribution is — lower temperature makes the distribution more peaked (more deterministic/confident), higher temperature makes it flatter (more random/diverse).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.why_it_exists: The model's raw logits/softmax distribution reflects its trained confidence, but the 'right' amount of randomness for generation depends on the task — sometimes you want the model's most confident answer (low temperature), sometimes you want more variety/creativity (higher temperature). Temperature provides a single, simple knob to adjust this trade-off without changing the model itself.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.how_it_works: Given raw logits z, the softmax with temperature T computes P(token_i) = exp(z_i / T) / sum_j exp(z_j / T). As T -> 0, the distribution approaches a one-hot at the argmax (equivalent to greedy decoding). As T -> 1, it's the model's unmodified distribution. As T increases beyond 1, the distribution flattens toward uniform, increasing the relative probability of less-likely tokens being sampled. T must be > 0 (T=0 is typically implemented as a special case equal to argmax/greedy, since dividing by 0 is undefined).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.use_when: Creative/open-ended generation (stories, brainstorming, varied chat responses) benefits from temperature around 0.7-1.0. Factual/precise tasks (code, math, extraction) benefit from low temperature (0-0.3) or greedy decoding to favour the model's most confident predictions.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.avoid_when: Avoid very high temperatures (>1.5) for most practical applications — the distribution becomes close enough to uniform that output quality degrades into near-randomness/incoherence. Avoid relying on temperature alone for diversity if the underlying issue is the model's training (e.g. mode collapse to certain phrasings) — temperature adjusts sampling, not the model's learned distribution itself.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.what_goes_wrong: Temperature interacts with top-k/top-p in non-obvious ways — the order of operations (temperature scaling typically applied before top-k/top-p filtering) and combined parameter settings can produce different results than tuning each independently. Setting temperature to exactly 0 requires special-casing (division by zero) in implementations — most APIs treat temperature=0 as 'use greedy decoding' rather than literally computing softmax with T=0.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|T.real_example: For a creative writing prompt, temperature=1.2 might produce a more surprising/varied continuation ('The dragon, surprisingly, asked for a cup of tea') versus temperature=0.3 producing a more conventional one ('The dragon roared and breathed fire') — both technically sampled from the same underlying model, but temperature reshapes how much probability mass less-likely-but-still-plausible tokens receive, directly affecting perceived 'creativity' of outputs from chat APIs where this is a commonly exposed user-facing parameter.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.what_it_is: Repetition penalty is a decoding-time adjustment that reduces the probability of tokens that have already appeared in the generated sequence (or recent context), discouraging the model from repeating words/phrases.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.why_it_exists: Language models, especially with greedy or low-temperature decoding, are prone to degenerate repetition loops ('the the the' or repeating entire sentences) — repetition penalty directly counteracts this tendency by making previously-used tokens less attractive for re-selection.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.how_it_works: Two common implementations: (1) a multiplicative/divisive penalty — for each token that has appeared in the generated sequence so far, divide its logit by a penalty factor (>1) if positive or multiply if negative, before applying softmax, reducing its probability of being selected again; (2) frequency/presence penalties (as in OpenAI's API) — subtract a value proportional to how many times a token has appeared (frequency penalty) or a flat value if it has appeared at all (presence penalty) from its logit. A related but distinct technique, 'no-repeat n-gram', hard-blocks (sets probability to 0) any n-gram that would exactly duplicate one already generated.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.use_when: Any generation task prone to repetition — long-form generation (stories, articles), summarisation, or whenever a model exhibits the repetition-loop failure mode, especially with greedy/low-temperature decoding.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.avoid_when: Avoid high repetition penalties for tasks where legitimate repetition is needed — e.g. code generation (variable names, keywords like 'if'/'return' naturally repeat often), or text that legitimately requires repeated terms (technical/legal writing with consistent terminology) — over-penalising repetition can force the model to use awkward synonyms or avoid necessary repeated terms.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.what_goes_wrong: Setting the penalty too high can make the model avoid necessary function words or repeated technical terms, producing unnatural text that awkwardly substitutes synonyms to avoid repetition ('the the the' avoided by becoming 'the, that, this, said'). 'No-repeat n-gram' hard constraints can make the model unable to produce legitimately-repeated short phrases (e.g. a poem with an intentional refrain), causing it to generate something different (and possibly worse) just to satisfy the constraint.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|R.real_example: Without repetition penalty, a model generating a product description might fall into 'This product is great. This product is great. This product is great.' under greedy decoding — applying a repetition penalty of ~1.2 (dividing logits of already-used tokens by 1.2) makes 'This product is great' less likely to be re-selected verbatim, pushing the model toward 'This product is great. It also offers excellent durability.' — breaking the loop while still allowing the topic to continue.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.what_it_is: Contrastive search is a decoding method that selects, at each step, the token that has both high model probability AND low similarity to previous tokens' representations — explicitly balancing coherence (probability) against diversity/non-repetitiveness (representation dissimilarity), aiming to avoid both incoherent random sampling and degenerate repetition.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.why_it_exists: Greedy/beam decoding produces coherent but repetitive/degenerate text; sampling-based methods (top-k/top-p) introduce diversity but can sacrifice coherence and still don't directly address the 'model assigns artificially high probability to repeated content' issue (a phenomenon called the 'anisotropy' of language model representations, where repeated tokens' hidden states become very similar to each other). Contrastive search directly targets this by penalising candidates whose hidden representation is too similar to recent tokens' representations.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.how_it_works: At each step, identify the top-k candidate tokens by model probability (a small candidate set, like top-k sampling but used deterministically). For each candidate, compute a 'degeneration penalty' — the maximum cosine similarity between this candidate's hidden representation (if selected) and the hidden representations of all previous tokens in the generated sequence. The final score for each candidate is a weighted combination: (1-alpha) * model_probability - alpha * degeneration_penalty. The candidate with the highest combined score is selected deterministically (no random sampling involved, unlike top-k/top-p) — alpha controls the trade-off between fluency (probability) and diversity (low similarity to past tokens).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.use_when: Open-ended generation tasks (story generation, dialogue) where you want deterministic, reproducible outputs (unlike sampling) but also want to avoid the repetition degeneration that greedy/beam search exhibit — contrastive search has been shown to produce higher-quality open-ended generations than both greedy/beam and sampling-based methods in some evaluations, while remaining deterministic.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.avoid_when: Avoid when computational overhead matters significantly — contrastive search requires computing and comparing hidden-state similarities at each step, which is more expensive than simple probability-based selection (sampling or greedy). For tasks with a clear single correct answer (extraction, classification-as-generation), simpler greedy decoding suffices and the diversity-promoting mechanism of contrastive search is unnecessary.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.what_goes_wrong: The alpha hyperparameter (trade-off between probability and degeneration penalty) requires tuning — too high emphasises diversity at the cost of coherence/fluency, too low reduces to near-greedy behaviour with the repetition problems contrastive search was meant to solve. The technique's benefits are most pronounced for open-ended generation; for tasks with narrow correct-answer distributions, the added complexity may not yield measurable improvement over simpler methods.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|C.real_example: Generating a long story with greedy decoding might degenerate into repeating a character's name and a stock phrase ('Then John said, "I see." Then John said, "I see."'); contrastive search, by penalising tokens whose representation is too similar to the recent 'Then John said, "I see."' tokens, steers the generation toward a different (but still high-probability) continuation, breaking the loop deterministically — without introducing the randomness that top-p sampling would, which matters for applications needing reproducible outputs.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.what_it_is: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by using a small, fast 'draft' model to propose multiple tokens ahead speculatively, then having the large target model verify (in a single parallel forward pass) which of those drafted tokens it would have generated itself — accepting the matching prefix and only falling back to standard generation where they diverge.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.why_it_exists: Autoregressive generation with a large model is inherently sequential — one forward pass per token, dominated by memory-bandwidth (loading model weights) rather than compute, especially for a single sequence (low arithmetic intensity). Speculative decoding exploits the fact that verifying multiple tokens in parallel (one forward pass scoring K draft tokens) costs roughly the same as generating one token, since the large model's forward pass is memory-bound regardless of how many positions it scores in that pass — turning 'K sequential large-model steps' into 'K small-model steps + 1 large-model verification step'.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.how_it_works: A small draft model (much cheaper per-token, e.g. a distilled/smaller version of the target model, or even an n-gram model) generates K candidate tokens autoregressively (cheap, since it's small). The large target model then processes the original context PLUS these K draft tokens in a single forward pass, computing what ITS probability distribution would have been at each of those K positions. Tokens are accepted from left to right as long as they match what the target model would have sampled (using a rejection-sampling scheme that preserves the target model's exact output distribution, not an approximation); at the first mismatch, the target model's own sample replaces the draft token, and any remaining draft tokens are discarded. This guarantees outputs are distributed identically to standard target-model-only decoding, but with fewer expensive target-model forward passes overall.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.use_when: Latency-sensitive serving of large models where a smaller, faster draft model (from the same model family/tokenizer, or otherwise well-aligned with the target's distribution) is available — particularly effective when the draft model's predictions frequently match the target's (e.g. for predictable text like code, repeated patterns, or when draft and target are closely related models).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.avoid_when: Avoid when no suitable draft model exists or training/maintaining one adds more operational complexity than the latency gain justifies. Avoid when the draft model's predictions rarely match the target's (low acceptance rate) — speedup degrades toward zero (or even becomes a net slowdown due to draft model overhead) if acceptance rates are poor, e.g. for highly unpredictable/creative generation where even the target model's own top choices vary a lot.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.what_goes_wrong: The achievable speedup (commonly cited 2-3x) depends heavily on the draft model's 'alignment' with the target — a draft model that diverges from the target frequently provides little benefit since most draft tokens get rejected, wasting the draft model's compute. Maintaining two models (draft + target) in the serving stack adds operational complexity (two sets of weights to load/manage, potential version-sync issues if either model is updated). The acceptance-sampling scheme must be implemented correctly to preserve the exact target distribution — an incorrect implementation could subtly bias outputs toward the draft model's distribution.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|S.real_example: Serving a 70B-parameter target model with a 7B-parameter draft model from the same family (e.g. both LLaMA-2 variants): for predictable text (e.g. completing a common phrase or generating boilerplate code), the 7B draft model often correctly predicts several tokens in a row that the 70B model would also have chosen, so one 70B forward pass can verify and accept, say, 3-4 tokens at once — yielding close to the cited 2-3x throughput improvement for that portion of generation, with mathematically guaranteed output-distribution equivalence to running the 70B model alone.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.what_it_is: Quantisation reduces the numerical precision of a model's weights (and sometimes activations) from the original training precision (typically FP32/FP16/BF16) down to lower-bit representations like INT8 (8-bit integers) or INT4 (4-bit), reducing memory footprint and often increasing inference speed, at some cost to numerical accuracy. GGUF is a file format (used by llama.cpp and similar tools) for storing quantised models with various bit-widths and quantisation schemes.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.why_it_exists: LLM weights at FP16 require 2 bytes per parameter — a 7B-parameter model needs ~14GB just for weights, often exceeding consumer GPU memory or making CPU inference impractically slow. Quantisation to INT8 (1 byte/param, ~7GB) or INT4 (0.5 bytes/param, ~3.5GB) makes large models runnable on consumer hardware (including CPUs and smaller GPUs), and can also speed up inference on hardware with optimised low-precision kernels.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.how_it_works: Quantisation maps the continuous range of FP16/FP32 weight values to a smaller set of discrete integer levels, typically via a scale factor (and sometimes a zero-point offset) per tensor or per group of weights: quantised_value = round(weight / scale). At inference, weights are dequantised (or computed directly in low-precision with specialised kernels) on the fly. Techniques vary in granularity (per-tensor vs per-channel vs per-group quantisation, where smaller groups preserve more accuracy at the cost of more scale-factor storage) and in whether activations are also quantised (weight-only quantisation, common for INT4/INT8 LLM inference, keeps activations in higher precision since they're more sensitive to quantisation error). GGUF is a binary file format that packages quantised weights (in various schemes like Q4_0, Q4_K_M, Q8_0 — denoting bit-width and grouping strategy) along with model metadata/tokenizer, designed for efficient CPU/GPU-hybrid inference via llama.cpp.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.use_when: Running LLMs on consumer hardware (laptops, single consumer GPUs) where the full-precision model wouldn't fit in available memory, or in production serving where reduced memory footprint allows higher batch sizes/throughput on the same hardware, accepting a small accuracy trade-off.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.avoid_when: Avoid aggressive quantisation (INT4 and below) for tasks highly sensitive to precision (complex multi-step reasoning, precise numerical computation) where accuracy degradation, even if small on average benchmarks, could matter for specific failure cases. Avoid quantising models that will be further fine-tuned without using quantisation-aware fine-tuning techniques (e.g. QLoRA) — naive fine-tuning of quantised weights doesn't work well with standard full-precision gradient updates.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.what_goes_wrong: Quantisation error compounds through the many layers of a deep network — while INT8 is often nearly lossless for LLMs, INT4 and below can measurably degrade performance on harder tasks even if simple benchmarks look similar, and outlier weight values (which are common in trained LLMs) can be poorly represented by uniform quantisation grids unless handled specially (e.g. mixed-precision schemes that keep outliers in higher precision). Choosing the wrong GGUF quantisation level for available hardware (e.g. a quant level that doesn't fit in available RAM/VRAM, or one so aggressive that quality is unacceptable for the task) requires empirical testing per use case.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Decoding & Serving|Q.real_example: A 7B-parameter model at FP16 (~14GB) might be quantised to GGUF Q4_K_M format (~4-4.5GB), enabling it to run on a laptop with 8GB RAM via llama.cpp's CPU/GPU-hybrid inference — at a typically modest (a few percentage points on standard benchmarks) accuracy cost compared to the FP16 original, making the difference between 'cannot run at all on this hardware' and 'runs at usable speed', which is why quantised GGUF models are extremely popular in the local-LLM/hobbyist community.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.what_it_is: Whisper is OpenAI's encoder-decoder (sequence-to-sequence) Transformer model for automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speech translation, trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual, multitask, weakly-supervised audio-text data scraped from the internet.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.why_it_exists: Prior ASR systems typically required training on carefully curated, expensive transcribed datasets (often thousands of hours, manually labelled) and were brittle to accents, background noise, and domain shift. Whisper's bet was that massive scale of weakly-supervised (imperfect but abundant) data — internet audio paired with transcripts/subtitles — could produce a single model that generalises robustly across languages, accents, and acoustic conditions without per-dataset fine-tuning.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.how_it_works: Audio is converted to a log-Mel spectrogram and fed into a standard Transformer encoder (similar architecture to the original 'Attention is All You Need' encoder). A Transformer decoder then autoregressively generates output tokens, conditioned on the encoder output and a sequence of special task tokens (language ID, task type — transcribe vs translate, timestamps on/off) prepended to the decoder input — this multitask token format lets one model handle multiple tasks/languages via prompting rather than separate model heads. The model comes in multiple sizes (tiny through large-v3), trading speed for accuracy.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.use_when: General-purpose speech-to-text across many languages and acoustic conditions (podcasts, meetings, videos, phone calls), especially when you need a robust off-the-shelf model without fine-tuning, or need speech translation (audio in language X -> text in English) in addition to transcription.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.avoid_when: Avoid for real-time/streaming low-latency applications without modification — base Whisper is designed for offline (chunked) processing, not true streaming. Avoid when you need precise word-level timestamps without extra processing — Whisper's native timestamps are approximate and benefit from forced alignment tools. For narrow-domain, high-volume production ASR (e.g. a single language, specific accent/vocabulary like medical dictation), a smaller fine-tuned/specialised model may be more efficient and accurate.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.what_goes_wrong: Whisper is known to 'hallucinate' — generating plausible-sounding text not present in the audio, especially during silences, music, or non-speech segments (a consequence of being trained as a language model that always produces fluent output even with weak acoustic signal). It can also repeat phrases in a loop on long audio with certain decoding settings. Long-form transcription requires chunking audio into ~30-second windows (the model's training context), and naive chunking can cut words/sentences at boundaries, requiring careful handling (e.g. via libraries that implement sliding-window with overlap and timestamp-based stitching).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.real_example: Transcribing a 2-hour multilingual podcast with Whisper large-v3: the model automatically detects the spoken language(s), produces a transcript with reasonable accuracy despite background music and multiple speakers, and (with the 'translate' task token) can directly output an English translation of non-English segments — all from a single model checkpoint, without needing separate ASR + machine-translation pipelines.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.what_it_is: A key practical strength of Whisper is its breadth and robustness: it supports speech recognition and translation across 99 languages (with widely varying amounts of training data per language) and demonstrates strong robustness to background noise, recording quality, and speaker accents compared to prior ASR systems.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.why_it_exists: Real-world audio is messy — phone recordings, accented speech, background noise, overlapping speakers, and rare languages are all common, but most ASR benchmarks/training sets were historically clean, single-accent, single-language. Whisper's massive and diverse weakly-supervised training data (680K hours scraped broadly from the internet, covering many languages, accents, and recording conditions) was specifically intended to produce a model that performs well 'in the wild' rather than just on curated benchmarks.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.how_it_works: The training data's diversity (different languages, accents, recording qualities, and the presence of background noise/music in much of the scraped audio) acts as a form of data augmentation 'for free' — the model implicitly learns to be invariant to many of these nuisance factors because it has seen them at scale during training. Language coverage is highly imbalanced (English dominates, with progressively less data for lower-resource languages), so robustness/accuracy varies significantly by language — well-resourced languages (English, Spanish, German, etc.) perform much better than low-resource ones.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.use_when: Real-world deployment scenarios with unpredictable audio quality: user-generated content (videos, voice messages), call-center recordings, field recordings, or any application serving a global/multilingual user base where a single robust model is preferable to maintaining per-language/per-accent specialised systems.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.avoid_when: Avoid assuming uniform quality across languages — for low-resource languages in Whisper's training mix, accuracy can be substantially worse than for English, and a language-specific fine-tuned model (or a different ASR system entirely) may be necessary for production-quality results in those languages. Avoid for languages not in Whisper's 99-language set at all.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.what_goes_wrong: Performance disparity across languages is a real production risk — a system that 'supports 99 languages' may give excellent English transcripts but poor-quality output for a lower-resource language, creating an inconsistent user experience if not benchmarked per-language before deployment. Robustness to noise has limits — extremely low SNR audio, heavy crosstalk/overlapping speakers, or highly domain-specific jargon/acronyms (medical, legal) can still degrade accuracy significantly, sometimes triggering the hallucination failure mode described for Whisper generally.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Whispe.real_example: A voice-memo transcription app serving users globally might find that Whisper large-v3 produces near-perfect transcripts for English, French, and Spanish memos (even with background traffic noise), but noticeably more errors for a lower-resource language like Swahili or Welsh — prompting the team to either accept the gap, fine-tune on additional in-language data, or supplement with a language-specific ASR model for those locales.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.what_it_is: Wav2Vec 2.0 is a self-supervised representation-learning model for raw audio, pretrained using a contrastive objective that learns to distinguish true latent speech representations from distractors at masked positions — analogous to BERT's masked-language-modelling but applied to continuous audio.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.why_it_exists: Labelled speech data (audio paired with transcripts) is expensive and limited, especially for low-resource languages, while raw (unlabelled) audio is abundant. Wav2Vec 2.0 enables learning powerful audio representations from unlabelled speech alone, which can then be fine-tuned for ASR with much less labelled data than training from scratch.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.how_it_works: Raw audio waveform is passed through a CNN feature encoder to produce a sequence of latent speech representations, which are then partially masked (similar to BERT's token masking). A Transformer encoder processes the (partially masked) sequence to produce contextualised representations. A contrastive loss (similar to InfoNCE) trains the model to identify the true latent representation for a masked position among a set of distractors (other masked positions' quantized representations) — this requires the model to use context to predict what the masked audio segment 'should' represent. A separate quantization module (using Gumbel-softmax over a learned codebook) discretises the targets for the contrastive loss. After self-supervised pretraining, a small amount of labelled data plus a CTC head (or similar) fine-tunes the model for actual transcription.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.use_when: Low-resource ASR settings where labelled data is scarce but unlabelled audio in the target language/domain is available — pretrain (or use a pretrained checkpoint) on unlabelled audio, then fine-tune with limited labelled data. Also useful as a general audio feature extractor for downstream tasks beyond ASR (speaker identification, emotion recognition).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.avoid_when: Avoid when a strong supervised model already exists for your exact language/domain with sufficient labelled data (e.g. Whisper for general multilingual ASR) — the extra complexity of self-supervised pretraining + fine-tuning may not be worth it versus using/fine-tuning an off-the-shelf supervised model. Avoid for real-time streaming without architectural adaptation, similar to other Transformer-based audio models.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.what_goes_wrong: Self-supervised pretraining is computationally expensive (large amounts of unlabelled audio, long training times) — practitioners typically use publicly released pretrained checkpoints rather than pretraining from scratch. The contrastive pretraining objective and the downstream fine-tuning objective (typically CTC loss) are quite different, so the quality of the fine-tuned model depends on how well the self-supervised representations transfer — this transfer quality varies by domain/language match between pretraining and fine-tuning data.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Wav2Ve.real_example: For a low-resource language with only a few hours of transcribed speech, a team might take a Wav2Vec 2.0 model pretrained on a large multilingual unlabelled audio corpus (e.g. via the XLSR cross-lingual variant), then fine-tune it with a CTC head on the small labelled dataset — achieving substantially better ASR accuracy than training a model from scratch on the small labelled set alone, because the pretrained representations already capture general acoustic-phonetic structure.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.what_it_is: A CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) head is an output layer and loss function that allows a neural network to map a sequence of audio frames to a (typically much shorter) sequence of output tokens (characters/subwords) without requiring frame-level alignment labels between audio and transcript.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.why_it_exists: Audio has many more frames (time steps) than the corresponding transcript has characters/tokens, and the exact alignment between audio frames and transcript characters is unknown and variable (people speak at different speeds, with pauses). CTC solves the problem of training a sequence model to produce a shorter output sequence from a longer input sequence, marginalising over all possible alignments, without needing per-frame alignment annotations.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.how_it_works: The model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary (plus a special 'blank' token) at every input frame. CTC defines a many-to-one mapping from frame-level sequences (including blanks and repeated characters) to the final output sequence: consecutive repeated non-blank tokens are collapsed to one, and blanks are removed (e.g. 'h-h-e-_-l-l-o' with blanks/repeats collapses to 'hello'). The CTC loss sums the probabilities over ALL frame-level sequences that map to the correct target sequence, computed efficiently via a dynamic-programming (forward-backward) algorithm, and is differentiable end-to-end. At inference, greedy or beam-search decoding over the frame-level outputs (with the collapse rule applied) produces the final transcript.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.use_when: Building ASR systems where you want a simple, fast, non-autoregressive decoding path (CTC inference can be done in a single forward pass plus a collapse operation, much faster than autoregressive decoder generation) — common as the fine-tuning head for self-supervised audio encoders like Wav2Vec 2.0, or in streaming ASR systems where low latency matters.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.avoid_when: Avoid when you need the output to be a flexible transformation of the input rather than a monotonic alignment — CTC assumes the output sequence is produced in the same order as input frames with no reordering, which works for transcription but not for tasks like translation (where word order can change) — those require encoder-decoder attention-based models instead.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.what_goes_wrong: CTC's conditional-independence assumption (each frame's output is assumed independent given the input, no explicit language-model dependency between output tokens) means CTC-only models can produce locally-plausible-sounding but contextually odd transcriptions, especially for homophones or words requiring broader context to disambiguate — often mitigated by combining CTC with an external language model during decoding (CTC + LM beam search) or using a joint CTC/attention architecture.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|CTC he.real_example: Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuned for ASR adds a linear CTC head on top of the Transformer encoder's output: each of the (downsampled) audio frame representations is mapped to a probability distribution over characters plus blank; CTC loss trains this end-to-end against the transcript text, and at inference, greedy decoding (take argmax per frame, then collapse repeats/blanks) or beam search with a language model produces the final text — all without ever needing frame-by-frame alignment labels in the training data.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.what_it_is: A typical production automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipeline consists of three stages: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) to identify segments of audio containing speech, transcription (the core ASR model converting speech segments to text), and post-processing (formatting, punctuation, capitalisation, profanity filtering, etc.) to produce a final usable transcript.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.why_it_exists: Raw audio streams contain long stretches of silence, background noise, music, or non-speech sounds that waste compute if fed directly to an ASR model, and ASR models often have limited context windows (e.g. Whisper's 30-second chunks) requiring audio to be segmented sensibly. Additionally, raw ASR output is often unformatted (no punctuation, inconsistent casing, filler words) and needs cleanup before being useful to end users or downstream NLP systems.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.how_it_works: VAD (using a lightweight model, e.g. based on energy thresholds or a small neural classifier like Silero VAD) scans the audio stream and outputs timestamps of speech vs non-speech segments, discarding or skipping non-speech regions and producing speech segments of manageable length for the ASR model. The transcription stage runs the ASR model (e.g. Whisper, Wav2Vec2+CTC) on each speech segment, producing raw text (and possibly timestamps/confidence scores). Post-processing then applies steps such as: punctuation restoration (if the ASR model doesn't produce it natively), true-casing/capitalisation, number formatting (e.g. 'twenty twenty four' -> '2024'), removal of filler words/disfluencies if desired, and potentially profanity filtering or PII redaction depending on the application.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.use_when: Any production speech application — call transcription, meeting notes, voice assistants, captioning — benefits from this pipeline structure because it improves efficiency (skip silence), handles long audio (segment appropriately), and produces output that's actually usable (formatted text vs raw model tokens).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.avoid_when: For very short, controlled audio clips (a single short command to a voice assistant) where the entire clip is known to contain speech, VAD may be unnecessary overhead — directly transcribing the clip suffices. Avoid over-engineering post-processing for internal/debugging use cases where raw transcript output is sufficient.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.what_goes_wrong: Poorly tuned VAD can cut off the beginning/end of speech segments (clipping words) or fail to merge segments separated by brief pauses, causing the ASR model to receive fragmented context and produce worse transcriptions at segment boundaries. Post-processing steps like punctuation restoration and true-casing are themselves models/heuristics that can introduce their own errors (e.g. incorrect sentence boundaries changing meaning). Pipeline latency is the sum of all stages — for real-time applications, each stage must be fast enough, and buffering/segmentation strategy directly impacts perceived responsiveness.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|ASR pi.real_example: A meeting-transcription product processes a 1-hour recording by first running VAD to identify ~200 speech segments (skipping silent pauses and background noise between speakers), transcribing each segment with Whisper, then post-processing the concatenated output to add punctuation, capitalise proper nouns, and format numbers/times — turning raw model output like 'so the meeting is at three pm tomorrow right' into 'So the meeting is at 3 PM tomorrow, right?'

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.what_it_is: Speaker diarisation is the task of partitioning an audio stream into segments labelled by 'who spoke when' — answering 'speaker A said this, then speaker B said that' — without necessarily knowing the speakers' actual identities (unless combined with speaker identification/recognition).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.why_it_exists: ASR alone produces a single stream of text without attribution to individual speakers, but many applications (meeting transcripts, call-centre analytics, podcast transcription) need to know which speaker said what — diarisation adds this 'who' dimension to the 'what' that ASR provides.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.how_it_works: A typical pipeline: (1) VAD to find speech regions; (2) segment the speech into short windows and extract speaker-embedding vectors for each window (using a model trained for speaker verification, producing embeddings where same-speaker segments are close in embedding space and different-speaker segments are far apart); (3) cluster these embeddings (e.g. via agglomerative clustering or spectral clustering) to group segments by speaker, without knowing the number of speakers in advance (often estimated from the clustering structure); (4) optionally refine segment boundaries with resegmentation. The output is a sequence of (start_time, end_time, speaker_label) tuples, which can then be merged with ASR transcripts to produce speaker-attributed text.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.use_when: Multi-speaker audio where speaker attribution matters: meeting transcription, interview/podcast transcripts, call-centre conversations (agent vs customer), or any analytics that need per-speaker statistics (talk time, sentiment per speaker).
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.avoid_when: Avoid for single-speaker audio (no diarisation needed) or when speaker identity doesn't matter for the application (e.g. simple voice commands). Diarisation adds latency and complexity that's wasted if the use case never needs 'who said what'.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.what_goes_wrong: Diarisation error rate (DER) is affected by overlapping speech (multiple people talking simultaneously) — most diarisation systems struggle with overlap since they assign one speaker label per time segment, missing or misattributing overlapping speech. Estimating the correct number of speakers automatically is error-prone (especially with brief contributions from minor speakers). Combining diarisation output with ASR transcripts requires careful timestamp alignment — mismatches between ASR segment boundaries and diarisation segment boundaries can cause text to be attributed to the wrong speaker, especially at speaker-change points.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Speake.real_example: A call-centre QA tool processes recorded calls by running diarisation to separate 'Speaker 1' (agent) and 'Speaker 2' (customer) segments, then runs ASR on each segment and merges results into a transcript like 'Agent: How can I help you today? / Customer: I'm having trouble with my order. / Agent: I'm sorry to hear that...' — enabling per-speaker analytics (e.g. agent talk-time ratio, sentiment analysis per speaker) that wouldn't be possible from an undifferentiated transcript.

4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.what_it_is: Text-to-speech (TTS) is the task of converting written text into spoken audio — the inverse of ASR — typically involving converting text into an intermediate acoustic representation (e.g. a mel-spectrogram) via a text-to-spectrogram model, then converting that representation into a raw audio waveform via a vocoder.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.why_it_exists: Many applications need to produce spoken output from text: voice assistants responding to users, accessibility tools (screen readers), audiobook/podcast generation, and conversational AI systems with voice interfaces. TTS provides the 'speaking' half of a voice-based interaction, complementing ASR's 'listening' half.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.how_it_works: Modern neural TTS typically uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) a text-to-spectrogram model (historically models like Tacotron 2, or newer Transformer/diffusion-based architectures) takes input text (often after normalisation — expanding abbreviations, numbers, etc. — and sometimes phoneme conversion) and predicts a mel-spectrogram representing the target audio's time-frequency content, often with an attention or duration-prediction mechanism to align text units with output frames; (2) a vocoder (e.g. WaveNet, HiFi-GAN, or other neural vocoders) converts the mel-spectrogram into a raw audio waveform. Some newer end-to-end systems combine these stages or use other generative approaches (flow-based, diffusion, or large audio-language-model-based generation) to go directly from text/tokens to waveform. Voice characteristics (timbre, prosody, accent) can be controlled via speaker embeddings (for multi-speaker/voice-cloning models) or explicit prosody controls.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.use_when: Any application needing synthesised speech output: voice assistants, accessibility (screen readers, audiobooks), IVR systems, language-learning apps, or conversational AI products with audio responses.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.avoid_when: Avoid TTS for applications where text output suffices and audio adds no value (most chat interfaces) — TTS adds computational cost and latency. For applications requiring extremely natural, emotionally nuanced, or specific celebrity/cloned voices, off-the-shelf TTS may not meet quality bars without significant fine-tuning, and voice cloning raises consent/ethical/legal considerations that must be addressed.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.what_goes_wrong: Text normalisation errors (e.g. mishandling abbreviations, numbers, or unusual proper nouns) lead to mispronunciations — '$5' might be read as 'dollar five' instead of 'five dollars' if normalisation rules are incomplete. Prosody (intonation, stress, rhythm) can sound unnatural or robotic, especially for long/complex sentences, questions, or text with emotional content the model wasn't trained to express. Voice cloning capabilities raise misuse concerns (deepfake audio) — production systems often include safeguards (consent verification, watermarking) to mitigate this.
4|🔴 T1 Transformers|Speech Models|Text-t.real_example: A navigation app converts the text 'Turn left on Main St. in 200 ft' to speech: text normalisation expands 'St.' to 'Street' and 'ft' to 'feet', a TTS model (e.g. a Tacotron-2-style model + HiFi-GAN vocoder) generates a mel-spectrogram and then a waveform with natural-sounding prosody emphasising 'left' and '200 feet', producing clear spoken directions — issues arise if abbreviation expansion is incomplete (e.g. 'St.' ambiguously meaning 'Saint' vs 'Street' depending on context, like 'St. Mary's St.').

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_it_is: Sentence-BERT (SBERT) is a modification of BERT that fine-tunes it in a Siamese/twin-network configuration (two copies of the same model with shared weights, processing two inputs in parallel) to produce sentence-level embeddings whose cosine similarity (or Euclidean distance) directly reflects semantic similarity, enabling efficient sentence comparison.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.why_it_exists: Vanilla BERT produces token-level contextual embeddings, and computing sentence similarity with BERT requires feeding sentence pairs jointly through the model (cross-encoder style) — accurate but O(n^2) for finding similar pairs among n sentences, since every pair must be processed together. SBERT enables encoding each sentence independently into a fixed-size vector once, after which similarity is a cheap vector operation (cosine similarity) — reducing pairwise comparison from a full model forward pass per pair to a dot product, making large-scale semantic search/clustering feasible.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.how_it_works: Two sentences are each passed through the same BERT encoder (shared weights — a Siamese network) to get token embeddings, which are pooled (commonly mean-pooling over token embeddings, sometimes with the [CLS] token or max-pooling) into a single fixed-size sentence embedding per sentence. During fine-tuning, the two sentence embeddings are combined (e.g. concatenated with their element-wise difference, for classification objectives like NLI; or compared via cosine similarity for regression objectives like semantic textual similarity) and a loss (cross-entropy for classification, MSE for similarity regression, or contrastive/triplet losses) trains the model so that semantically similar sentences end up with high cosine similarity in embedding space.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.use_when: Any task requiring fast similarity computation across many sentences/documents: semantic search, clustering, deduplication, paraphrase mining, or as the encoder in a retrieval system (bi-encoder retrieval) — essentially any time you need to compare a sentence against many others efficiently.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.avoid_when: Avoid when maximum accuracy on a single pair comparison matters more than speed — a cross-encoder (processing the pair jointly) is generally more accurate for pairwise similarity/relevance scoring than the independently-pooled SBERT embeddings, because it can model token-level interactions between the two texts directly.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_goes_wrong: The choice of pooling strategy (mean vs CLS vs max) significantly affects embedding quality and isn't always obvious — mean-pooling over all tokens is generally found to work better than using the [CLS] token for SBERT-style models, but this isn't true for all base models. Off-the-shelf SBERT models trained on general-domain data (e.g. NLI, STS benchmarks) may not transfer well to specialised domains (legal, medical, code) without domain-specific fine-tuning — embeddings might cluster by superficial lexical similarity rather than the semantic relationships that matter for the target domain.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.real_example: To deduplicate a database of 1 million customer support tickets, encoding each ticket once with SBERT into a 384 or 768-dimensional vector allows finding near-duplicate tickets via approximate nearest-neighbour search over the precomputed vectors (e.g. using FAISS) in seconds — whereas a cross-encoder approach comparing every pair would require ~5*10^11 model forward passes, computationally infeasible at this scale.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_it_is: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, E5, and BGE are families of widely-used open-source sentence/text embedding models: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a small, fast, distilled SBERT-style model (6 layers, 384-dim embeddings) popular for general-purpose semantic similarity; E5 (from Microsoft) and BGE (from BAAI) are families of embedding models trained with large-scale contrastive pretraining plus instruction-aware fine-tuning, generally achieving stronger retrieval performance, especially at larger sizes.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.why_it_exists: Different applications have different trade-offs between embedding quality, model size/speed, and embedding dimensionality (which affects storage and search cost in vector databases). This spectrum of models — from MiniLM's lightweight efficiency to E5/BGE's higher accuracy at larger compute cost — gives practitioners options across this trade-off space, and their open-source availability (vs proprietary API-only embeddings) enables self-hosting and fine-tuning.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.how_it_works: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is produced via knowledge distillation from a larger BERT-based model into a 6-layer MiniLM architecture, then fine-tuned with SBERT-style contrastive/similarity objectives on large sentence-pair datasets. E5 and BGE models are typically pretrained with weakly-supervised contrastive learning on massive web-scraped text pairs (e.g. titles paired with passages, question-answer pairs) using an InfoNCE-style loss, then fine-tuned on labelled retrieval/similarity datasets — both also commonly use 'instruction prefixes' (e.g. prepending 'query: ' or 'passage: ' to inputs, or task-specific instructions for E5) that the model was trained to expect, which significantly affects embedding quality if omitted at inference time.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.use_when: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for resource-constrained settings, prototyping, or applications where speed/cost matters more than top-tier accuracy. E5/BGE (especially larger variants, e.g. BGE-large or E5-large) for production retrieval systems where embedding quality directly impacts search relevance and the additional compute cost is justified — both are common choices for self-hosted RAG pipelines.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.avoid_when: Avoid all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for highly nuanced semantic distinctions or specialised domains where its smaller capacity limits representational power. Avoid E5/BGE without using their expected instruction/prefix format — using them 'naively' (without the prefixes they were trained with) can significantly underperform their benchmarked results.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting model-specific input formatting conventions (E5's 'query:'/'passage:' prefixes, or BGE's instruction prefixes for queries) is a common and easy-to-miss mistake that silently degrades retrieval quality without throwing any error — the model still produces embeddings, just lower-quality ones for the intended task. Mixing embeddings from different model versions/dimensions in the same vector index is invalid (cosine similarity between embeddings from different models is meaningless) — re-indexing is required after switching embedding models.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.real_example: A RAG pipeline switching from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim, fast) to BGE-large (1024-dim, more accurate) for better retrieval quality must: (1) re-embed and re-index the entire document corpus (since the embedding spaces are incompatible), (2) update the vector DB schema for the new dimensionality, and (3) for BGE, prepend the recommended instruction prefix to queries (e.g. 'Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ') — skipping step 3 is a common oversight that leaves retrieval quality below BGE's benchmarked potential despite the larger model.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_it_is: A bi-encoder is a retrieval architecture where the query and each candidate document are independently encoded into fixed-size vectors (using the same or different encoder models), and relevance is computed as a similarity metric (cosine similarity or dot product) between these vectors — enabling document embeddings to be precomputed and indexed for fast retrieval.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.why_it_exists: For retrieval over large document collections (millions+), comparing a query against every document via a joint model (cross-encoder) is computationally infeasible at query time. Bi-encoders solve this by separating encoding (done once, offline, for all documents) from comparison (a cheap vector operation at query time), enabling sub-linear search via approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indices.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.how_it_works: An encoder model (often a fine-tuned BERT/SBERT variant) maps each document to a dense vector, computed offline and stored in a vector index (e.g. FAISS, HNSW). At query time, the same (or a paired query-specific) encoder maps the query to a vector in the same embedding space; the index returns the k nearest document vectors by cosine similarity or dot product, which become the retrieved candidates. Because document encoding happens offline and query encoding is a single forward pass, retrieval latency is dominated by the ANN search, not model inference over the full corpus.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.use_when: First-stage retrieval over large corpora — almost all production semantic search and RAG systems use a bi-encoder for initial candidate retrieval, often followed by a cross-encoder for reranking (two-stage retrieval).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.avoid_when: Avoid relying on bi-encoder similarity scores alone when precise relevance ranking matters for a small set of top candidates — bi-encoders sacrifice some accuracy for speed by compressing each text into a single vector, losing fine-grained token-level interaction information that cross-encoders capture.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_goes_wrong: Bi-encoders can struggle with queries/documents that require fine-grained token-level matching (e.g. exact phrase matches, negation, numerical comparisons) since all information is compressed into a single fixed-size vector — this 'representation bottleneck' is a known limitation. Domain mismatch between the bi-encoder's training data and the target corpus can cause embeddings to cluster by superficial features (length, topic at a coarse level) rather than the fine-grained relevance signal needed for good retrieval, requiring domain-specific fine-tuning.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.real_example: A documentation search feature encodes all 50,000 help-center articles offline using a bi-encoder (e.g. all-MiniLM-L6-v2) into 384-dim vectors stored in a FAISS HNSW index; when a user searches 'how do I reset my password', the query is encoded once (milliseconds) and the index returns the 20 nearest article vectors in milliseconds — total retrieval latency dominated by the single query encoding plus fast ANN lookup, independent of corpus size beyond the index's sub-linear scaling.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_it_is: A cross-encoder is an architecture where the query and a candidate document are concatenated (with a separator token) and processed jointly through a single Transformer (typically BERT-based), which outputs a single relevance score for that pair — allowing full token-level cross-attention between query and document but requiring a separate forward pass for every query-document pair.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.why_it_exists: Bi-encoders compress each text into a single vector independently, losing information about how specific query terms relate to specific document terms. Cross-encoders allow every query token to attend to every document token (and vice versa) within the Transformer's self-attention, capturing fine-grained interactions (e.g. exact term matches, negation, numerical relationships) that significantly improve relevance scoring accuracy — at the cost of needing to run the model once per query-document pair.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.how_it_works: The input is formatted as '[CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP]' and fed through a BERT-style Transformer; the [CLS] token's final representation (or a pooled representation) is passed through a small classification/regression head to produce a relevance score (e.g. a probability that the document is relevant to the query, or a continuous relevance score). Because the model processes the concatenated pair jointly, self-attention layers allow direct interaction between query and document tokens at every layer — but this means the document's representation depends on the specific query, so document representations cannot be precomputed/cached independently.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.use_when: Reranking a small set of candidates (typically the top 10-100 retrieved by a faster method) where accuracy matters more than speed — cross-encoders consistently outperform bi-encoders on relevance-ranking benchmarks when applied to a manageable candidate set.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.avoid_when: Avoid using a cross-encoder as the sole retrieval mechanism over a large corpus — running it against every document for every query is computationally prohibitive (O(n) expensive forward passes per query, vs O(1) for bi-encoder + ANN index).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_goes_wrong: Latency scales linearly with the number of candidates being scored — reranking too many candidates (e.g. 1000 instead of 50) with a cross-encoder can introduce unacceptable latency for interactive applications. Cross-encoder scores from one model aren't directly comparable across different queries in absolute terms in all cases (they're typically used for relative ranking within a single query's candidate set, not as an absolute relevance threshold across queries, without calibration).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.real_example: A search system retrieves the top 100 candidates via a fast bi-encoder + FAISS index (milliseconds), then reranks those 100 candidates with a cross-encoder (e.g. ms-marco-MiniLM cross-encoder) — each of the 100 query-document pairs gets a fresh forward pass (perhaps 50-200ms total for all 100 on a GPU), producing a much more accurate final ranking than the bi-encoder alone, while keeping total latency acceptable because only 100 (not millions) of pairs are scored this way.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.what_it_is: Two-stage retrieval is the standard production architecture for high-quality semantic search: a fast bi-encoder (with an ANN index) retrieves a broad set of candidates (e.g. top 50-200) from the full corpus, and a more accurate but slower cross-encoder reranks just those candidates to produce the final top-k results shown to the user.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.why_it_exists: Bi-encoders are fast enough to search millions of documents but less accurate at fine-grained relevance ranking; cross-encoders are more accurate but too slow to run against an entire corpus per query. Two-stage retrieval combines the strengths of both: bi-encoder for recall (don't miss relevant documents among millions), cross-encoder for precision (get the ranking of the most-likely-relevant documents right).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Embeddings & Retr.how_it_works: Stage 1 (retrieval): encode the query with a bi-encoder, search a precomputed ANN index of document embeddings, retrieve the top-N candidates (N typically 20-200, chosen to balance recall vs stage-2 cost). Stage 2 (reranking): for each of the N candidates, concatenate query+document and score with a cross-encoder; sort candidates by cross-encoder score; return the top-k (k << N, e.g. top 5-10) as final results.
