4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.use_when: Self-supervised pretraining of Vision Transformers, especially when downstream applications can benefit from DINO's emergent attention-map properties (e.g. unsupervised object localisation/segmentation, or as a strong general-purpose visual feature extractor for retrieval/classification).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.avoid_when: Avoid if working with CNN architectures where DINO's benefits (particularly the emergent attention-map interpretability, which is closely tied to ViT's patch-based self-attention) may be less pronounced — though DINO's core self-distillation training framework can still apply, the headline interpretability result is most associated with ViTs specifically.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_goes_wrong: Like BYOL, DINO requires careful mechanisms (centering and sharpening of the teacher's output distribution, momentum/EMA update rate for the teacher) to avoid representation collapse — getting these hyperparameters wrong can lead to the student and teacher converging to a trivial uninformative solution. The multi-crop strategy (multiple global and local crops per image) increases computational cost during training compared to simpler two-view contrastive setups.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.real_example: A ViT trained with DINO on unlabelled ImageNet images, when its self-attention maps from the [CLS] token to image patches are visualised, often show attention concentrated on the main object in the image (e.g. an animal's outline) — emerging purely from the self-distillation training objective, without any segmentation labels — making DINO-pretrained ViTs useful as feature extractors for tasks like unsupervised object discovery or as strong backbones for retrieval (e.g. DINOv2 is widely used as a general-purpose visual feature extractor).

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_it_is: Triplet loss is a metric-learning loss function that operates on triplets of examples — an anchor, a positive (similar to the anchor), and a negative (dissimilar to the anchor) — and trains the model so the distance between anchor and positive is smaller than the distance between anchor and negative by at least a margin.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.why_it_exists: Many tasks (face recognition, image retrieval, sentence similarity) care about relative similarity rather than absolute classification — the goal is an embedding space where similar items are close and dissimilar items are far apart, regardless of absolute category labels (useful when the number of classes is huge or unbounded, e.g. 'is this the same person' across millions of identities, where a standard classification head over all identities would be impractical).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.how_it_works: For a triplet (anchor a, positive p, negative n), the loss is defined as max(0, d(a,p) - d(a,n) + margin), where d is a distance function (e.g. Euclidean or 1-cosine_similarity) and margin is a hyperparameter specifying how much further the negative should be than the positive. The loss is zero once d(a,n) >= d(a,p) + margin (the constraint is satisfied with sufficient margin), and positive (providing gradient signal) otherwise — training pushes positives closer and negatives further from the anchor until the margin constraint is satisfied for each triplet.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.use_when: Tasks requiring a learned embedding space for similarity/retrieval where positive/negative relationships are known (e.g. same identity vs different identity for face recognition, same product vs different product for visual search) — triplet loss is a classic, well-understood choice for such metric-learning problems, including as one of several losses used to train sentence embedding models.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.avoid_when: Avoid naive random triplet sampling for large datasets — most random triplets quickly satisfy the margin constraint (easy triplets contribute zero gradient), making training inefficient; triplet mining strategies (selecting 'hard' or 'semi-hard' negatives) are essentially required for triplet loss to train efficiently at scale, adding complexity that contrastive losses with in-batch negatives (e.g. InfoNCE) sometimes avoid.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_goes_wrong: Training with triplet loss is highly sensitive to triplet selection — too many 'easy' triplets (where the margin is already satisfied) waste compute with zero gradients, while too many extremely 'hard' triplets (e.g. mislabelled data appearing as a hard negative) can destabilise training. The margin hyperparameter itself requires tuning — too small a margin doesn't enforce meaningful separation, too large can make the loss difficult to ever satisfy, keeping gradients large/unstable throughout training.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.real_example: Training a face-recognition model with triplet loss: anchor = a photo of person A, positive = a different photo of person A, negative = a photo of person B; the loss pushes the embedding distance between the two photos of person A to be smaller than the distance to person B's photo by at least the margin — after training on many such triplets (with hard-negative mining to select challenging same-vs-different-person pairs), the resulting embedding space allows face verification via simple distance thresholding, without needing a classification head over all known identities.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_it_is: Hard negative mining is the practice of deliberately selecting 'hard' negative examples — ones that are difficult for the current model to distinguish from positives (e.g. close in embedding space but actually dissimilar/irrelevant) — for use in contrastive or triplet-loss training, rather than relying on randomly-sampled (typically 'easy') negatives.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.why_it_exists: For most contrastive/metric-learning objectives, randomly-sampled negatives are usually already 'easy' for a reasonably-trained model to separate from positives — these easy negatives contribute little useful gradient signal once the model has learned basic discrimination. The examples that actually drive further improvement are 'hard negatives' — cases where the model currently (incorrectly) considers a negative to be similar to the anchor/positive. Without explicitly surfacing these hard cases, training can plateau on easy examples while remaining weak on the confusable cases that matter most for real-world performance.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.how_it_works: Several strategies exist: (1) In-batch hard negative mining — within a training batch, for each anchor, select the negative(s) with the smallest distance (highest similarity) to the anchor among the batch's negatives, rather than using all/random batch negatives equally. (2) Offline hard negative mining — periodically run the current model over the full dataset (or a retrieval index) to find, for each training example, other examples that the model currently ranks as highly similar but are actually negatives (e.g. for retrieval: documents that score highly for a query but aren't the correct/relevant document) — these become hard negatives for the next training phase. (3) 'Semi-hard' negative selection (used in some triplet-loss formulations) — select negatives that violate the margin but aren't so close that they might actually be mislabelled positives, balancing learning signal against training stability.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.use_when: Any contrastive/metric-learning training (dense retrieval like DPR, sentence embedding fine-tuning, face recognition, image retrieval) where final performance on confusable/near-miss cases matters — which is essentially always the case for production retrieval/similarity systems, making hard negative mining a near-universal component of serious embedding-model training pipelines.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.avoid_when: Avoid overly aggressive hard-negative mining early in training, before the model has learned basic representations — mining 'hard' negatives against an undertrained model can surface noise (essentially random examples that happen to be close due to the model's current poor representations) rather than meaningfully confusable cases; some pipelines start with easier negatives and progressively introduce harder ones (curriculum-style) as training progresses.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_goes_wrong: If hard negative mining surfaces examples that are actually mislabelled (a 'negative' that's actually relevant/similar but mislabelled in the dataset), training is pushed to incorrectly separate genuinely-similar examples — hard negative mining can amplify label noise. Mining hard negatives requires either an auxiliary retrieval/scoring pass over the dataset (offline mining, adding computational overhead and pipeline complexity — the model used to mine negatives may itself need periodic updating as training progresses, a moving-target problem) or larger batches (for in-batch mining to have a chance of containing genuinely hard examples).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.real_example: Training a dense retrieval model (DPR-style): initial training with random/in-batch negatives gets the model to a reasonable baseline; then, using this baseline model to retrieve top results for training queries, any retrieved passage that scores highly but is NOT the labelled correct answer becomes a 'hard negative' for a second training round — these hard negatives (passages that are lexically/topically similar to the query but don't actually answer it) teach the model the fine-grained distinctions that random negatives (typically totally unrelated passages) never would, often producing the largest single improvement in retrieval accuracy of any training intervention.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_it_is: InfoNCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation, Information-theoretic variant) is a contrastive loss function that frames learning as a classification problem: given one 'positive' example and a set of 'negative' examples, the loss is the cross-entropy of correctly identifying the positive among all candidates, based on a similarity score (e.g. dot product or cosine similarity) between a query/anchor representation and each candidate's representation — it underlies most modern contrastive learning methods (SimCLR's NT-Xent, MoCo, dense retrieval training, CLIP).
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.why_it_exists: InfoNCE provides a general, theoretically-motivated (related to mutual information maximisation between representations of related views/pairs) and practically effective way to train representations using only relative comparisons (positive vs negatives) rather than absolute labels — unifying the objective across many self-supervised and contrastive learning methods under a common mathematical form, with the specific differences between methods (SimCLR, MoCo, CLIP, SimCSE, DPR) largely coming down to HOW positive/negative pairs are constructed, not the loss formula itself.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.how_it_works: Given an anchor representation q and a set of candidate representations {k_0, k_1, ..., k_{N-1}} where k_0 is the positive (matching) candidate and k_1...k_{N-1} are negatives, InfoNCE loss = -log( exp(sim(q,k_0)/tau) / sum_i exp(sim(q,k_i)/tau) ), where sim is typically cosine similarity or dot product, and tau is a temperature hyperparameter controlling how 'sharp' the softmax distribution is (lower tau makes the loss more sensitive to small similarity differences, effectively focusing gradient on hard negatives). This is exactly the cross-entropy loss for an (N-way) classification problem where the 'correct class' is always the positive — minimising it pushes sim(q, positive) up and sim(q, negatives) down relative to each other.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.use_when: As the underlying training objective for essentially any contrastive representation-learning task — image self-supervised learning (SimCLR, MoCo), sentence embeddings (SimCSE, Sentence-BERT variants), dense retrieval (DPR), and vision-language alignment (CLIP) all use InfoNCE or a close variant as their core loss.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.avoid_when: InfoNCE itself is rarely 'avoided' outright when doing contrastive learning — but be aware it requires meaningful negatives (random/easy negatives provide weak signal, as discussed under hard negative mining) and a well-chosen temperature; for tasks where absolute (not just relative) calibration of similarity scores matters for downstream use (e.g. needing a probability-like 'are these the same' score with a meaningful threshold), additional calibration beyond InfoNCE-trained similarities may be needed.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_goes_wrong: The temperature parameter tau significantly affects training dynamics — too low a temperature makes the loss extremely sensitive to the hardest negatives (can cause instability if those 'hard negatives' are actually noise/mislabelled), too high a temperature makes the loss insensitive to meaningful similarity differences (weak gradient signal, slow learning). The number and quality of negatives (N) directly affects how informative the loss is — too few negatives, or negatives that are all trivially dissimilar (no hard negatives), provide a weaker training signal than a well-curated negative set, connecting InfoNCE's effectiveness directly to the hard-negative-mining considerations discussed separately.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.real_example: CLIP's training loss is InfoNCE applied across a batch of (image, text) pairs: for each image, the matching text caption is the positive and all other captions in the batch are negatives (and symmetrically for each text, the matching image is positive and other images are negatives) — the resulting symmetric InfoNCE loss, computed over a large batch (providing many negatives), is what trains CLIP's joint image-text embedding space, the same loss formula (just with different positive/negative construction) underlying SimCLR's purely-visual self-supervised pretraining.

4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_it_is: This refers to the application of contrastive learning objectives (InfoNCE-style losses) specifically to produce sentence-level embeddings, with SimCSE (covered in the Embeddings & Retrieval subtopic) as the canonical example — using contrastive training (positive pairs from dropout-based augmentation or NLI labels, negatives from the batch) to shape an embedding space where semantically similar sentences are close.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.why_it_exists: Sentence embeddings are foundational to semantic search, clustering, and retrieval (covered extensively elsewhere in this phase), and contrastive learning has proven to be the most effective general training paradigm for producing such embeddings — this entry connects the broader contrastive-learning concepts (InfoNCE, hard negatives, SimCLR/MoCo-style ideas from vision) to their concrete application in NLP via SimCSE and related sentence-embedding training methods.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.how_it_works: As detailed under SimCSE: positive pairs for sentence embeddings can come from dropout-based self-augmentation (unsupervised SimCSE), NLI entailment pairs (supervised SimCSE), or other pair-construction strategies (e.g. query-passage pairs for retrieval-oriented embeddings, as in E5/BGE training); the InfoNCE loss is applied with in-batch negatives (other sentences in the training batch serve as negatives for each positive pair), often augmented with hard negatives (e.g. NLI contradiction pairs, or retrieval-mined hard negatives) for stronger training signal. The result is an embedding space where cosine similarity between sentence embeddings correlates with semantic similarity — the same underlying contrastive machinery (InfoNCE, temperature, hard negatives) discussed for vision (SimCLR, MoCo) applied to text.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.use_when: Training or fine-tuning any sentence/text embedding model — this contrastive framework is the standard approach across the field (general-purpose models like SBERT/E5/BGE, and domain-fine-tuned embeddings) and connects directly to the broader contrastive learning principles (positive/negative construction, hard negative mining, InfoNCE temperature) that apply across modalities.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.avoid_when: As with SimCSE specifically, avoid relying purely on weak/unsupervised contrastive signals (dropout-based pairs alone) when better supervision (labelled similarity pairs, retrieval click data, NLI labels) is available — supervised or retrieval-augmented contrastive training generally produces embeddings better-suited to downstream retrieval tasks than unsupervised contrastive pretraining alone.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.what_goes_wrong: The same pitfalls as InfoNCE and hard-negative-mining generally apply here: weak/easy negatives limit how discriminative the resulting embedding space becomes, temperature requires tuning, and positive-pair construction quality (how well 'two views of the same sentence' or 'entailment pair' actually reflects the target notion of semantic similarity for your application) directly determines what the embeddings end up encoding — a model contrastively trained on NLI entailment pairs learns an embedding space tuned for 'logical entailment similarity', which may or may not align with what a specific retrieval application considers 'relevant'.
4|🔴 T1 Semantic Search|Contrastive Learn.real_example: The progression from raw BERT -> SimCSE (dropout-based unsupervised contrastive) -> supervised SimCSE (NLI-based contrastive) -> E5/BGE (large-scale weakly-supervised contrastive pretraining on web text pairs, plus supervised fine-tuning with hard negatives) illustrates how the same core contrastive/InfoNCE framework, applied with progressively better-curated positive/negative pairs and at larger scale, produces progressively stronger general-purpose sentence embedding models — the architecture and loss function are similar throughout; the main driver of improvement is the quality and scale of the contrastive pair construction.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Linguistic resources are structured collections of language data and knowledge — corpora (large bodies of text), lexicons/dictionaries, treebanks (syntactically annotated sentences), ontologies (like WordNet), and annotated datasets — that provide the raw material and ground truth for building and evaluating NLP systems.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Statistical and neural NLP methods require data to learn from and gold-standard annotations to evaluate against — linguistic resources provide the standardised, often expert-curated, foundation that both classical rule-based/statistical NLP systems and modern ML models rely on, whether directly (training data) or indirectly (evaluation benchmarks, lexical knowledge bases used as features or constraints).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Resources are built through varying combinations of manual annotation (linguists/annotators labelling text with part-of-speech tags, syntactic trees, semantic roles, etc.), automatic extraction (mining patterns from large corpora), and crowdsourcing. Examples include: raw text corpora (e.g. large web crawls, Wikipedia dumps) for language modelling; treebanks (e.g. Penn Treebank) with hand-annotated syntactic parse trees for training/evaluating parsers; WordNet, a lexical database organising words into synsets (sets of synonyms) with semantic relations (hypernymy, meronymy) between them; and annotated datasets for specific tasks (NER-tagged corpora, sentiment-labelled reviews, NLI pairs). These resources are distributed (often with licensing restrictions) and used as training data, fine-tuning data, or evaluation benchmarks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Building or evaluating any NLP system that requires structured language knowledge: training classical statistical parsers/taggers, evaluating modern models against gold-standard annotations, using WordNet-style relations for tasks like word-sense disambiguation, or sourcing domain-specific corpora for fine-tuning embedding/language models.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid relying on outdated or narrow-domain resources (e.g. a treebank of 1990s newswire text) as the sole training/evaluation signal for modern applications involving different domains (social media, code, multilingual text) — such resources may not reflect the linguistic phenomena of the target domain.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Many classic linguistic resources (treebanks, WordNet) were built for specific languages (often English) and specific text genres (newswire), and models/systems evaluated only on these resources can have blind spots for other languages, dialects, or informal text (social media, code-switching) not represented in the resource. Licensing restrictions on some resources (e.g. certain corpora requiring paid licenses via LDC) can limit reproducibility and accessibility for some researchers/practitioners.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: A word-sense disambiguation system might use WordNet's synsets as the inventory of possible senses for each word (e.g. 'bank' having senses for 'financial institution' and 'river bank'), while a syntactic parser might be trained and evaluated on the Penn Treebank's hand-annotated parse trees — both illustrating how linguistic resources provide the structured ground truth that defines what a 'correct' output looks like for these tasks.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Word-level analysis encompasses the NLP processing steps that operate on individual words/tokens — including tokenisation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, morphological analysis (identifying word forms/inflections), and lemmatisation/stemming — forming the foundational layer of the classical NLP pipeline before sentence-level (syntactic) and discourse-level analysis.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Before any higher-level analysis (parsing, semantic interpretation) can occur, text must be broken into meaningful units (words/tokens) and each unit characterised — what part of speech is it, what's its base form, what grammatical features does it carry (tense, number, case)? Word-level analysis provides this foundational characterisation that subsequent pipeline stages depend on.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Tokenisation splits raw text into words/tokens (handling punctuation, contractions, etc.). POS tagging assigns each token a grammatical category (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) — historically via Hidden Markov Models or CRFs using surrounding-word context, now often via neural sequence taggers. Morphological analysis examines word-internal structure to identify the stem/root and any affixes conveying grammatical information (e.g. 'running' = 'run' + '-ing', indicating progressive aspect). Lemmatisation maps inflected forms to their dictionary base form (e.g. 'ran', 'running' -> 'run') using morphological rules or lookup tables, while stemming uses simpler heuristic rules (e.g. Porter stemmer) to strip suffixes, potentially producing non-words (e.g. 'running' -> 'runn').
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: As a preprocessing step for classical NLP pipelines (rule-based systems, traditional ML feature engineering) where POS tags, lemmas, or morphological features serve as input features for downstream tasks; also useful for linguistic analysis/research on a language's morphological structure.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid heavy reliance on word-level preprocessing (POS tagging, lemmatisation) as a prerequisite for modern Transformer-based models — these models typically operate on subword tokens learned directly from data and don't require explicit POS/lemma features, which were more central to pre-neural (or early neural, e.g. feature-based CRF) NLP pipelines.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Word-level analysis tools (POS taggers, lemmatisers) are often language-specific and trained on particular domains/genres — applying an English newswire-trained POS tagger to social media text or a different language produces unreliable tags. Morphologically rich languages (e.g. Turkish, Finnish, with extensive agglutinative morphology) pose particular challenges for word-level analysis designed around English's relatively simple morphology, often requiring language-specific morphological analysers.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: Analysing the sentence 'The cats were running quickly' at the word level: tokenisation yields ['The', 'cats', 'were', 'running', 'quickly']; POS tagging assigns [DET, NOUN, AUX, VERB, ADV]; morphological analysis identifies 'cats' as 'cat' + plural, 'running' as 'run' + present participle; lemmatisation reduces 'cats'->'cat', 'were'->'be', 'running'->'run' — this structured information historically fed into rule-based grammar checkers or statistical parsers as input features.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit of language — a word may consist of a single morpheme (e.g. 'cat') or multiple morphemes combined (e.g. 'cats' = 'cat' + '-s' plural marker; 'unhappiness' = 'un-' + 'happy' + '-ness'); morphemes are categorised as free (can stand alone as words, e.g. 'cat') or bound (must attach to other morphemes, e.g. '-s', 'un-', '-ness').
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Morphological structure is fundamental to how languages convey grammatical information (tense, number, case, possession) and derive new words from existing ones — understanding morphemes is essential for tasks like stemming/lemmatisation, morphological analysis, and for languages with rich morphology where a single word can encode information that would require multiple separate words in English.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Morphemes combine via processes like inflection (adding grammatical information without changing the word's core meaning/category, e.g. 'walk' -> 'walked' for past tense) and derivation (creating a new word, often changing its category, e.g. 'happy' (adjective) -> 'happiness' (noun) via the derivational suffix '-ness'). Morphological analysis (computational) decomposes words into their constituent morphemes, which can be rule-based (for languages with regular morphology) or require finite-state transducers/statistical models for languages with complex, irregular, or agglutinative morphology (where many morphemes chain together, e.g. Turkish words that translate to entire English phrases).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Relevant for building morphological analysers/generators (especially for morphologically-rich languages), understanding subword tokenisation's linguistic basis (BPE/WordPiece subwords often roughly align with morphemes for many words, though not always), and tasks like lemmatisation/stemming that explicitly operate at the morpheme level.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: For most modern NLP work with Transformer models and subword tokenisers (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece), explicit morpheme-level analysis usually isn't necessary — these tokenisers learn subword units statistically from data, which may or may not correspond to linguistically 'correct' morphemes, but the models learn to work with whatever units the tokeniser produces regardless.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Subword tokenisation (used by virtually all modern Transformers) does not guarantee morphologically meaningful splits — a BPE tokeniser might split 'unhappiness' into chunks that don't align with the linguistic morphemes 'un-', 'happy', '-ness', instead splitting based on statistical frequency in the training corpus, which can occasionally produce splits that obscure rather than reveal meaningful structure (though in practice this rarely causes major issues for model performance).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: The word 'internationalization' can be morphologically decomposed as 'inter-' (prefix: between/among) + 'nation' (root) + '-al' (adjective-forming suffix) + '-ize' (verb-forming suffix) + '-ation' (noun-forming suffix) — five morphemes combining to form one word; a BPE tokeniser might instead split this into subwords like 'international' + 'ization' or other frequency-based chunks that don't cleanly map to these five linguistic morphemes, illustrating the difference between linguistic morpheme analysis and statistical subword tokenisation.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Syntactic analysis (parsing) is the process of determining the grammatical structure of a sentence — typically represented as a parse tree showing how words group into phrases and how phrases relate to each other according to the grammar of the language (e.g. subject-verb-object relationships, modifier attachments).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Understanding a sentence's meaning often depends on its syntactic structure — the same words in different syntactic arrangements can mean different things (e.g. 'I saw the man with a telescope' is ambiguous depending on whether 'with a telescope' attaches to 'saw' or 'the man'). Syntactic parsing makes this structure explicit, providing a foundation for semantic interpretation, grammar checking, and various downstream NLP tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Two major paradigms: constituency parsing represents sentence structure as a tree of nested phrases (noun phrases, verb phrases, etc.) following a context-free grammar; dependency parsing represents structure as directed relationships between words (e.g. 'saw' has a subject dependency to 'I' and an object dependency to 'man'), without explicit phrase nodes. Parsing algorithms range from classical chart-parsing algorithms (CYK, Earley — covered separately) for constituency parsing with formal grammars, to statistical parsers (e.g. PCFGs — probabilistic context-free grammars, which assign probabilities to grammar rules and find the most likely parse), to modern neural parsers (Transformer-based models that directly predict dependency arcs or constituency trees, often as a sequence-labelling or graph-prediction task).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Tasks requiring explicit structural understanding of sentences: grammar checking, information extraction (identifying who did what to whom), question answering systems that need to identify the grammatical role of query terms, or as a feature/preprocessing step for tasks where syntactic structure provides useful signal beyond what raw token sequences capture.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid assuming explicit syntactic parsing is necessary for modern Transformer-based NLP — these models implicitly learn syntactic regularities through their training objectives (next-token prediction, masked-language-modelling) without requiring an explicit parse tree as input or intermediate representation, and for most tasks (classification, generation, QA) end-to-end neural models without explicit parsing outperform pipelines with explicit parsing stages.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Syntactic ambiguity (a sentence having multiple valid parses, like the 'telescope' example) means parsers must choose among possibilities, and statistical/neural parsers can choose incorrectly, especially for unusual or long sentences — parsing errors compound if downstream tasks depend on the (possibly incorrect) parse. Parsers trained on one domain/genre (e.g. formal newswire text used in the Penn Treebank) often perform worse on other domains (informal text, technical text with unusual constructions) due to domain mismatch.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: Parsing 'The old man the boat' (a classic 'garden path' sentence) initially seems ungrammatical under the natural reading where 'old man' is a noun phrase and 'the boat' has no verb — but the correct parse treats 'man' as a verb (meaning 'to staff/operate'), giving 'The old [people] man [i.e., operate] the boat' — illustrating how syntactic parsing must consider multiple structural hypotheses and how garden-path sentences specifically challenge parsers (and human readers) by initially suggesting an incorrect structure.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: The CYK (Cocke-Younger-Kasami) algorithm is a dynamic-programming algorithm for parsing sentences according to a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form, determining whether (and how) a sentence can be derived from the grammar, with O(n^3) time complexity in sentence length n.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Naive parsing approaches (trying all possible ways to combine grammar rules) have exponential complexity in sentence length. CYK provides an efficient, guaranteed-polynomial-time algorithm for context-free grammar parsing by exploiting dynamic programming — building up parses for larger spans of the sentence from parses of smaller sub-spans, avoiding redundant recomputation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: The grammar must first be converted to Chomsky Normal Form (every production rule is either A -> BC, two non-terminals, or A -> a, a single terminal). CYK fills a triangular dynamic-programming table where cell (i,j) contains the set of non-terminals that can derive the substring spanning positions i to j. The table is filled bottom-up: first, cells for single-word spans (length 1) are filled based on which non-terminals can directly produce that word (A -> a rules); then, for increasing span lengths, cell (i,j) is filled by checking, for every way to split the span into two sub-spans, whether there's a rule A -> BC where B can derive the left sub-span and C can derive the right sub-span — if so, A is added to cell (i,j). The sentence is grammatical if the start symbol appears in the cell spanning the entire sentence; the table also implicitly encodes all possible parse trees (for ambiguous grammars, multiple non-terminals/derivations can populate a cell).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Educational/theoretical contexts for understanding context-free grammar parsing fundamentals, or in applications using explicitly-defined small/formal grammars (e.g. parsing programming languages, formal query languages, or constrained-domain natural language interfaces) where CYK's guarantees (polynomial time, finds all parses for ambiguous grammars) are valuable.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid for parsing natural language with large, ambiguous, hand-written or learned grammars at scale — CYK's O(n^3) complexity (with a constant factor depending on grammar size) becomes impractical for the very large grammars needed to cover natural language's complexity, and modern NLP uses statistical/neural parsers instead, which don't require explicit CNF grammars.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Converting an arbitrary context-free grammar to Chomsky Normal Form can significantly increase the number of grammar rules, and natural-language grammars are often highly ambiguous — CYK will find ALL possible parses for an ambiguous sentence, which for natural language can be combinatorially enormous (a sentence might have thousands of grammatically valid parses under a broad-coverage grammar), requiring additional mechanisms (probabilistic weighting, as in PCFG-CYK) to select the most plausible parse rather than enumerating all of them.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: For a toy grammar in CNF (e.g. S -> NP VP, NP -> Det N, VP -> V NP, Det -> 'the', N -> 'cat' | 'dog', V -> 'chased') parsing the sentence 'the dog chased the cat', CYK builds a table where cell (1,1) contains Det (for 'the'), cell (2,2) contains N (for 'dog'), cell (1,2) contains NP (since Det N -> NP for the span 'the dog'), and so on, ultimately determining that S spans the entire sentence — confirming grammaticality and providing the parse structure, all computed via this bottom-up table-filling in O(n^3) time.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: The Earley algorithm is a chart-parsing algorithm for context-free grammars that works with ANY context-free grammar (no Chomsky Normal Form conversion required), processes the input left-to-right, and has worst-case O(n^3) complexity but performs better (closer to linear) for many practical (non-pathologically-ambiguous) grammars.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: CYK requires converting grammars to Chomsky Normal Form, which can be inconvenient and obscure the original grammar's structure; CYK also processes the input in a way that doesn't naturally support 'incremental' left-to-right parsing (useful for some applications, e.g. providing partial-parse feedback as input is read). The Earley algorithm parses with the grammar in its original form and processes input incrementally left-to-right, while still guaranteeing polynomial-time worst-case complexity for arbitrary context-free grammars (including those with ambiguity or even certain forms of recursion that some other algorithms struggle with).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Earley maintains a set of 'states' (representing partially-recognised grammar rules, each tracking how much of a rule has been matched and the position in the input where matching began) for each position in the input, organized into 'Earley sets'. Three operations update these sets as the algorithm processes the input left-to-right: 'prediction' (if a state expects a non-terminal next, add states for all rules that could derive that non-terminal), 'scanning' (if a state expects a terminal next and the current input symbol matches, advance the state to the next input position), and 'completion' (if a state has fully matched a rule's right-hand side, advance any states in earlier sets that were waiting for that non-terminal). The input is successfully parsed if, after processing all input, a state representing a complete derivation of the start symbol (spanning the entire input) exists.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Parsing with grammars not naturally in (or awkward to convert to) Chomsky Normal Form, applications needing incremental/left-to-right parsing behaviour (e.g. providing real-time parse feedback), or parsing grammars with characteristics (like certain ambiguity patterns or epsilon productions) that are more naturally handled by Earley's approach than CYK's.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid for production natural-language parsing at scale, similar to CYK — both are primarily of theoretical/educational interest or niche formal-grammar applications in modern NLP, where statistical and neural parsers dominate practical use due to better handling of ambiguity resolution (assigning probabilities/scores to choose among parses) and scalability to broad-coverage natural language grammars.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: While Earley's worst-case complexity is O(n^3), for highly ambiguous grammars (common in natural language) the constant factors and the size of the Earley sets can still make it impractically slow for long sentences with broad-coverage grammars — similar to CYK, Earley by itself doesn't address the problem of CHOOSING among many valid parses for ambiguous input, which requires additional probabilistic/statistical machinery layered on top.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: Earley parsing is commonly used in implementations of formal/domain-specific grammars where the grammar is written directly in a natural (non-CNF) form — e.g. parsing a configuration language or a constrained natural-language command grammar for a voice interface — where the grammar's rules can be written in whatever form is most natural for the grammar author, and Earley's algorithm handles parsing against that grammar directly without requiring a CNF transformation step.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Semantic Role Labelling (SRL) is the NLP task of identifying the predicate (typically the main verb) in a sentence and labelling its arguments with semantic roles — answering 'who did what to whom, when, where, and how' by assigning labels like Agent, Patient/Theme, Instrument, Location, and Time to the relevant phrases.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Syntactic structure alone (subject, object) doesn't fully capture meaning — the same semantic role can be filled by different syntactic positions across different sentence constructions (e.g. 'John broke the window' vs 'The window was broken by John' — 'John' is the Agent in both, despite being the syntactic subject in one and part of a prepositional phrase in the other). SRL provides a layer of meaning representation that's more invariant to syntactic variation, useful for tasks needing to extract 'who did what' regardless of how it's phrased.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Given a sentence and a target predicate (verb), SRL identifies the spans of text that fill each of the predicate's semantic roles and labels them — common role inventories include PropBank-style numbered arguments (Arg0 typically = Agent/causer, Arg1 typically = Patient/Theme, etc., with the exact meaning depending on the specific verb's 'frame') or more general thematic roles (Agent, Patient, Instrument, Location, Time, Manner). Modern SRL systems are typically neural sequence-labelling models (often BERT-based) that, given a sentence with a marked predicate, label each token with its role (using a BIO-tagging scheme, similar to NER) — trained on resources like PropBank, which provides verb-specific 'frames' defining each verb's possible argument structure.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Information extraction tasks needing to identify event participants and their roles regardless of syntactic phrasing (e.g. extracting 'who acquired whom' from financial news with varying sentence structures), question answering (answering 'who/what/where' questions by mapping them to semantic roles), or as a feature for downstream tasks benefiting from predicate-argument structure.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks where end-to-end neural models (e.g. an LLM directly answering 'who did X' questions, or directly extracting structured information via prompting) achieve sufficient accuracy without an explicit SRL intermediate step — modern LLMs often implicitly capture predicate-argument relationships well enough for many practical extraction tasks without a dedicated SRL pipeline stage.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: SRL's role labels (especially PropBank's numbered Arg0/Arg1/etc.) are verb-specific — Arg1 for one verb might correspond to a different semantic role than Arg1 for another verb, requiring a 'frame' lookup to interpret the labels meaningfully, which adds complexity. SRL systems can struggle with long-distance dependencies (where an argument is far from its predicate in the sentence, e.g. due to relative clauses or coordination) and with predicates that have unusual or rare argument structures not well-represented in training data.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: For the sentence 'Yesterday, the company acquired its rival for $2 billion', SRL applied to the predicate 'acquired' would identify: Arg0 (Agent) = 'the company', Arg1 (Patient) = 'its rival', ArgM-TMP (temporal modifier) = 'Yesterday', ArgM-MNR or a purpose/manner argument = 'for $2 billion' — this structured output enables downstream systems to answer 'who acquired what, when, for how much' directly from the SRL output, regardless of whether the sentence had been phrased actively or passively.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Discourse processing is the analysis of structure and meaning ABOVE the sentence level — how multiple sentences in a text relate to each other, including discourse relations (e.g. cause-effect, contrast, elaboration between sentences/clauses), coherence, and topic structure across a document or conversation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Understanding a text fully often requires more than understanding each sentence in isolation — sentences relate to each other (one might elaborate on, contradict, or give the cause of another), and these relationships affect overall meaning, summarisation, and tasks like determining what a pronoun refers to (which may depend on discourse-level context, not just the immediate sentence). Discourse processing addresses this 'beyond the sentence' layer of language understanding.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Discourse processing covers several sub-problems: discourse parsing/relation classification identifies relationships between adjacent or related text spans (e.g. using frameworks like Rhetorical Structure Theory, which organises text into a hierarchical tree of relations like 'elaboration', 'contrast', 'cause'); discourse segmentation divides text into coherent units/topics; and coreference/anaphora resolution (covered separately) links referring expressions across sentences. Computationally, these tasks have been approached with both classical rule-based/statistical methods (using cue phrases like 'however', 'because', 'therefore' as signals of discourse relations) and modern neural models (often Transformer-based, processing multi-sentence/document-level context to classify relations or track entities/topics across the discourse).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Tasks requiring document-level (not just sentence-level) understanding: summarisation (understanding which sentences elaborate on others to avoid redundancy), dialogue systems (tracking conversational coherence and topic shifts), and any analysis where inter-sentence relationships affect the correct interpretation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid treating discourse processing as a separate explicit pipeline stage for tasks where modern long-context Transformer models, processing the full document/conversation as input, implicitly capture much of the relevant inter-sentence structure through their attention mechanisms without needing an explicit discourse-relation-labelling step.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Discourse relations can be implicit (not signalled by an explicit cue word like 'because' or 'however') — a sentence pair might have a causal relationship purely inferable from world knowledge/context, which is much harder to detect than explicitly-cued relations, and discourse parsers historically perform notably worse on implicit relations. Long-range discourse phenomena (a relationship between a sentence and something many paragraphs earlier) remain challenging even for models with large context windows, since attention must correctly identify the relevant earlier context among much intervening material.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: In the two-sentence text 'The company's profits fell sharply. They had invested heavily in a failed product line', a discourse parser would ideally identify an implicit 'cause/explanation' relation between the second sentence and the first (the investment failure explains the profit decline) — even though no explicit connective like 'because' signals this relationship, requiring the system to infer the discourse relation from the content/world-knowledge relationship between the two statements, a much harder problem than detecting relations signalled by explicit discourse markers.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Anaphora resolution is the task of determining what a referring expression (typically a pronoun like 'it', 'he', 'they', or a definite noun phrase like 'the company') refers back to (its antecedent) earlier in the text — a specific and prominent form of coreference resolution focused on backward-pointing references.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Natural language relies heavily on pronouns and other referring expressions to avoid constantly repeating full names/descriptions — but this means understanding a text fully requires figuring out what these expressions refer to. Anaphora resolution is essential for any task requiring tracking of entities across a text: summarisation, question answering, information extraction, and machine translation (where pronoun translation can depend on the antecedent's gender/number, which may differ across languages).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Given a referring expression (anaphor), the system identifies candidate antecedents (earlier mentions of entities in the text) and scores/ranks them based on features like: recency (closer mentions are often more likely antecedents), grammatical agreement (a pronoun's number/gender must match its antecedent — 'she' can't refer to a previously-mentioned 'company' unless personified), syntactic constraints (certain configurations rule out coreference, e.g. binding-theory constraints from linguistics), and semantic plausibility (does the candidate antecedent make sense as a filler for the anaphor's role in its sentence). Classical approaches used hand-crafted rules/heuristics (e.g. Hobbs' algorithm, which searches syntactic trees in a specified order) or statistical classifiers over these features; modern approaches use neural models (often span-based, scoring all pairs of mention spans for coreference likelihood, sometimes as part of a broader end-to-end coreference resolution system).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Any task where correctly tracking 'who/what is being talked about' across sentences matters: summarisation (avoiding ambiguous pronouns in summaries), information extraction (attributing extracted facts to the correct entity when pronouns are used), dialogue systems (resolving 'it'/'that' references to earlier conversation turns), and machine translation between languages with different pronoun/gender systems.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid assuming anaphora resolution is a solved/trivial problem for ambiguous cases — for sentences with genuinely ambiguous pronoun reference (where multiple antecedents are grammatically/semantically plausible), even state-of-the-art systems can struggle, and downstream applications should be designed to be robust to occasional resolution errors rather than assuming perfect resolution.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: The famous 'Winograd Schema' sentences ('The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it's too big/small' — 'it' refers to the trophy if 'big', the suitcase if 'small') illustrate cases requiring world knowledge/commonsense reasoning to resolve correctly, not just syntactic/grammatical features — these remain genuinely challenging even for large language models in some constructions. Cataphora (forward reference, where the referring expression appears BEFORE its antecedent, e.g. 'Before he left, John locked the door') and long-distance anaphora (antecedent many sentences earlier) are additional sources of difficulty beyond the simple 'nearest matching antecedent' heuristic.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: In 'The city council refused the demonstrators a permit because they feared violence', resolving 'they' requires understanding that 'fearing violence' is more plausibly attributed to the council (the entity granting/refusing permits, motivated by concern about violence) than to the demonstrators — this is a Winograd-schema-style example where grammatical agreement (both 'council' and 'demonstrators' could plausibly be referred to by 'they', ignoring number mismatch with 'council' as singular) doesn't resolve the ambiguity, and correct resolution depends on commonsense reasoning about why permits get refused.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Lexical semantics is the study of word meanings — including how words relate to each other (synonymy, antonymy, hypernymy/hyponymy), how words can have multiple meanings (polysemy) requiring disambiguation in context, and how word meaning can be represented computationally (from dictionary-style sense inventories to distributional/vector-based representations).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: Words are the basic units carrying meaning in language, but word meaning is rich and context-dependent — the same word can mean different things in different contexts (polysemy: 'bank' as financial institution vs riverbank), and words relate to each other in structured ways (synonyms, broader/narrower terms) that matter for tasks like search (matching queries to documents using related terms) and reasoning (knowing that a 'dog' is a kind of 'animal'). Lexical semantics provides the theoretical and computational frameworks for capturing these meaning relationships.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Classical lexical semantics uses structured resources like WordNet, organising words into 'synsets' (sets of words with the same meaning in a given sense) connected by relations: hypernymy/hyponymy (is-a: 'dog' is a hyponym of 'animal'), meronymy/holonymy (part-of: 'wheel' is a meronym of 'car'), antonymy (opposite meaning), etc. Word-sense disambiguation (WSD) — determining which sense of a polysemous word is intended in a given context — uses these sense inventories plus contextual features (surrounding words) to select the correct sense, via classical statistical classifiers or modern contextual embeddings (where a Transformer's contextual representation of a word implicitly captures which 'sense' is active, often without needing an explicit discrete sense inventory at all). Distributional semantics (the basis for word embeddings like Word2Vec/GloVe, covered in Phase 4's Classical NLP group) represents meaning via vectors derived from co-occurrence patterns, an alternative/complementary approach to discrete sense-based representations.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Tasks requiring explicit reasoning about word meaning relationships: query expansion in search (matching 'car' searches to documents about 'automobile' via synonymy), word-sense disambiguation for tasks sensitive to the specific meaning of ambiguous words, and building/using structured knowledge bases that encode lexical relationships.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid relying on discrete sense inventories (WordNet senses) as the sole representation of word meaning for modern neural NLP — contextual embeddings from Transformers capture context-dependent meaning variation continuously (without needing to commit to one of a fixed set of discrete 'senses'), often more flexibly than discrete WSD for downstream tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: WordNet's sense distinctions are sometimes finer-grained than is useful for practical tasks (a word might have a dozen WordNet senses with subtle distinctions that don't matter for a given application), making WSD against the full sense inventory harder than necessary — coarser sense groupings are sometimes used instead. Word-sense distinctions and relationships (synonymy, hypernymy) are language-specific and don't always translate directly across languages, complicating multilingual lexical-semantic resources.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: The word 'bank' has (at least) two common senses: 'financial institution' and 'land alongside a river'. Lexical semantics would represent these as distinct WordNet synsets with different hypernyms ('financial institution' is a hyponym of 'organization'; 'river bank' is a hyponym of 'slope'/'land'); a word-sense-disambiguation system given the sentence 'He deposited money at the bank' would use the context ('deposited money') to select the financial-institution sense — whereas a contextual embedding model (BERT) would simply produce a different vector for 'bank' in this sentence vs in 'He sat on the bank fishing', implicitly capturing the sense distinction without an explicit discrete label.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Pragmatic analysis is the study of how context, speaker intent, and real-world knowledge affect the interpretation of language beyond its literal/grammatical meaning — covering phenomena like implicature (meaning more than what's literally said), speech acts (what an utterance DOES, e.g. requesting, promising), and context-dependent interpretation of deictic expressions (words like 'here', 'now', 'I' whose meaning depends on the utterance context).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: The literal/semantic meaning of a sentence often differs from what a speaker actually intends to communicate — 'Can you pass the salt?' is literally a yes/no question about ability, but pragmatically functions as a request. Understanding language as humans do requires modelling this gap between literal meaning and communicative intent, which depends on shared context, social conventions, and reasoning about the speaker's goals.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Pragmatic phenomena include: implicature (Gricean — what's implied but not stated, e.g. 'Some students passed' implicating 'not all students passed', based on conversational maxims about being informative); speech acts (categorising utterances by their function — assertions, questions, requests, promises — following speech act theory); presupposition (background assumptions an utterance takes for granted, e.g. 'Have you stopped smoking?' presupposes the addressee used to smoke); and deixis (context-dependent reference — 'I', 'you', 'here', 'now', 'this' require knowing the utterance context to resolve). Computationally, these phenomena are difficult to handle with rule-based methods alone (requiring extensive world/social knowledge); modern large language models, trained on vast amounts of text reflecting pragmatic language use, often capture many pragmatic inferences implicitly (e.g. correctly interpreting indirect requests), though systematic evaluation of pragmatic competence remains an active research area.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: Relevant for dialogue systems/conversational AI needing to correctly interpret indirect requests, sarcasm, or politeness conventions; also relevant for evaluating whether language models correctly capture implicature and other pragmatic inferences (an active area of LLM evaluation/benchmarking, e.g. testing whether models recognise indirect speech acts).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid expecting rule-based pragmatic analysis to scale to open-domain conversation — the context-dependence and world-knowledge requirements of pragmatic inference make rule-based approaches brittle outside narrow, well-defined domains; this is an area where large-scale learned models (capturing pragmatic patterns implicitly from training data) have largely superseded explicit rule-based pragmatic analysis.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: Pragmatic inference is highly context- and culture-dependent — what counts as an appropriate implicature or polite indirect request varies across languages/cultures, and models trained primarily on data from one cultural/linguistic context may misinterpret or fail to generate appropriate pragmatic forms in another. Sarcasm and irony (where the literal meaning is the OPPOSITE of the intended meaning) are notoriously difficult, even for humans without sufficient context, and remain a challenging case for automated pragmatic analysis.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: If someone asks 'Do you know what time it is?' and the response is 'Yes' (a literal, technically-correct answer to the literal yes/no question about knowledge), this fails pragmatically — the utterance functions as an indirect request for the time, and a pragmatically-competent system should respond with the actual time, not just confirm knowledge of it; correctly handling such indirect speech acts is a pragmatic-analysis challenge relevant to building conversational AI that responds the way humans actually expect.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_it_is: Information retrieval (IR) is the field concerned with finding relevant documents/information from a large collection in response to a user's query — encompassing the classical foundations (indexing, ranking, relevance models like TF-IDF/BM25) that underpin modern search engines and, by extension, the retrieval components of semantic search and RAG systems.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.why_it_exists: As document collections grow far beyond what any user could read exhaustively, IR provides the theoretical and practical foundations for efficiently finding the small subset of documents relevant to a specific information need — a problem central to search engines, digital libraries, enterprise search, and (in its modern dense-retrieval form) the retrieval stage of RAG pipelines.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.how_it_works: Classical IR builds an inverted index (mapping each term to the documents containing it) for efficient lookup, and ranks matching documents by relevance models — TF-IDF and BM25 (covered in the Semantic Search group) being the canonical lexical relevance scores, considering term frequency, document frequency, and document length. Evaluation of IR systems uses metrics like precision (fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant), recall (fraction of relevant documents that are retrieved), and ranking-aware metrics like nDCG (normalised discounted cumulative gain, rewarding relevant documents appearing higher in the ranked list) and MAP (mean average precision). Modern IR extends these foundations with learned ranking (machine-learned ranking functions combining many features), dense/neural retrieval (covered extensively in the Semantic Search group — bi-encoders, cross-encoders, hybrid search), and large-scale infrastructure (distributed indices, caching) for web-scale search.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.use_when: As the conceptual foundation for any retrieval-based system — understanding classical IR concepts (inverted indices, TF-IDF/BM25, precision/recall/nDCG evaluation) provides the vocabulary and evaluation framework that modern dense/hybrid retrieval systems (and RAG pipelines) build upon and are evaluated against.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.avoid_when: Avoid treating classical IR (purely lexical, BM25-based) as sufficient for modern semantic search/RAG applications where query-document vocabulary mismatch is common — as discussed under sparse vs dense retrieval, lexical IR alone misses semantically-related-but-lexically-different matches, motivating the dense/hybrid approaches covered in the Semantic Search group.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.what_goes_wrong: IR evaluation requires relevance judgments (which documents are actually relevant to which queries) — obtaining these at scale is expensive (human annotation) or noisy (using implicit signals like clicks, which can be biased by ranking position — users click higher-ranked results more regardless of true relevance, a 'position bias' that must be accounted for when using click data as relevance signal). Precision/recall trade-offs mean optimising for one can hurt the other — a system returning very few results might have high precision but miss many relevant documents (low recall), while a system returning many results has the opposite issue, and the right balance depends on the application (e.g. legal discovery prioritises recall, while a quick web search prioritises precision of top results).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Ling.real_example: Evaluating a search system's quality might involve computing nDCG@10 over a set of test queries with human relevance judgments (each query-document pair rated as highly relevant, somewhat relevant, or not relevant) — nDCG@10 rewards the system more for placing highly-relevant documents near the top of its top-10 results than for placing them lower, and this same evaluation framework (originally developed for classical lexical IR systems) is directly applied to evaluate modern dense/hybrid retrieval systems and RAG retrieval components, illustrating IR's foundational role across both classical and modern retrieval paradigms.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformers replace the dense feed-forward layer in some Transformer blocks with multiple parallel 'expert' feed-forward networks plus a learned 'router' that, for each token, selects a small subset of experts (often just 1 or 2) to process that token — drastically increasing total model parameters without proportionally increasing the compute cost per token.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Scaling dense Transformers (where every parameter is used for every token) requires proportionally more compute as parameters grow — doubling parameters roughly doubles compute per token. MoE decouples total model capacity (number of parameters) from per-token compute: a model can have, say, 8x more total parameters than a dense equivalent, but each token only activates a small fraction (e.g. 2 of 8 experts) of those parameters, so per-token compute stays comparable to a much smaller dense model while total capacity (and thus potential knowledge/specialisation) is much larger.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: In each MoE layer, instead of one feed-forward network, there are N expert feed-forward networks (each with its own weights). A small router network (typically a linear layer + softmax) takes each token's representation and computes a score for each expert; the top-k experts (commonly k=1 or k=2) are selected, and the token is processed by only those experts, with their outputs combined (often weighted by the router's scores). Training requires load-balancing techniques (e.g. auxiliary losses encouraging the router to distribute tokens roughly evenly across experts) to prevent 'expert collapse' where the router always picks the same few experts, leaving others undertrained/unused. At inference, only the selected experts' weights need to be loaded/computed for each token, though all experts' weights must still be stored in memory.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Scaling model capacity for tasks/domains needing broad knowledge coverage while keeping per-token inference cost manageable — MoE architectures (e.g. Mixtral, and reportedly some large proprietary models) are used when the benefits of larger total capacity (better performance) outweigh the added complexity of routing and the memory overhead of storing all experts.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid MoE for smaller-scale models or settings where the engineering complexity (routing, load balancing, distributed serving of experts across devices) isn't justified by the scale — for models that fit comfortably as dense architectures, the added complexity of MoE may not yield proportional benefits. Avoid in memory-constrained deployment (e.g. single consumer GPU) where storing all experts' weights (even if only a few are used per token) may exceed available memory despite lower compute.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Load balancing is a persistent challenge — without effective auxiliary losses/routing strategies, the router can collapse to using only a few experts, wasting the capacity of unused experts and effectively reducing the model to a smaller dense model with extra unused parameters. MoE models require more total memory (to store all experts) even though compute per token is lower, creating a memory-vs-compute trade-off that complicates deployment compared to dense models of similar per-token compute cost. Distributed serving of MoE models (sharding experts across devices) adds infrastructure complexity, especially when token routing causes uneven load across devices hosting different experts.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: Mixtral 8x7B is an MoE model with 8 experts per MoE layer, each ~7B parameters, but only 2 experts are activated per token — giving the model access to roughly 47B total parameters' worth of specialised knowledge while keeping per-token compute closer to that of a ~13B dense model (2 active experts of ~7B each, plus shared components), achieving strong performance with significantly less inference compute than a dense 47B model would require.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Sparse Transformers (in the attention sense) are Transformer variants that replace full O(n^2) self-attention — where every token attends to every other token — with sparse attention patterns where each token attends to only a subset of other tokens (e.g. nearby tokens, or tokens at fixed strided intervals), reducing the computational and memory cost of attention for long sequences.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Standard self-attention's O(n^2) cost in sequence length n becomes prohibitive for long sequences (e.g. long documents, high-resolution images treated as long token sequences, or long audio) — both compute and memory scale quadratically. Sparse attention patterns reduce this to O(n*sqrt(n)) or O(n*k) for some fixed k, enabling Transformers to process much longer sequences than full attention would allow, while (ideally) retaining most of the modelling capability since most relevant dependencies tend to be either local or can be reached via a combination of local and strided/global connections.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Various sparse attention patterns have been proposed: strided/fixed patterns (each token attends to a local window of nearby tokens plus tokens at regular strided intervals further away, providing both local context and some long-range connectivity); block-sparse patterns (attention computed only within and between certain blocks of the sequence); and combinations with a small number of 'global' tokens that attend to (and are attended to by) all other tokens, providing a pathway for information to propagate across the whole sequence despite most attention being local. The specific pattern is fixed by architecture design (not learned), trading some modelling flexibility (a token can't attend to an arbitrary distant token outside its sparse pattern, except via global tokens or multi-layer propagation) for the efficiency gain.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Processing long sequences (long documents, genomic sequences, high-resolution images-as-sequences) where full O(n^2) attention would be computationally prohibitive, and where the sparse attention pattern's locality+global-token structure is a reasonable match for the data's dependency structure (most relevant relationships are local or can route through global tokens).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid for shorter sequences where full attention is computationally feasible — sparse attention's reduced connectivity is an approximation/trade-off that's unnecessary when the quadratic cost isn't actually a bottleneck. Avoid when the task fundamentally requires arbitrary long-range token-to-token interactions that the chosen sparse pattern can't capture even indirectly through global tokens or layer-stacking.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: A fixed sparse attention pattern is a structural assumption about which token relationships matter — if the actual task requires dependencies that fall outside the pattern (e.g. two distant tokens that are highly relevant to each other but neither is a 'global' token and they're not within each other's local windows), the model may struggle to capture that relationship, potentially only through many layers of indirect propagation (each layer can only 'reach' as far as its pattern allows, so long-range info must hop through intermediate positions across layers). Choosing the right sparsity pattern (window size, stride, number of global tokens) requires understanding the data's typical dependency structure, and a poor choice can hurt performance more than the compute savings are worth for some tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: The Sparse Transformer architecture (and related approaches like Longformer) might use a pattern where each token attends to its 256 nearest neighbours (local window) plus a set of designated 'global' tokens (e.g. the first few tokens, or task-specific tokens like [CLS]) that attend to and are attended to by everything — for a 16,000-token document, this might reduce attention computation by a factor of 50-100x compared to full attention, while the global tokens ensure that information can still propagate across the entire document within a reasonable number of layers.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Retrieval-Augmented Transformers are architectures that integrate a retrieval mechanism directly into the model's architecture/training (not just as an external pipeline step, as in typical RAG) — the model retrieves relevant text/knowledge from an external corpus during its forward pass (e.g. via cross-attention to retrieved passages, or by retrieving and incorporating nearest-neighbour examples at the token level) and this retrieval is part of the model's learned computation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Standard Transformers store all 'knowledge' implicitly in their parameters, requiring enormous parameter counts to memorise facts and making updating knowledge require retraining/fine-tuning. Architecturally integrating retrieval allows a model to access a large external knowledge source dynamically — potentially using far fewer parameters for 'memorisation' while achieving comparable or better factual accuracy, and allowing the knowledge source to be updated without retraining the core model.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Approaches vary: RETRO-style architectures retrieve, for chunks of the input, the nearest-neighbour text chunks (by embedding similarity) from a large external database, and incorporate these retrieved chunks via cross-attention layers interspersed in the Transformer's decoder — the retrieval happens for every chunk during both training and inference, and the cross-attention layers learn to use the retrieved content. kNN-LM style approaches interpolate the model's next-token distribution with a distribution derived from the nearest-neighbour matches (in a datastore of context-representation -> next-token pairs) for the current context, blending parametric and non-parametric (retrieval-based) predictions. Unlike typical RAG (where retrieval happens once, producing text that's concatenated into the prompt), architecturally-integrated retrieval can occur multiple times during generation and is trained jointly with (or specifically integrated into) the model's parameters.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Research/architectures aiming to reduce parameter count needed for factual knowledge while maintaining/improving factual accuracy, or settings where the knowledge base needs frequent updates without retraining the core model (since the retrieval datastore can be updated independently of the trained model weights).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid for production systems where simpler prompt-based RAG (retrieve relevant text, concatenate into the prompt of an off-the-shelf LLM) suffices — architecturally-integrated retrieval requires specialised model architectures and training procedures, a much higher engineering bar than prompt-based RAG which works with any standard LLM.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Retrieval at training time means the training data distribution (and the retrieval datastore used during training) must be representative of what will be retrieved at inference — a mismatch (e.g. updating the datastore significantly after training) can cause the model's learned cross-attention/integration mechanisms to behave unexpectedly with retrieved content quite different from what they were trained to integrate. The retrieval step itself (nearest-neighbour search over a potentially massive datastore) adds latency and infrastructure requirements beyond a standard Transformer's forward pass.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: RETRO (Retrieval-Enhanced Transformer) demonstrated that a model with significantly fewer parameters than GPT-3, but augmented with retrieval from a multi-trillion-token database (retrieving relevant chunks for cross-attention during generation), could achieve comparable performance on certain language modelling benchmarks — illustrating the core trade-off: architecturally-integrated retrieval can substitute external, updatable, non-parametric knowledge access for some of the parametric knowledge that would otherwise need to be baked into model weights via scale alone.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: A Prefix Language Model (PrefixLM) is a Transformer architecture/training setup where the input is divided into a 'prefix' portion that uses bidirectional (non-causal) attention among its own tokens, and a 'target' portion that's generated autoregressively (causal attention, can attend to the full prefix plus previously-generated target tokens) — combining the bidirectional context-encoding strength of encoder-style models with the generative capability of decoder-style models, within a single Transformer stack.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Standard decoder-only (GPT-style) models use causal attention everywhere, meaning even the 'input'/context portion of a prompt can only attend to earlier tokens (not later ones within the input itself) — potentially limiting how well the model encodes the input context compared to a bidirectional encoder. PrefixLM addresses this by allowing the input/prefix to be encoded bidirectionally (each prefix token can see the whole prefix), while still supporting autoregressive generation for the output — aiming to get encoder-like input understanding with decoder-like generation in one architecture.
