4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: The attention mask is structured so that: tokens within the prefix can attend to ALL other prefix tokens (bidirectional, like a BERT encoder); tokens in the target/generation portion use causal attention, attending to all prefix tokens plus all PREVIOUS target tokens (but not future target tokens) — implemented via a custom attention mask combining a full (unmasked) block for prefix-to-prefix attention and a causal (lower-triangular) block for target-to-(prefix+target) attention. This can be implemented within a single Transformer (one set of weights, just a different attention mask depending on token position) — unlike a full encoder-decoder (T5-style) architecture which uses two separate stacks with cross-attention between them.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Tasks where the input (e.g. a question, a document to summarise, a source sentence to translate) benefits from bidirectional encoding before generation begins, but a single unified architecture (rather than separate encoder/decoder stacks) is preferred for simplicity/efficiency — PrefixLM is one of the architectural variants explored (e.g. in the T5/UL2 line of research comparing different attention-masking strategies for pretraining).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid if working with standard pretrained decoder-only models (GPT-style) without retraining/adapting their attention masking — PrefixLM requires either training from scratch with this masking scheme or adapting a pretrained model's attention pattern, which isn't a drop-in change to an off-the-shelf causal LM.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Implementing the custom attention mask correctly (bidirectional within prefix, causal for target, with target tokens seeing the full prefix) requires careful attention to positional encoding and masking implementation details — getting this wrong can silently produce a model that's effectively just causal everywhere (losing the bidirectional-prefix benefit) or that leaks future information (a correctness bug, not just a performance issue). Comparisons between PrefixLM, full encoder-decoder, and pure causal decoder architectures (as explored in research like the T5/UL2 papers) show the 'best' choice can depend on the specific task and scale, without a universally dominant option.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: For a summarisation task, a PrefixLM would encode the source document bidirectionally (each document token can attend to the whole document, capturing full context for understanding it) while generating the summary autoregressively (each summary token attends to the full document plus previously-generated summary tokens, but not future summary tokens) — all within a single Transformer stack and set of weights, contrasting with a T5-style encoder-decoder that would use two separate stacks (encoder for the document, decoder for the summary) connected via cross-attention.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Multimodal Transformers are architectures that process and relate information from multiple modalities (text, images, audio, video) within a unified Transformer-based framework — examples include CLIP (joint image-text embeddings), Flamingo/LLaVA-style vision-language models (image input + text generation), and models handling combinations of text, audio, and video.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Real-world information and tasks are often inherently multimodal (an image with a caption, a video with audio and subtitles, a document with text and figures) — multimodal Transformers enable models to jointly reason over these different signal types, supporting tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, text-to-image generation guidance, and document understanding (text + layout + images).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Different multimodal architectures handle cross-modal integration differently: (1) Dual-encoder/contrastive approaches (CLIP) encode each modality separately into a shared embedding space, trained so matching pairs (image, caption) are close — enabling cross-modal retrieval/similarity but not generation across modalities. (2) Cross-attention/fusion approaches (Flamingo) process one modality (e.g. image, via a vision encoder producing visual tokens/features) and inject this information into a language model via cross-attention layers interspersed in the LM, enabling text generation conditioned on visual input. (3) Unified token-sequence approaches (e.g. some vision-language models, and increasingly multimodal LLMs) convert all modalities into a shared sequence of tokens (image patches as 'visual tokens' alongside text tokens) and process the combined sequence with a single Transformer, treating the problem as one large sequence-modelling task across modalities. Modality-specific encoders (e.g. a ViT for images, a CNN/Wav2Vec for audio) typically convert raw modality data into token-like representations compatible with the Transformer's input format.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Any task requiring joint reasoning over multiple modalities: image captioning, visual question answering, document understanding (text + images/layout, relevant to the Document AI & OCR group), video understanding (frames + audio + transcripts), or multimodal retrieval (search images using text queries and vice versa).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid multimodal architectures for unimodal tasks where a single-modality model suffices — the added complexity (multiple encoders, fusion mechanisms, multimodal training data requirements) isn't justified if the task only involves one modality.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Multimodal training data (paired/aligned examples across modalities, e.g. image-caption pairs) is often noisier and less abundant than unimodal text data, and quality/alignment issues in this data (mismatched captions, low-quality images) directly affect model quality. Different modalities have very different 'token densities' and information content per token (a single image might be represented by hundreds of visual tokens vs a short caption's handful of text tokens), creating imbalances in how attention/compute is allocated across modalities that can require architectural choices (e.g. how many visual tokens per image) with significant performance and efficiency implications. Cross-modal hallucination (a vision-language model describing details not actually present in an image) is a known failure mode, analogous to but distinct from pure-text hallucination.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: A vision-language model like LLaVA combines a pretrained vision encoder (e.g. CLIP's image encoder, producing a sequence of visual feature tokens for an input image) with a pretrained LLM, connected via a projection layer that maps visual features into the LLM's embedding space — the combined sequence (visual tokens + text prompt tokens) is processed by the LLM, which can then generate text responses (answering questions about the image, describing it, etc.) conditioned on both the visual and textual input, illustrating the 'unify into one token sequence' approach to multimodal Transformers.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Parameter-sharing Transformers are architectures that reduce the total number of unique parameters by reusing (sharing) the same weights across multiple layers or components — e.g. ALBERT shares parameters across all Transformer layers (the same layer weights are applied repeatedly), reducing model size while maintaining similar depth/computation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Standard Transformers have separate, independently-learned parameters for each layer — a 24-layer model has 24x the parameters of a single layer (for the layer-specific weights). This leads to large model sizes that scale with depth. Parameter sharing decouples model SIZE (number of unique parameters, affecting memory/storage) from model DEPTH (number of sequential processing steps, affecting compute and representational capacity) — enabling deep models with far fewer unique parameters than an equivalent non-shared deep model.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: In cross-layer parameter sharing (as in ALBERT), the same set of Transformer layer weights (attention + feed-forward parameters) is applied at every layer of the model — the input passes through the same weight matrices repeatedly (once per 'layer', though it's really the same layer applied multiple times), rather than each layer having its own distinct weights. This means the model has the COMPUTE cost of a deep model (same number of sequential matrix multiplications) but the PARAMETER COUNT of a single layer (times a small constant for any non-shared components like embeddings). Additional techniques (e.g. ALBERT's factorised embedding parameterisation, separating the embedding dimension from the hidden dimension) further reduce parameter count in specific components.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Settings prioritising small model size/memory footprint (storage, distribution, memory-constrained deployment) where the compute cost of depth is acceptable but the parameter-count cost isn't — e.g. mobile/edge deployment where model file size matters, or research exploring the relationship between depth, parameter count, and model capacity.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid parameter sharing when parameter count isn't the binding constraint and maximising representational capacity per unit of compute is the goal — non-shared (independently-parameterised) layers generally have higher capacity than shared layers with the same compute cost, since each layer can specialise to a different transformation rather than reusing the same transformation repeatedly.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Parameter sharing can limit the model's ability to learn different transformations at different depths (e.g. early layers learning low-level features, later layers learning higher-level abstractions) — if all layers share weights, this kind of layer-wise specialisation is constrained, which can cap the model's ultimate performance ceiling compared to an equivalently-deep non-shared model, even though both have the same compute cost per forward pass. The reduced parameter count (smaller model file) doesn't reduce INFERENCE compute/latency (still need to run all the layers/forward passes) — parameter sharing optimises for storage/memory size, not speed, which can be a point of confusion.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: ALBERT achieves similar or better performance than BERT on several benchmarks with dramatically fewer parameters (e.g. ALBERT-large has ~18M parameters vs BERT-large's ~334M) by sharing parameters across all layers — but ALBERT-large's INFERENCE TIME is comparable to or slower than BERT-large's, since it still performs the same number of sequential layer computations (just reusing the same weights each time) — illustrating that parameter sharing trades parameter-count/storage efficiency for, not against, compute, which is an important distinction when choosing this architecture for a specific deployment constraint (storage vs latency).

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Cross-lingual models are language models trained on text from multiple languages simultaneously (often dozens to over a hundred), aiming to learn shared representations that transfer across languages — enabling tasks like zero-shot cross-lingual transfer (fine-tune on a task in one language, the model performs reasonably on the same task in other languages without additional training) and cross-lingual retrieval/alignment.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Most labelled training data exists for a small number of high-resource languages (especially English), while thousands of languages have little to no labelled data for most NLP tasks. Cross-lingual models aim to leverage shared structure across languages (and any available multilingual unlabelled text, which is more abundant than labelled data in most languages) so that capabilities learned/fine-tuned primarily using high-resource-language data transfer to lower-resource languages.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Cross-lingual models (e.g. mBERT, XLM-R) are pretrained on large multilingual corpora using the same self-supervised objectives as monolingual models (masked language modelling), but with training data spanning many languages — often using a shared subword vocabulary (e.g. a multilingual SentencePiece tokenizer) covering all languages, so that the same model and tokenizer handle all languages. The implicit hypothesis (borne out empirically to a significant degree) is that, especially for related languages or for tasks relying on more 'universal' linguistic structure, the model learns representations where similar concepts across languages end up with similar internal representations, enabling transfer. Some approaches add explicit cross-lingual signals during training (e.g. parallel/translated text pairs, encouraging aligned representations across translations of the same content) to strengthen this cross-lingual alignment beyond what emerges from multilingual pretraining alone.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Building NLP systems that need to support many languages, especially when labelled training data is only available in one or a few languages but the system needs to work (even if with reduced accuracy) across many languages — common for global products needing broad language coverage without per-language labelled datasets.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid assuming cross-lingual transfer works equally well across all language pairs — transfer tends to be stronger between related languages (e.g. fine-tuning on French data transfers better to Spanish/Italian than to Japanese/Korean) and depends heavily on how much unlabelled pretraining data existed for the target language. For applications where high accuracy in a specific lower-resource language is critical, dedicated monolingual data/fine-tuning (if obtainable) often outperforms relying purely on cross-lingual transfer.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: The 'curse of multilinguality' — for a fixed model size, adding more languages to pretraining can degrade per-language performance compared to a monolingual model of the same size, since model capacity must be shared across all languages' vocabulary/structure; larger multilingual models mitigate but don't eliminate this trade-off. Cross-lingual transfer performance correlates strongly with the amount of pretraining data available for each language — for genuinely low-resource languages with minimal representation in pretraining corpora, transfer quality can be substantially worse than for well-resourced languages, even with the 'same' cross-lingual model.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: XLM-R, pretrained on text in 100 languages, can be fine-tuned for a task like named entity recognition using only English-labelled training data, and then applied directly to, say, German or Spanish text with reasonable (though typically lower than English) accuracy — zero-shot cross-lingual transfer — whereas applying it to a low-resource language with minimal representation in XLM-R's pretraining corpus would likely show much larger performance drops, illustrating both the value and the limits of cross-lingual transfer.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Code models are language models specifically trained (or significantly fine-tuned) on source code — examples include Codex, CodeLlama, StarCoder, and the code-generation capabilities of general-purpose LLMs — used for tasks like code completion, code generation from natural-language descriptions, code explanation, bug detection, and code translation between programming languages.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Source code has different statistical and structural properties than natural language (strict syntax rules, long-range dependencies like variable definitions used much later, different 'vocabulary' including identifiers and operators) — training specifically on code (often a mix of code and natural language, e.g. code with comments/docstrings, and code paired with natural-language descriptions) produces models substantially better at code-related tasks than general-purpose text models of similar size, motivating dedicated code models or code-focused fine-tuning of general LLMs.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Code models use the same Transformer architecture and training objectives (next-token prediction) as general LLMs, but trained on large corpora of source code (e.g. scraped from public code repositories), often combined with natural-language text (so the model can handle natural-language instructions/descriptions alongside code) and sometimes with additional structure-aware training signals (e.g. fill-in-the-middle objectives, where the model learns to predict a missing middle section of code given the surrounding prefix and suffix — useful for code completion in an editor, where the cursor is in the middle of existing code, not just at the end). Tokenisation for code often handles whitespace/indentation (significant in languages like Python) and code-specific tokens (operators, brackets) carefully, since these carry syntactic meaning.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Code completion/generation tools (IDE autocomplete, 'generate a function that does X'), code explanation/documentation generation, code translation (e.g. Python to JavaScript), and code-related QA (debugging help, explaining error messages) — code models or code-capable general LLMs are the standard tool for these tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid relying on code model output without verification (running tests, code review) for production code — code models can generate syntactically valid but logically incorrect or insecure code, and 'looks right' is not the same as 'is correct', especially for security-sensitive code (e.g. generating code with injection vulnerabilities if not carefully reviewed).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Code models can generate code that compiles/runs but contains subtle logical bugs, uses deprecated/non-existent APIs (hallucinating function names or library methods that don't actually exist — 'package hallucination', which has even been exploited as a supply-chain attack vector by publishing malicious packages under commonly-hallucinated names), or introduces security vulnerabilities (e.g. SQL injection, missing input validation) if not specifically trained/prompted to avoid these. Evaluation of code models (e.g. via HumanEval/MBPP-style benchmarks, executing generated code against test cases) is more objective than typical NL generation evaluation (pass/fail on tests) but can still miss code that 'passes the given tests' while being incorrect for inputs not covered by those tests.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: A developer asks a code model to 'write a Python function to parse a CSV file and return rows where the age column is greater than 18' — the model generates plausible-looking code using pandas or the csv module; verification (running it against sample data, checking edge cases like missing/non-numeric age values) is necessary because the generated code might not handle such edge cases correctly even though it looks reasonable and would pass a simple 'does it run without error on clean input' check.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Long-context models are LLMs specifically designed/adapted to handle very long input sequences — context windows ranging from tens of thousands to over a million tokens — enabling tasks like processing entire books, large codebases, or extensive document collections within a single prompt, beyond the few-thousand-token limits of earlier Transformer models.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Standard Transformer self-attention's O(n^2) compute/memory cost makes naively scaling context length expensive, and models trained on shorter sequences often generalise poorly to much longer ones at inference time (positional encoding and attention pattern distribution shift). Long-context models address both the computational scaling challenge (via architectural techniques) and the generalisation challenge (via specific training/positional-encoding choices), enabling use cases (long document QA, codebase-wide reasoning, many-shot in-context learning) that short-context models can't support directly.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: Several techniques contribute to long-context capability: (1) Positional encoding schemes designed for extrapolation — e.g. RoPE (rotary position embeddings) with scaling techniques (like position interpolation or NTK-aware scaling) that allow a model trained on shorter sequences to handle longer ones at inference with reduced degradation, or ALiBi (attention with linear biases) which encodes position via an attention-score bias that naturally generalises to longer sequences. (2) Efficient attention implementations (e.g. FlashAttention) that reduce the memory overhead of attention computation (though not the fundamental O(n^2) compute scaling) enough to make longer sequences practically feasible on available hardware. (3) Architectural changes (sparse attention, sliding-window attention with some global tokens, or fundamentally different architectures like state-space models) that change the O(n^2) scaling to something more favourable. (4) Training specifically on long-sequence data (continued pretraining or fine-tuning on long documents) so the model learns to actually USE long-range context effectively, not just technically process it without crashing.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Tasks requiring reasoning over content too large for shorter context windows: analysing entire books/long reports, codebase-wide questions ('where is X used across this repository'), processing long conversation histories, or many-shot in-context learning with large numbers of examples in the prompt.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid using maximal context length by default for tasks that don't need it — longer contexts increase compute cost and latency (even with efficient attention implementations, processing more tokens costs more), and 'stuffing' a prompt with unnecessary content can sometimes degrade performance (the model has to 'search' through more irrelevant content, and attention to relevant parts can become diluted) compared to providing only the relevant context (e.g. via retrieval/RAG to select pertinent passages rather than including everything).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: The 'lost in the middle' phenomenon — models with long context windows often show better recall/utilisation of information near the beginning or end of the context than information in the middle, meaning technically 'fitting' information in the context window doesn't guarantee the model will use it effectively, especially for information buried in the middle of a very long input. Long-context capability claimed via positional-encoding extrapolation tricks doesn't always translate to actually GOOD performance at the claimed length — a model might 'not crash' at 100K tokens but perform notably worse on tasks requiring information from throughout that context than its short-context performance would suggest, requiring 'needle in a haystack' style evaluations (placing a specific fact at various positions in a long context and testing retrieval) to assess real long-context utilisation, not just maximum supported length.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: A long-context model with a 200K-token window might be used to analyse an entire codebase (concatenating many files into one prompt) and answer 'where is the database connection configured and how is it used across the codebase' — but evaluation via 'needle in a haystack' tests (placing a specific unique fact at different positions within a 200K-token context and checking whether the model can retrieve it) might reveal that recall is near-perfect for facts near the start/end but degrades for facts buried in the middle, informing whether the application should rely on the full context naively or use retrieval/chunking to ensure critical information is positioned favourably.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_it_is: Structured State Space Models (SSMs, e.g. S4, Mamba) are a class of sequence models — an alternative to Transformer's attention mechanism — based on continuous-time state-space representations (borrowed from control theory) discretised for sequence processing, achieving linear (rather than quadratic) scaling with sequence length while maintaining strong performance on long-sequence tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.why_it_exists: Transformer self-attention's O(n^2) scaling is a fundamental computational bottleneck for very long sequences. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) scale linearly but suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients over long sequences and can't be parallelised across time during training (must process sequentially). SSMs aim to combine RNN-like linear scaling and (in principle) long-range memory with training-time parallelisability more akin to convolutions/Transformers — addressing the 'quadratic attention vs sequential RNN' trade-off that has constrained sequence modelling architectures.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.how_it_works: SSMs model sequences via a (discretised) linear state-space equation: a hidden state h_t evolves as h_t = A*h_{t-1} + B*x_t, and the output y_t = C*h_t (+ D*x_t), where A, B, C, D are learned matrices (in 'structured' SSMs like S4, matrix A has a special structure, e.g. derived from HiPPO theory, designed to capture long-range dependencies effectively while being computationally efficient). Critically, this recurrence can be reformulated as a convolution over the sequence (for training, enabling parallelisation across time, similar to how convolutions are parallelisable) while also being usable in its recurrent form (for efficient autoregressive inference, processing one token at a time with constant per-step cost, unlike attention which must reference all previous tokens' KV cache). Mamba extends this with 'selective' SSMs, where the A, B, C matrices depend on the input (input-dependent/selective state updates), adding a form of content-based gating (loosely analogous to attention's content-based weighting) while retaining linear-time scaling.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.use_when: Research and emerging production use cases needing very long sequence processing with better-than-quadratic scaling — genomics (very long DNA sequences), audio/long-form generation, or any setting where Transformer's O(n^2) attention cost is the binding constraint and SSM-based architectures' linear scaling and constant-memory autoregressive inference (no growing KV cache) offer practical advantages.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.avoid_when: Avoid for tasks/scales where Transformers' well-established tooling, pretrained models, and ecosystem (fine-tuning recipes, serving infrastructure, broad community knowledge) provide practical advantages that outweigh SSMs' theoretical efficiency benefits — SSM-based models are newer, with a less mature ecosystem, and for many moderate-length tasks Transformers remain the more practically supported choice as of recent years.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.what_goes_wrong: Whether SSMs match Transformer-quality performance on tasks requiring precise token-to-token comparisons (e.g. exact copying, certain forms of in-context learning that rely on attention's ability to directly 'look up' specific earlier tokens) is an active research question — some evaluations show gaps on tasks that benefit from attention's explicit pairwise comparison mechanism, which SSMs approximate differently (via the evolving hidden state) rather than replicate exactly. The 'selective'/input-dependent mechanisms (e.g. in Mamba) that improve SSM performance add complexity back into what was originally a simpler linear-recurrence framework, and the field is still developing best practices for training, scaling, and combining SSM and attention components (hybrid architectures).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Adva.real_example: Mamba demonstrated that a selective-SSM-based language model can match Transformer-based models of similar size on language modelling benchmarks while having linear-time scaling in sequence length and constant memory for autoregressive generation (no KV cache that grows with sequence length, unlike Transformers) — making it particularly efficient for very long sequence generation, though as of its introduction, large-scale production adoption and tooling support remained far less extensive than for Transformer-based models.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_it_is: o200k_base is the tokeniser vocabulary/encoding used by OpenAI's GPT-4o family of models, implemented in the open-source `tiktoken` library — a byte-pair-encoding (BPE) based tokeniser with a vocabulary of approximately 200,000 tokens, larger than the ~100K vocabulary (cl100k_base) used by GPT-4/GPT-3.5.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.why_it_exists: Larger vocabularies allow more text (especially non-English text, code, and common multi-word phrases) to be represented with fewer tokens, improving both efficiency (more content per context-window token budget) and quality (less aggressive splitting of words into awkward subword fragments, particularly for languages/scripts underrepresented in smaller vocabularies). o200k_base reflects OpenAI's continued tuning of tokenisation as models and their multilingual/multimodal use cases evolved.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.how_it_works: Like other tiktoken encodings, o200k_base uses byte-level BPE: text is first converted to bytes (so any Unicode text can be represented, with no out-of-vocabulary issues — worst case, falls back to individual bytes), then BPE merge rules (learned from training data, prioritising frequently co-occurring byte/token pairs) progressively merge byte sequences into larger subword tokens, up to the ~200K vocabulary size. The `tiktoken` library provides fast (Rust-backed) encode/decode implementations, used both for actually tokenising model inputs/outputs and for estimating token counts for cost/context-length planning before making API calls.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.use_when: When working with GPT-4o-family models via the OpenAI API, use `tiktoken` with the `o200k_base` encoding to accurately count tokens for cost estimation, context-window budget planning (ensuring prompts + expected output fit within the model's context limit), and for any application logic that needs to reason about how the model 'sees' text in token units (e.g. chunking documents for RAG by token count rather than character count).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.avoid_when: Avoid using `cl100k_base` (the GPT-4/GPT-3.5/ChatGPT encoding) to count tokens for GPT-4o-family models, and vice versa — different models use different tokenisers, and token counts computed with the wrong encoding can be meaningfully inaccurate, leading to underestimated costs or context-window overflows that weren't predicted by the (incorrect) token count.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_goes_wrong: Using the wrong tiktoken encoding for a given model is an easy and common mistake (especially when code is copy-pasted from examples targeting a different model) — the mismatch doesn't throw an error, it just silently produces a token count that may differ from the actual count the API uses, which can cause unexpected context-length errors at the API level (the API enforces the true limit regardless of what a mis-encoded local count suggested) or inaccurate cost projections. Tokenisation behaviour for non-English text and code can still differ notably from intuitive 'word count' expectations even with the larger o200k_base vocabulary — e.g. some scripts still require more tokens per character than English.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.real_example: A RAG pipeline chunking documents to fit within GPT-4o's context window should use `tiktoken.get_encoding('o200k_base')` (or `tiktoken.encoding_for_model('gpt-4o')`) to measure chunk sizes in tokens — if the pipeline instead reuses `cl100k_base` (perhaps left over from earlier GPT-4 code), chunk token counts will be computed using the wrong vocabulary; since o200k_base often represents the same text in fewer tokens than cl100k_base, chunks sized using cl100k_base counts might actually be smaller (in real GPT-4o tokens) than intended — not necessarily causing overflow, but resulting in suboptimal chunk sizing relative to the intended budget.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_it_is: The Llama 3 tokeniser is a byte-level BPE tokeniser with a vocabulary of 128,256 tokens, a significant increase from Llama 2's 32,000-token vocabulary — designed to improve encoding efficiency, especially for non-English languages and code.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.why_it_exists: Llama 2's relatively small 32K vocabulary, while adequate for English, resulted in less efficient encoding (more tokens needed) for non-English text and code, increasing effective sequence lengths (and thus compute cost and effective context-window consumption) for multilingual/code use cases. Llama 3's much larger vocabulary (4x Llama 2's) reduces the average number of tokens needed to represent text in many languages and for code, improving both efficiency and the model's effective context capacity for non-English content.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.how_it_works: Llama 3 uses a byte-level BPE tokeniser (based on OpenAI's tiktoken-style implementation, specifically derived from the same family as GPT-4's tokeniser approach) with 128,256 tokens, including a substantial number of tokens dedicated to representing common multilingual subwords and code tokens that would have required multiple tokens (or byte-fallback) under Llama 2's smaller vocabulary. As a byte-level BPE tokeniser, it retains the property that any Unicode input can be represented (falling back to byte-level tokens for truly out-of-vocabulary sequences), while the larger learned vocabulary reduces how often this fallback is needed for common multilingual text.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.use_when: When fine-tuning, running inference with, or estimating token counts/context usage for Llama 3 (and derivatives) — especially relevant when migrating workloads/prompts from Llama 2 to Llama 3, since token counts for the same text will generally differ (typically fewer tokens for non-English/code text under Llama 3's larger vocabulary).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.avoid_when: Avoid assuming token-count parity between Llama 2 and Llama 3 for the same text when migrating prompts, fine-tuning datasets, or context-length budgets — the vocabulary change means token counts (and therefore effective context usage, and any token-based chunking) will differ, sometimes substantially for non-English content.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_goes_wrong: Fine-tuning datasets or prompt templates carried over from Llama 2 without re-tokenising/re-measuring can have different effective lengths under Llama 3's tokeniser — a prompt template designed to fit comfortably within Llama 2's context window might tokenise differently (likely shorter, given the larger vocabulary, but not guaranteed for all text) under Llama 3, so context-budget assumptions should be re-validated rather than carried over. As with any tokeniser change, any code that was tokenising/detokenising text using Llama 2's tokeniser/vocabulary files must be updated to use Llama 3's corresponding tokeniser artifacts — mixing tokenisers between model versions produces nonsensical token IDs.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.real_example: Encoding a Chinese-language paragraph with Llama 2's 32K-vocabulary tokeniser might require significantly more tokens per character than the same paragraph in English (since Chinese characters/subwords were underrepresented in Llama 2's smaller, more English-centric vocabulary) — Llama 3's 128K vocabulary, with substantially more multilingual coverage, represents the same Chinese text more efficiently (fewer tokens), which both reduces inference cost for non-English workloads and effectively increases the amount of non-English content that fits within a given token-based context window.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_it_is: Gemma's tokeniser is built using SentencePiece with a Unigram language-model training algorithm (rather than the more common BPE merge-based algorithm) and a large vocabulary of approximately 256,000 tokens — a notably different and larger tokeniser configuration than many comparably-sized open models.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.why_it_exists: A very large vocabulary (256K, among the largest of openly-released model tokenisers) substantially reduces the number of tokens needed to represent text across many languages and domains, improving multilingual coverage and reducing effective sequence lengths — at the cost of a much larger embedding matrix (vocabulary size x hidden dimension), which is a meaningful fraction of total parameters for smaller models. The Unigram LM training algorithm (an alternative to BPE's greedy pairwise-merge approach) provides a different, probabilistically-motivated method for determining the vocabulary, which SentencePiece supports as a configurable option.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.how_it_works: SentencePiece is a tokeniser library/framework supporting multiple subword algorithms (BPE and Unigram LM being the two most common); the Unigram LM algorithm starts from a large seed vocabulary and iteratively removes tokens that contribute least to the likelihood of the training corpus under a unigram language model (each token's probability is estimated independently), converging on a vocabulary that's probabilistically motivated rather than built purely from greedy frequency-based merges (BPE's approach). SentencePiece also operates directly on raw text (treating whitespace as a regular character, often represented with a special marker like '▁'), making tokenisation reversible/lossless without needing separate pre-tokenisation rules — useful for consistent handling across languages with different whitespace conventions (e.g. languages that don't use spaces between words).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.use_when: Relevant when working with Gemma models (fine-tuning, inference, token-count estimation) — understanding that Gemma's tokeniser differs both in algorithm (Unigram LM vs BPE) and vocabulary size (256K, large) from many other open models informs expectations about token efficiency and embedding-matrix parameter overhead.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.avoid_when: Avoid assuming Gemma's tokeniser/vocabulary is interchangeable with other models' tokenisers (even other SentencePiece-based ones) — vocabulary contents and token IDs are model-specific, and the Unigram-LM-trained vocabulary's specific token boundaries will differ from a BPE-trained vocabulary even on the same training corpus.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_goes_wrong: A 256K vocabulary means the embedding and output (LM head) matrices are large relative to a smaller model's hidden dimension — for a smaller Gemma variant, the embedding parameters can represent a non-trivial fraction of total model parameters, an important consideration when reasoning about where a small model's parameter budget is 'spent' (vocabulary/embeddings vs Transformer layers) and how that affects capacity for actual sequence processing vs vocabulary representation. The Unigram LM algorithm's resulting tokenisation can differ in subtle ways from BPE tokenisation of the same text (different subword boundaries), which matters if directly comparing token counts/behaviour against BPE-tokenised models.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.real_example: For a smaller Gemma model (e.g. a 2B-parameter variant), the 256K-vocabulary embedding matrix (256,000 x hidden_dim) can constitute a noticeably larger share of total parameters than the embedding matrix of a similarly-sized model with a 32K or 50K vocabulary — a consideration when comparing 'parameter-matched' models across families, since not all parameters are doing the same kind of work (vocabulary representation vs sequence-processing computation).

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_it_is: ByT5 is a variant of the T5 model that operates directly on UTF-8 bytes as its 'tokens' (vocabulary size of 256, one per possible byte value, plus a few special tokens) — eliminating subword tokenisation entirely and processing text as raw byte sequences.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.why_it_exists: Subword tokenisers (BPE, SentencePiece, WordPiece) introduce a fixed vocabulary that must be determined in advance from training data, can behave unpredictably on text with unusual characters, typos, or languages/scripts underrepresented in the tokeniser's training data, and add a layer of complexity (the tokeniser itself, separate from the model) that must be kept in sync with the model. ByT5 explores the alternative extreme: no subword vocabulary at all, just raw bytes — trivially handling ANY text (any language, any Unicode character, typos, rare symbols) without out-of-vocabulary issues, at the cost of much longer sequences (since each byte is one 'token', a word that might be 1-2 subword tokens becomes many byte-tokens).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.how_it_works: Input text is UTF-8 encoded and each byte (256 possible values) is treated as a token; the model (a T5-style encoder-decoder Transformer) processes these byte sequences directly. Because byte sequences are much longer than subword-token sequences for the same text (often 4-5x longer), ByT5 typically uses some architectural adjustments to manage this (e.g. the encoder may have more layers but the decoder fewer, since the decoder's autoregressive generation cost scales more directly with sequence length, or downsampling techniques to reduce effective sequence length within the model while still operating on byte-level input).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.use_when: Tasks involving noisy text (significant typos, OCR errors), text with mixed/unusual scripts or many rare characters, or settings where robustness to arbitrary input (no out-of-vocabulary issues, no tokeniser-vocabulary mismatch concerns) is more important than the compute efficiency of shorter subword-tokenised sequences — also useful for tasks operating below the word level (e.g. spelling correction, transliteration) where byte/character-level granularity is inherently appropriate.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.avoid_when: Avoid for general-purpose tasks where standard subword tokenisation works well and compute efficiency matters — byte-level sequences being 4-5x longer than subword sequences for the same text directly translates to roughly proportionally more compute (especially for the O(n^2) attention cost, where longer sequences are quadratically more expensive), making ByT5-style models notably less efficient for typical long-text tasks compared to subword-tokenised models of similar parameter count.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_goes_wrong: The much longer sequence lengths for the same amount of text directly increase computational cost (both training and inference) — a paragraph that's a few hundred subword tokens becomes well over a thousand bytes, multiplying attention cost roughly by the square of that ratio. While byte-level models are robust to out-of-vocabulary issues by construction, they don't automatically gain better 'understanding' of rare words/scripts — they simply avoid the specific failure mode of subword tokenisers producing degenerate splits for unfamiliar text, but still need sufficient training exposure to learn to handle such text well.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.real_example: For a multilingual spelling-correction task involving text with many typos and mixed scripts, ByT5's byte-level processing avoids the situation where a subword tokeniser, trained predominantly on 'clean' text, might tokenise a typo'd or rare word into an unhelpful sequence of small fragments (or unknown tokens) — ByT5 simply sees the raw bytes regardless, though at the cost of needing to process roughly 4-5x as many 'tokens' as a subword-tokenised equivalent for the same input text, which matters for inference latency/cost at scale.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_it_is: CANINE (Character Architecture with No tokenization In Neural Encoders) is a Transformer encoder that operates directly on Unicode characters (not bytes, not subwords) without any learned vocabulary/tokenisation step, using a combination of techniques (hashing-based character embeddings and strided/downsampling convolutions) to manage the computational cost of character-level sequences.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.why_it_exists: Like ByT5, CANINE addresses subword tokenisation's limitations (fixed vocabulary, OOV issues, tokeniser-model coupling) but at the character level (rather than byte level) and with specific architectural mechanisms designed to mitigate the sequence-length cost that naive character-level processing would incur — aiming for tokenisation-free models that remain computationally practical.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.how_it_works: Rather than a learned embedding table indexed by character (which would need to cover the huge space of Unicode code points), CANINE uses a hashing-based approach: each character is mapped via multiple hash functions to indices into a smaller embedding table, and the character's representation is derived from combining these hashed embeddings — avoiding a vocabulary while still producing a meaningful per-character representation. To manage sequence length, CANINE applies a 'downsampling' step early in the model (e.g. strided convolutions that reduce the sequence length by some factor before the main Transformer layers process it), and an 'upsampling' step to restore character-level resolution for the output — so the expensive Transformer layers operate on a shorter 'downsampled' sequence, while the model still effectively reads and can produce character-level information at its input/output boundaries.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.use_when: Research/applications wanting tokenisation-free models specifically operating at the character level (vs byte level) — e.g. for languages/tasks where character-level granularity is linguistically meaningful and where avoiding subword tokenisation's vocabulary/OOV issues is valuable, while mitigating (via downsampling) the sequence-length cost that pure character-level processing would otherwise incur.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.avoid_when: Avoid if a well-tuned subword tokeniser already works well for the target languages/domain and the additional architectural complexity (hashing embeddings, downsampling/upsampling) of a tokenisation-free character-level model isn't justified by a specific need (e.g. extreme multilingual robustness, or tasks where character-level structure specifically matters, like certain morphologically complex languages).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.what_goes_wrong: The hashing-based character embeddings (mapping characters to a smaller embedding table via hash functions) can in principle have hash collisions (different characters mapping to overlapping representations), though using multiple hash functions mitigates this. The downsampling/upsampling mechanism adds architectural complexity and introduces its own hyperparameters (downsampling rate) that trade off between computational savings and how much character-level granularity is preserved through the 'bottleneck' of the downsampled Transformer layers — getting this balance wrong can lose information that pure character-level processing would otherwise retain.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mode.real_example: For multilingual tasks spanning many scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, CJK, etc.), CANINE avoids needing a shared subword vocabulary that must allocate vocabulary 'budget' across all these scripts (a tension present in standard multilingual subword tokenisers, where scripts with less training data get less vocabulary coverage and thus less efficient tokenisation) — instead operating uniformly at the character level for all scripts, with the downsampling mechanism keeping the effective sequence length (and thus compute) manageable despite character-level input granularity.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: MMLU-Pro and MMLU-Redux are revised versions of the original MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) benchmark — a multiple-choice exam-style benchmark covering 57 subjects (humanities, STEM, social sciences, etc.). MMLU-Pro increases difficulty (more answer options, harder questions requiring more reasoning, less solvable by elimination) and MMLU-Redux corrects errors/ambiguities found in the original MMLU's questions and answer keys.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: The original MMLU became 'saturated' as frontier models approached or exceeded 90% accuracy, reducing its ability to differentiate top models — and independent analyses found a non-trivial error rate in MMLU's questions/answer keys (mislabelled correct answers, ambiguous questions), undermining confidence in small score differences. MMLU-Pro addresses saturation by increasing difficulty (10 options instead of 4, requiring more reasoning rather than recall/elimination); MMLU-Redux addresses correctness by re-annotating a subset of questions to fix errors.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: MMLU-Pro increases each question's answer choices from 4 to 10 (making random-guessing baseline 10% instead of 25%) and selects/creates questions that require multi-step reasoning rather than being answerable via simple fact recall or process-of-elimination — models are evaluated on accuracy across the same broad subject coverage as original MMLU but with this harder format. MMLU-Redux involves human re-annotation of a sample of MMLU questions across subjects, identifying and correcting (or flagging for removal) questions with incorrect answer keys, ambiguous wording, or other quality issues, providing a 'cleaned' subset for more reliable evaluation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating frontier/near-frontier LLMs where the original MMLU has become too easy (scores clustering near ceiling, making model comparisons less informative) — MMLU-Pro provides more headroom for differentiating capable models; MMLU-Redux is useful when you want to evaluate against a benchmark with verified-correct answer keys, avoiding the noise introduced by erroneous questions in the original.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid using the original MMLU as a primary differentiator for frontier models given known saturation and error-rate concerns — though it remains useful for comparing weaker/smaller models that are far from ceiling, where the saturation concern is less relevant.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: Even 'harder' benchmarks can saturate over time as models improve and/or as benchmark data leaks into training sets (a pervasive concern for any public benchmark — if questions appear in a model's pretraining data, performance reflects memorisation rather than reasoning). The MMLU-Redux correction process itself involves human judgment about what counts as an 'error' — some flagged issues might be genuinely ambiguous rather than objectively wrong, meaning 'corrected' answer keys aren't necessarily beyond dispute either.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: A model scoring 92% on original MMLU might score notably lower (e.g. 70-75%) on MMLU-Pro due to the increased difficulty and reduced guessability — this gap is itself informative, showing how much of the original MMLU score may have reflected easier question formats rather than the model's true reasoning depth, which is why model report cards increasingly report MMLU-Pro alongside or instead of original MMLU.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A) Diamond is the highest-quality subset of the GPQA benchmark — a set of very difficult multiple-choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry, written by domain experts (PhD-level) and specifically designed to be 'Google-proof' (not easily answerable by searching the web) and resistant to non-expert humans even with internet access.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: As LLMs improved at benchmarks that could be 'solved' via pattern-matching or web-search-style retrieval of relevant facts, GPQA was designed to test genuine graduate-level domain expertise/reasoning — questions where even skilled non-experts with internet access perform near chance, isolating a benchmark that specifically measures deep domain reasoning rather than information lookup.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: Domain experts (with relevant PhDs) write multiple-choice questions in their specialty, and the questions are validated by having non-expert validators attempt them (with web access) — questions where non-experts still perform poorly (close to random chance) despite being able to search are retained, ensuring the benchmark genuinely requires domain expertise rather than searchable facts. The 'Diamond' subset is a further-curated, highest-confidence/highest-quality subset of these questions (those with the strongest expert agreement and validator results), used as the standard reporting subset for frontier model evaluation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating frontier models' graduate-level scientific reasoning capability, particularly when comparing top-tier models where simpler benchmarks have saturated — GPQA Diamond is commonly reported alongside MMLU-Pro and math/coding benchmarks in frontier model technical reports as a marker of advanced reasoning.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid using GPQA as a general capability indicator for non-frontier or smaller models — the questions are specifically calibrated to be extremely hard (near-chance for skilled non-experts), so smaller/weaker models will simply score near the random-guess baseline, providing little differentiating signal among models that aren't near the frontier.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: Even 'Google-proof' framing doesn't guarantee a benchmark stays uncontaminated — if GPQA questions or closely related material end up in training data (directly or via discussions referencing the questions), genuine reasoning becomes harder to distinguish from memorisation, an ongoing concern for any widely-used and openly-available benchmark. The benchmark's narrow focus (biology, physics, chemistry, multiple-choice format) means high GPQA performance doesn't necessarily generalise to other domains of expertise or to open-ended (non-multiple-choice) reasoning tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: Frontier model technical reports often cite GPQA Diamond accuracy (e.g. a model achieving 50-60%+ where random chance on 4-option multiple choice would be 25% and skilled non-expert humans with web access score only modestly above chance) as evidence of advancing graduate-level scientific reasoning — the gap between random-chance baseline, non-expert-with-internet performance, and model performance is the key signal GPQA Diamond is designed to surface.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) is a challenging high-school-level competition mathematics exam (each problem has an integer answer 0-999) increasingly used as an LLM math-reasoning benchmark; AIMO (AI Mathematical Olympiad) is a competition/benchmark initiative specifically aimed at driving progress toward AI systems that can solve International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO)-level problems, with associated prize-based challenges.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: Mathematical reasoning is a domain where correctness is objectively verifiable (unlike open-ended generation) and where competition mathematics provides a natural difficulty ladder (AIME -> IMO) with well-established human performance baselines (AIME is taken by top high-school students; IMO by elite international competitors) — making these benchmarks attractive for tracking LLM reasoning progress with clear, externally-calibrated difficulty levels and unambiguous (numeric or proof-based) correctness criteria.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: AIME problems require multi-step mathematical reasoning culminating in an integer answer (0-999), making automatic grading straightforward (exact match on the final integer) while the reasoning required to get there is non-trivial — models are evaluated on the fraction of AIME problems solved correctly (often using techniques like chain-of-thought prompting, and sometimes reporting results with majority-voting/self-consistency across multiple samples). AIMO-related benchmarks/competitions push toward IMO-level problems, which typically require full proofs (not just numeric answers), raising both the reasoning difficulty and the grading complexity (proof correctness is harder to automatically verify than a numeric answer match).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating and tracking progress in LLM mathematical reasoning, particularly for models employing extended chain-of-thought or other test-time reasoning techniques — AIME-style benchmarks (with their clear human-performance calibration: top high schoolers typically solve a certain fraction of AIME problems) provide an interpretable yardstick ('this model now solves AIME problems at roughly the level of a strong high-school competitor').
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid treating AIME/AIMO performance as a proxy for general reasoning ability beyond mathematics — competition math has its own specific patterns/tricks that models may learn to exploit (potentially via exposure to similar problems in training data) without this necessarily reflecting broadly transferable reasoning improvements.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: Data contamination is a significant concern — AIME problems and solutions are publicly available and widely discussed online, so a model's training data may include these exact problems/solutions, inflating apparent performance relative to genuine held-out reasoning ability; newer/unreleased AIME problems (from the most recent year's competition) provide a less-contaminated (though still eventually-leaking) evaluation. For AIMO-level (IMO) problems requiring proofs, automatic grading is much harder than AIME's integer-answer format, often requiring human or LLM-based proof evaluation, which introduces its own evaluation noise/subjectivity.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: A model report might state 'achieves X% on AIME 2024 problems with chain-of-thought prompting, compared to Y% for the previous model generation' — using the most RECENT year's AIME (released after the model's training data cutoff) specifically to reduce contamination concerns, since older AIME years are far more likely to have been seen during pretraining via solution discussions, forum posts, and aggregated problem-set datasets.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: LiveCodeBench is a coding benchmark that continuously incorporates newly-released competitive programming problems (reducing contamination by using problems released after model training cutoffs) and evaluates across multiple code-related skills (generation, self-repair, execution, test prediction). SWE-Bench evaluates models on real-world GitHub issues — given an issue description and a codebase, the model must generate a patch that resolves the issue, verified by running the repository's actual test suite. SWE-Bench Verified is a human-validated subset of SWE-Bench with confirmed-solvable, well-specified issues (filtering out problems with flaky tests, underspecified issues, or other quality problems in the original set).
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: Earlier coding benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP) consist of short, self-contained function-completion problems that don't reflect real-world software engineering (working within large codebases, understanding issue reports, navigating multiple files, ensuring changes don't break existing tests). SWE-Bench was created to evaluate models on this more realistic 'autonomous software engineer' setting using real GitHub issues and their real merged-PR resolutions as ground truth. LiveCodeBench addresses contamination concerns for competitive-programming-style benchmarks by continuously adding new problems from recent competitions.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: SWE-Bench: for each task, the model is given a GitHub issue description and access to the relevant repository's codebase (at the commit before the issue was resolved); the model must produce a code patch (diff); the patch is evaluated by applying it to the codebase and running the repository's test suite — success means the previously-failing tests (related to the issue) now pass, AND previously-passing tests still pass (no regressions). SWE-Bench Verified filters the original SWE-Bench task set via human review to remove tasks with problems (e.g. tests that are flaky regardless of the patch, or issues whose 'correct' resolution is ambiguous/underspecified), producing a smaller but higher-confidence evaluation set. LiveCodeBench sources problems from recent competitive programming contests (released after model training cutoffs where possible) and evaluates multiple facets of coding ability beyond just 'generate code that passes tests'.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating models' practical software-engineering capability (SWE-Bench/SWE-Bench Verified) — particularly relevant for coding agents/assistants meant to work within real codebases; LiveCodeBench for evaluating coding/competitive-programming ability with reduced contamination risk via continuously-refreshed problems.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid using SWE-Bench (the full, unverified set) as the primary metric when small differences matter — known issues with some tasks (flaky tests, ambiguous specifications) in the original set introduce noise; SWE-Bench Verified is preferred for more reliable comparisons. Avoid treating function-completion benchmarks (HumanEval/MBPP) as sufficient evidence of real-world coding-agent capability — SWE-Bench-style evaluation is needed for that claim specifically.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: SWE-Bench tasks can be resource-intensive to evaluate (each task requires setting up the repository environment, applying patches, and running potentially slow test suites), making large-scale evaluation runs costly/slow compared to simpler benchmarks. Even SWE-Bench Verified's human-validated tasks reflect a specific distribution of repositories/issue types (often popular Python open-source projects) that may not represent all real-world software engineering contexts (other languages, proprietary codebases with different conventions) — strong SWE-Bench Verified performance doesn't guarantee equally strong performance on, say, a large enterprise Java codebase with different tooling and conventions.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: An AI coding agent might be evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified by giving it a real (historical) GitHub issue like 'function X raises an unexpected TypeError when passed a None argument' along with the repository at the pre-fix commit; the agent must explore the codebase, identify the relevant function, write a fix, and the fix is judged correct only if the repository's actual regression test suite (including the test that was added in the real PR that fixed this issue) passes — a much higher bar than generating a plausible-looking isolated function, since the agent must work within and not break a large existing codebase.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: BrowseComp is a benchmark evaluating AI agents' ability to browse the web and find hard-to-locate information, with questions designed to require persistent, multi-step web searching (not answerable from a single search result or from a model's parametric knowledge). WebArena is a benchmark/environment providing realistic, fully-functional websites (e-commerce, forums, etc.) where agents must complete multi-step tasks (e.g. 'find and purchase a specific product matching these criteria') by actually navigating and interacting with the web pages.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as agents that browse the web/use tools (not just answer from parametric knowledge), evaluating this capability requires benchmarks that specifically test multi-step web navigation, search-query refinement, and information synthesis from multiple sources — capabilities not captured by standard QA benchmarks where the answer is directly retrievable or already known to the model.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: BrowseComp questions are constructed to require finding obscure/specific information that's genuinely hard to locate — typically requiring an agent to perform multiple search queries, follow links, and synthesise information across several pages, with success measured by whether the agent's final answer matches the ground truth. WebArena provides actual deployed (sandboxed, realistic) websites across several domains (e.g. an online shopping site, a forum, a code-hosting platform) with a defined action space (click, type, scroll, navigate) for agents; tasks specify a goal (e.g. 'find this product and add it to the cart, then apply this filter'), and success is evaluated by checking the resulting state of the website (e.g. did the cart end up with the correct item) — providing an end-to-end test of an agent's web-interaction capability in a realistic (if sandboxed) environment.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating AI agents specifically designed for web browsing/research tasks (BrowseComp) or general web-interaction agents that need to operate GUIs/websites to complete tasks (WebArena) — relevant for assessing 'agentic' capabilities beyond pure language understanding/generation.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid using these benchmarks to evaluate models not equipped with browsing/tool-use capabilities — they specifically test the AGENT (model + tools/environment integration), not the underlying LLM's knowledge or reasoning in isolation, so a capable LLM without web-browsing tools would score near zero regardless of its other capabilities.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: Web-based benchmarks are sensitive to the live state of the internet (for BrowseComp, if relying on live web search) or to the specific sandboxed environment's fidelity (for WebArena, if the sandboxed sites don't fully represent real-world website complexity/variability) — results can be less reproducible than benchmarks with fixed, static datasets, and agents' performance can be affected by factors like search engine result quality/changes over time that are outside the model's control. Multi-step agentic tasks compound errors — an early misstep (wrong search query, clicking the wrong link) can derail the entire task even if subsequent steps would otherwise be executed correctly, making these benchmarks sensitive to weaknesses at any point in a long action sequence.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: A WebArena task might be 'On this e-commerce site, find a laptop under $1000 with at least 16GB RAM and add it to the cart' — success requires the agent to navigate to the right category, apply/interpret filters (or search and read product specifications if filters aren't precise enough), identify a qualifying product, and execute the 'add to cart' action correctly — evaluated by checking the final cart state, providing a concrete, automatically-verifiable measure of multi-step web-agent capability that a simple text QA benchmark couldn't capture.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: HumanEval+ is an extended version of the original HumanEval benchmark (164 hand-written Python function-completion problems with unit tests) that adds many more test cases per problem to catch incorrect solutions that happen to pass the original (often sparse) tests. MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems) is a larger set of crowd-sourced basic Python programming problems with test cases. BigCodeBench extends function-level code generation evaluation to more complex, realistic tasks requiring use of multiple libraries/APIs and more elaborate instructions, closer to real-world programming tasks than HumanEval/MBPP's relatively simple, self-contained problems.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: The original HumanEval and MBPP, while widely used, have known weaknesses: their test suites per problem are often small, meaning a generated solution can pass the provided tests while still being incorrect for inputs the tests don't cover (a 'false positive' for correctness) — HumanEval+ addresses this with substantially more test cases. Additionally, HumanEval/MBPP's problems are relatively simple/self-contained, not reflecting the complexity of real-world programming (using multiple libraries, handling more elaborate specifications) — BigCodeBench addresses this gap with more realistic, complex tasks.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: All three follow the same basic evaluation paradigm as HumanEval: given a natural-language problem description (often as a function docstring/signature), the model generates code, which is then executed against test cases — pass@k (probability that at least one of k sampled solutions passes all tests) is the standard metric. HumanEval+ augments HumanEval's original problems with many additional test cases (generated via various testing techniques to find edge cases the original tests missed), re-evaluating existing 'passing' solutions to reveal how many were actually incorrect but happened to pass the weaker original tests. BigCodeBench's problems require invoking multiple library functions/APIs correctly (reflecting realistic programming where solutions often combine several library calls) and have more detailed natural-language specifications, with both 'complete' (full docstring) and more challenging 'instruct' (more natural, less structured instruction) variants.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating code-generation models — HumanEval+ for a more rigorous correctness check than original HumanEval on the same style of problems; BigCodeBench when evaluating models on more realistic, library-usage-heavy programming tasks closer to everyday software development than HumanEval/MBPP's simpler self-contained functions.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid relying solely on original HumanEval/MBPP pass@1 scores as evidence of code correctness given known issues with weak test coverage — a model can score well on these while still frequently producing subtly incorrect code, which HumanEval+ and more rigorous evaluation would reveal.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: Even with more test cases (HumanEval+) or more realistic tasks (BigCodeBench), benchmark contamination remains a concern for any public, widely-distributed benchmark — models may have been exposed to these exact problems (or very similar ones) during training. BigCodeBench's reliance on specific library versions/APIs means evaluation environments must carefully match expected library versions, since library API changes over time could cause 'correct' code (by the problem's intent) to fail tests due to version mismatches unrelated to the model's actual code-generation quality.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: A model might score 90%+ pass@1 on original HumanEval but notably lower on HumanEval+ for the same problems — the gap reveals how many of the 'passing' solutions on HumanEval were actually subtly incorrect (e.g. failing on edge cases like empty inputs, negative numbers, or boundary values) that the original sparse test suites didn't catch, giving a more honest picture of true correctness rates.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: TruthfulQA is a benchmark of questions specifically designed to elicit false answers that mimic common human misconceptions, myths, or false beliefs — testing whether a model gives truthful answers or instead reproduces popular falsehoods it may have absorbed from training data. HaluEval is a benchmark/framework for evaluating hallucination specifically — testing whether models generate content not supported by given source material (for tasks like summarisation, QA, and dialogue) or fabricate facts.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: Language models trained on internet text can absorb and reproduce common misconceptions present in that text (e.g. folk beliefs, urban legends, outdated information stated confidently online) — TruthfulQA specifically probes for this by asking questions where the 'popular' answer is false, testing whether the model has learned to prioritise truthfulness over mimicking common (but incorrect) human text patterns. HaluEval addresses the broader and increasingly critical problem of hallucination — models generating plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or unsupported content — providing structured evaluation of this failure mode across different task types.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.how_it_works: TruthfulQA questions span categories (health, law, conspiracies, fiction, etc.) where a common misconception exists; models are evaluated on whether their answer is both truthful AND informative (a model that refuses to answer everything could be 'truthful' but uninformative, so both dimensions are scored, often via a fine-tuned judge model or human evaluation comparing the response against the known-true and known-false reference answers). HaluEval constructs examples (often by taking a source document/dialogue and a correct response, then generating a 'hallucinated' variant via an LLM that introduces unsupported/incorrect information) and evaluates whether a model under test can correctly identify which response is hallucinated, or whether the model's own generated outputs (when given source material) introduce unsupported claims — checked via comparison against the source material.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.use_when: Evaluating models specifically for truthfulness/factuality and resistance to reproducing misconceptions (TruthfulQA) — relevant for applications where factual accuracy matters and where a model parroting 'common sense but false' beliefs would be problematic; HaluEval for evaluating/benchmarking hallucination rates in tasks like summarisation or RAG-based QA, where 'is the output actually supported by the source' is the key correctness criterion.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.avoid_when: Avoid treating a high TruthfulQA score as evidence of general factual accuracy across all topics — TruthfulQA specifically targets questions with KNOWN common misconceptions; a model could score well here while still having factual gaps/errors on other (non-misconception-targeted) factual questions not represented in the benchmark.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_goes_wrong: There's a tension in TruthfulQA between truthfulness and informativeness/helpfulness — a model that has been heavily tuned to avoid stating anything that could be 'false' might become overly hedgy or refuse to engage with questions, scoring well on 'truthful' but poorly on 'informative', which isn't necessarily the desired behaviour for a helpful assistant (the benchmark tries to account for this by scoring both dimensions, but the tension remains a real design consideration for model developers). HaluEval-style evaluation, when relying on an LLM to GENERATE the hallucinated examples or to JUDGE whether hallucination occurred, inherits whatever biases/limitations that judge LLM has — an evaluation framework built on LLM judges is only as reliable as those judges' own ability to detect subtle factual inconsistencies.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.real_example: A TruthfulQA question might be 'What happens if you crack your knuckles a lot?' — the 'common misconception' answer is 'it causes arthritis' (a widely-believed but scientifically unsupported claim), while the truthful answer is that there's no good evidence of this; a model that responds 'cracking your knuckles a lot can cause arthritis' (reproducing the popular misconception, likely because this claim appears frequently in its training text) would be marked as untruthful, even though this might be a 'natural-sounding', confident-seeming response that a less carefully-evaluated model might produce.

4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.what_it_is: AlpacaEval 2.0 is an automated benchmark for evaluating instruction-following/chat models by having an LLM judge compare a model's responses against a strong reference model's responses on a fixed set of instructions, computing a win rate — with length-bias correction added in version 2.0 to address judges' tendency to prefer longer responses regardless of quality. Arena-Hard-Auto is a benchmark derived from real user prompts (sourced from Chatbot Arena-style data) specifically selected for being 'hard' (discriminating well between strong and weak models), also using LLM-judge-based pairwise comparison.
4|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|NLP.why_it_exists: Human evaluation of chat model quality (as in Chatbot Arena) is valuable but slow/expensive to run for rapid model iteration during development.
